THE MILL. Five storeys high, huge, sooty, and grim, Packed with machinery up to the brim, Stands the mill in its shroud of smoke and steam; Towering aloft, the chimney hard by, Belches its smoke in the murky sky, While dark below rolls the foul inky stream.

'Tis six o'clock; with rousing voice The mill bell calls; and now the noise Of trampling feet, hurrying on from yard and street, Till gathered up like sheep in a pen; A motley crowd of women and men, •The huge mass moves to the time of the engine's beat.. What but awhile was silence and death, Is now alive with the engine's breath, And atl is business, throng, and commotion; . Hark! to the throbbing, buzzing, and knocks, Of scribblers and mules, power-looms, and stocks; A wonderful sight is machinery in motion. 'Tis the engine's strength, with am so stout, Like a giant poised with arms stretched out, Tnat grasp the crank and turn the wheels around; Thus goes merrily on like a hive, • From six in the morn to half-past five, The mill with a roaring and rumbling sound. What a world is the mill! Hopes and fears, Success and failure, with changing years, Are part and parcel of all business life; How many a fight and well sustained. Has merit freight, and pluck obtained, Masters and workmen brethren in the strife. Every breath, each throbbing of the heart, Has in the mill its own counterpart— A living body, with organs, sinews, mind— Functions and motions hard to comprehend— The workman's daily hope, the master's friend, Perchance his enemy, if Fate'', unkind. J. T. Witten, Carlisle.

'Owed Politeness.—Bowing to necessitV. gimantic Death.—A young; lady drowned in tears. en can never expect a blacksmith to give up all his

vices. . Gravity does not indicate wisdom, any mro than ' silenes. nor is a turn for conversation of a cheerful, in- structive character the distinctive mark of fools, what- ever stupid dulness may hint on the subject. A gentleman having brought ma action for an assault, his servant was called as a witness to support it, who. after a few nueetione, observed that he was certain if his /nester "had not a very thick head the blow which defendent gave him would-Ilitre cracked his skull." A story is told of the Essex North Medical Society that is too good to keep. PrevionS to the recent meeting in the city the secretary wrote to one of the members ask- ing. him if he could depend upon him for an eneay which L: had sometime before premises! to give. The doctor replied that be could. He would, read the essay—" Dee volente"—itt the time stated. Upon this the secretary sent a notice to the Press stating that, the subject of Dr. esear would be "1)"o Voleate." DR. JOHNSON'S FORESIGHT.—Mr. Thisbe reminds us of another story of Dr. Johnson, which will not be out of place here. It is an excellent illustration of the keen sagacity and forethought of that great man's mind. One reening Dr. Johnson, looking from his dim Bolt Court window, saw the slovenly lamp-lighter of those days ascending a ladder (just est alnearth has drawn him in the "Rake's Progress "), and fill the little receptacle in the globular lamp with detestable whale-oil. Just as he got down the ladder the dull light wavered out. Skip- ping up the ladder again, the son of Prometheus lifted the cover, thrust the torch he carried into the heated vapour rising from the wick, and instantly the ready farce :imams restored to life. " Ah," said the old seer, "one of these days the streets of London will be lighted by smoke."—Cessell's Old and Nein London. THE ROYAL AC tDEMY Scnoors.—ln its schools the Hovel Academy is carrying, out, according to its lights, a frilly great Work. It has instructed in its time over four thousand students, entirely without fee or exacting payment of any kind, at an expense to itself of nearly a quarter of a million sterling while the increased cost of maintenance averages £6,000 a year, as against £926 at the date of formation. These figures alone, without counting the amount of time and thought freely given by the members, in addition to their private benefac- tions, should convey some idea of the importance and influence of this institution, and sheuld be sufficient to prove that, whatever the shortcomings with which it may be rightly chargeable. they are the result of honest if mistaken views, and certainly in no vrav attributable to want of liberality or lack of zeal. That the schools, even more than the exhibi- tions, are the object of constant solicitude to the Aca- demic body is beyond dispute ; so that with the im- provements which have been plentifully introduced into them of late, and will be continued, if report says true, in tbe future, we may look forward with confidence for the best results which the perfection of the present system can vield.---The Magazine of Art. NATIONAL- CHAR.ACTERISTICS —Tlie French say of other peoples hard things: "Cheating as an American, drunken as a swiss, jealous as a Spaniard, revengeful as a Corsi- can. quarrelsome as a German, proud as a Scotchman, and cold as a Dutchman." Another French saying is, "The Italian is wise in time, the German at the time, the Frenchman after time." The Emperor Maximilian I. said that "the King of France is a king of asses, for he lades his subjects with heavy burdens; the Kine of England is a king of men, for he lays anthem nothing they do not consent to bear; but. the Emperor is a kin,, of princes who do 'nothing but follow their own caprices." A true snying. • one he lind learned by ex- perience. The German Emperor was a snvereien in name, hut without power; he inherited a magnificent title, had splendid pretensions. but was flouted by every prince who pretended to owe him allegiance. To Maxi- milian several such characterisations are attributed. He is reported to have spoken first. of the Englishman as a typical shopkeeper, an identification, which the first Napoleon often had on his lips. Maximilian said, "An English shopkeeper, aJewish usurer, an old min, a Ger- man courtier, an ape, and a man of Basle are the devil's best servants." In Spain, it is said, "The Englishman is a drunkard, the Frenchman a scamp, the Dutchman a butterman and the Spaniard a cavalier ;" and again, "It is best to t'ai horn in Italy, to live in France, and to die in Spain."—Cessen's Magazine. Ammons AN'to READINO.--DT. Johnson himself laid down the law that reading should he done as inclination prompts one. He was in the habit of dipping and skim- ming himself, as he tore over the pages with knife or finger. He resented being asked if he had read a hook through, Raying that he had read it tee "one does read such books." Scott had accumulated his rich and mis- cellaneous stores by casual studies of congenial subjects; it was only when he was beggared and slaving !for his creditors that the author Of " Waverley" and editor of Swift consented to "cram" for his" Life of Buonaparte." 'Therein something pitiful in his rueful praise of the magnificent notions of Constable, who kept crushing the enslaved genius ot the night-lamp under piles of con- temporary treatises and ponderous files of the " Moni- tour." But Southey was perhaps the most melancholy example of the literary voluptuary broken into harness. Be could seldom write except on subjects that pleased him. In the face of disappointments he fondly believed in fame and a future as an English classic. He be- queathed to the more kindly appreciation of posterity the poems that had scarcely cleared the publishing ex- penses; he devoted invaluable time and untold trouble to unpopular histories of the Brazils and abstruse an- notations of Spanish literature; and labouring inde- fatigably all the time to maintain his family, he only managed to make the two ends meet by more paying "pot-boilers" for the periodicals. Leadiog the existence of a hard-working hermit among the Cumberland hills, he was compelled to surround himself with a costly library. Yet for the life of him, unless for special pur- poses when the collar was chafing, he could spare no time to the books in which he could have revelled; andl when the literary Tantalus died worn out, the collection was dispersed which had never been enjoyed.—Black- seee,i's Magazine. A DAY'S Wong.—The amount of work some people get through is simply enormous. Pew people are harder worked than a London physician in active practice. We know a doctor who seldom gets more than four hours' sleep out of the 24. He says thief it is not that be couldn't do with more, but it is as much as he can get. Many busy men are constantly at work of some kind or the other from eight in the morning till past 12 at night. Some of course break down, but others can do tkis year after year, apparently without any detriment to their health. Instances are known of professional men who have not slept for five days together. and who have not been in bed for three weeks at a time. These sound almost like travellers' tales, but they are true, although, of course, they are exceptional cases. It is astonishing what interest and energy will do in enabling a :man to dispense with rest. It has been said that the 24 hours might be advantageously divided into three equal parts, eight hours for sleep,eight for meals,exercise, recreation, Esc., and eight for mental wark. Few men really require naore than eight hours' sleep, but the majority of us have to do considerably more than eight hours' work in the day. It is not so much that a man wishes for the work, as that it is forced upon him. He, perhaps, is the only person who can perform a certain duty, and when, as is often the case, it is a question of life and death, it is almost impossible to refuse. Many people CM neves force themselves to do more than a certain amount of .mental work, they get nervous and headachy, and then it is all over with them. Forced work, as a rule, tells on a man Much more rapidly. than purely _voluntary woraa for in the former case it is usually rossiciated with anxiety. Real overwork gives rise to isoes of memory, a general sense of fatigue, and particu- latly of discomfort it:lout the head, poorness of appetite, lownesa of spirits, and other similar symptoms. It is worry that injures more than real work—care killed the cat. Some people are so happily constituted that they never worry much about anything, while others es in a fever of anxiety on every trivial occasion.— Family Physician. The engraving which we have selected its the illustration of our large sheet Almanac for 1888 is a combination picture possessing alike historical, archaeological, and personal interest. In the first place we have a representation of 'Lathom House, near Ormskirk, as it appeared before and during the sieges in 1644-4E'. the second of which ended in its capture and partial demolition, and there are also portraits of James, Earl of Derby, the lord of the mansion, of the ceuntess of Derby, its heroic de- fender, and the Colonel Alexander Rigby,of Preston, and M.P. for Wigan, who had the direction of the operations of the first siege on the side of Parlia- ment. , Of the old Lathom House there is not, we believe, the smallest piece of wall left standing. Its site is scarcely definable, but is said to have been "be- tween the north-east offices of the present modern house and the kitchen garden." There is, so far as we have heard, no painted picture or drawing of the House as it stood in its ancient strength and glory, extant, and the copy is from an imaginary restoration prepared for Mr. John Roby's "Tradi- tions of Lancashire." But, seeing that we know that the place consisted, first, of a thick embattled outer wall, surrounded by a moat, at intervals of which were nine square towers. thah the principal geta- way we% an imposing arch Way, flanked by bigh towers that there was an inner court, separated from the Outer by a second wall and buildings, and that in the midst st'ood the lofty Eagle Tower, dominating the whole pile, with domestic build- ings, chapel, &c., standing about it, we may accept this attempted restoration on paper as a fair repre- sentation of the general aspect of Lathom House before it fell into vaeldal hands. Camden, who traversed the western parts of England in 161)7, describes Lathom House as "A 'House large and, stately, which, from the time of Henry the Fourth, has been continually enlarging." The first of the famous sieges of Lathom House began. in" March 1643-4, and continued until the middle of May in the same year (1644.) During this siege the Goun- teas of Derby, whose portrait we give, was in com- mand of the beleaguered garrison, and she conducted &successful defence with remarkable determination and spirit. Sortie after sortie was made against the besieging Parliamentarians, who at length re- tired with some precipitation on the approach of the "fiery Rupert," accompanied by Lord Derby and an army of 8,000 or 10,000 Royalists. A few weeks later, however. Rupert, Lord Derby. and.their fellow supporters of the King were in hot retreat from the disastrous field of Marston Moor, and it was nct long before. Lathom House again met with I the unfriendly attentions of the victorious Common- wealth men. On this occasion the animating spirit of the Countess. of Derby was absent, and as the result of a blockade at first carried on laxly, but , afterwards with vigour the stronghold was yielded up by its starving garrison. As to the treatment of the House at the hands of its captors, we have an account in "A. Discohrse upon the War in Lanca- shire." written about that time by a Lancashire Parliamentarian officer. Says this writer, "The House with all the goods within it was to gee , amongst the Souldiers, who pulled the lead off all the Turret; • with all those leaden troughes, like hunt° cisterens, which they salted Beefe, in were all ' pulledisunder and sould. And this was remark- able, that Wiggan men, great Cavillers, much is. the favour of the Earle—A town which he had great confidence in above any other in the county , —these very men were most forward to buy the Leades. and to deface that Honourable House more than any others. It appeared the tyde was turned. I Much of that famous House (like a little towne in itselfe) was pulled down and cast into the Mote that is about it, so that it is nothing in comparison to what it was. It was the glorie of the Conntie. The Earles, Lords thereof, were esteemed by most about them with little lesse respect° than Kings. It I was the wilfulness and headiness of the Countesse. that brought this downefall upon it. When it will I be repaired again is doubtful'. JAMES, SEVENTH RIM, Ot DERET. The portrait in our almanac of James; seventh Earl of Derby. his Countess. and one child, is copied from a tine family picture by Vandyke, which was engraved on steel for the first edition of Baine's "History of Lancashire." There are other portraits of the Earl. An authentic one is photographed as frontispiece to a ChethamSociety's volume, "A dis- course sn the Warr in Lancashire," edited by Mr. Beamont, of Orford Hall, Warrington. The seventh Earl of Derby was born on the 31st January,l6o6-7. In early manhood, whilst abroad at the Hague, to perfect his education, he met with the 'lady who afterwards became his wife, and whom he married •in England in the year 1626. This lady was Charlotte, daughter of Claude de Tremouille, and of her we give a further notice below. In 1623 the Earl was elected one of the Knights of the Bath at the coronation of Charles 1., and on the 18th February, 1627, was summoned to Parliament as Baron Strange, under the impression that such a barony was enjoyed by his father; this being a mis- take, the summons was tantamount to the creation of a new peerage. Lord Strange in 1630 was ap- pointed Lord-Lieutenant of the counties of Lancas- ter, Chester, and Flint. About this time he retired, somewhat suddenly and strangely, from court and from public life. But when the war between the King and the Parliament became inevitable, in 1642, he came forth from his seclusion, and placed his sword at the service of King Charles. He mustered his own retainers and tenants, and all other forces he could raise. in support of the King's interest in Lancashire. Yet he was at first distrusted by Charles, whose mind had been prejudicM against. him, and he was actually at this juncture deprived ,of the Lieutenancy of Cheshire and North Wales, and had Lord Rivers joined with him in that of Lancashire. In June, 1642, he attended the County Meeting on Preston Moor, called by the High Sheriff, and did all that in him lay to cause Lanca- shire to declare for the King. In this he was not successful. The county was divided in that conflict. The strong Puritan party in East Lancashire was as resolutely opposed to the King's pretension to rule without a Parliament as the Hirsh hurch, and Roman Catholic sections in West Lancashire were ardent in their espousal of Charles the First's cause and policy. The war commeribed, and its first action in this county was the attack on Manchester, by the Royalist forces, commanded by Lord Strange, in September, 1642. The Manchester Parliamentarians repulsed the enemy, and the Royalists departed. William, sixth Earl, died at this time, and his son succeeded him as seventh Earl of Derby. He com- menced to fortify Lathom House in realness for I contingencies. On the 17th March. 1642-3. the: Royalists, under the leadership of the Earl and Lord Molineux, marched from Lathom, and did not halt until Lancaster was reached, which. was held by a small garrison of Roundheads. Tile, town was as- saulted, and after one repulse \YIN carried. On the '2oth of March the Earl of Derby and his fighting- men were back at Preston, which, after a desperate struggle, was taken from the Parliamentarians. The slaughter was great on both sides. Towards the end of March the King ordered Lord Molineux to till up his regiment from Lord Derby's bands and to march

-7 -,-- v • southwards to Oxford. Lord Derby's protest was . .

unavailing, and he could only retire- wah the rem- nant of his forces from Chorley, where they were posted, to Lathom House. Thus shabbily and cruelly was the Edl of Derby treated by Charles tfilliAritst, for whom he was risking all—life, forruhe, and estates. Still he was resolved to continue _the

struggle-for the ascendancy in Lancashire; and he led. a .hastily-collected force, mo.lerately largetin numbers, but undisciplined, up the Ribble -valley, in April, 1643; occupying 131ackburn with a detach- ment, and advancing to Whalley, where he was sur- prised and defeated by Colonel Shuttleworth and his Parliamentarian Militia. Afterwards the Earl held the Isle of Man on behalf of .the King, and later • on, as .. stated above, took.part in the battle of Marston Moor, at which the Royalists were completely overthrown by Cromwell, Leslie, and Fairfax. He then returned to the Isle Of. Man, which he held against-the Par- lianient for seven years, and eve ri after Charles the First was beheaded and the monarchy for the tiMe being abolished. In 1651, the Earl reappeared in Lancashire with 300 gentlemen to join Charles the Second in his attempt to iecover the throne. The .Earl was deputed to raise Lancashire in the royal cause; but • his followers were defeated with .great loss by Colonel Lilburne at the battle of WiAan- lane. He himself was severely wounded, but, after lying in concealment for some time, escaped and pined ,the King before the battle of rcester. After that disastrous defeat he was miptiOl by the Roundheads, tried at Chester, and nom-We'd of hav- ing "traitorously borne arms for Charles Stuart against the Parliament" Szc. At the age of 45 • years, he was executed on the 15th Octolior 1651, at Bolton, the scene os a ruthless Slaughter of Parliamentarians, alleged, though without proof, to have taken place by command of the Earl. "In I person," writes one of his biographers, "lames, Earl of Derby, was rather below the common size, but of an athletic make; his countenance was one of those old Stanley faces which we love to look upon as they darken in their frames, and to associ- ate with deeds of chivalry. The .most remarkable feature, and in this he differs from the family, is the smallness of his forehead, which. is exaggerated by the straight combing of his lank brown hair; his eyes are large, and of a clear brown, not sparkling, but full of grave and thoughtful expression,; his nose is large, but not in the least degree aquiline, and the latest paintings represent his cheeks inn and ruddy, without marks of age. He wore mus- tachios, but had not the tuft on the chin usual in King Charles's days." THE COUNTESS OF DEBBY,

whose portrait we give, was not an Englishwoman, being the daughter of Claude de la Tremouille. Duke de Tremouille and Thomas, Prince of raiment and peer of France, by Charlotte his wife, daughter of William, the first Prince of Orange and Charlotte de Bourbon, of the Royal house et France. Thus her grandmother was 8, Royal prince.s of the liOuse of Bourbon the most distinguished royal family in Europe in that age; whilst her mother was a mem-- ber of the reigning family of Holland. For abme time after her marriage, she was doubtless a Cen- tral figure at the English court.' but -after a while the Earl, her husband, renounced court life and be- took himself to a country life, to his seats of Knowsley and Ludlow. It is related that "on the 18th of September, 1630, the Dowager Duchess of of Tretnouille, on her road to visit her daughter in Lancashire, was received near Chester by a greater number of knights, esquires, and gentlemen than ever had been assembled together in that part of the country: the Corporation, Gentlemen of Artillery, and 600 horsemen meeting her at Boole Heath, they rode in great state to the Penner, where a magni- ficent banquet was prepared. Tradition is not silent in the subject Of this Lady's reception in Lancas- hire; and there were, eatly in this century, ancient persons at Warrington who could recite verses in which the beauty" and prin?ely carriage of the young Lady Strange (our heroine), and the digni- fied presence of her mother, as they rode together over the bridge near that town, were fully set forth; nor was the gallant bearing of the Esquires of both counties, accompanying them on this occasion, for- gotten." During the war between King and Parlia- ment, as we have seen, the Countess of -Derby made a heroic defence of the family seat 3f Lathom on behalf of the. King, and subsequently she shared in the vicissitudes of her husband's life. After the execution of the Earl, she was allowed £2OO a year by Parliament, out of the revenues" of the Isle of Man, and Rushen Castle was appointed as "the place of her captivity." There she remained for nine , years until the return of Charles the Second, when she was restored to liberty. It is saiq that, through her misfortunes and captivity, she had become sour , and melancholy. "She was no longer the lady of the deceased Earl's love; her religion had grown , severe and morose; her feelings of regard for him ; that was no more had transformed themselves into L a settled purpose of avenging his death, and the pangs of a broken heart were, for a time, deadened by the presence of feelings that were neither' natu- ral to her sex, nor consistent with her former life." Tee Countess died at ,Knowsley, March 22nd, 1G133, 'and was buried at Ormskirk. COLONEL ALEXANDER. RIGBY,

whose portrait also appearp on our Almanac, was the eldest son of Alexander Rigby, of Wigan, gen- tleman. He was born at Wigan, in 1594, and en- tered the profession of the law in 1610. Later in life lie was enrolled as a burgess of Preston, but nevertheless he was elected to represent his native town of Wigan in 1640. In 1643 we -find him in command of forces he had raised in West Lancashire to fight far Parliament. Having captured Thurland Castle, in Lunesdale, Colonel Rigby was selected along with "Mr. Ashton, of Middletdn, and Mr. Moore, of Banckliall," other tw) "parliament colonels" to command the forces of the county in the siege of Lathom House. At the terminati nof this unsuccessful siege, Colonel Rigby withdrew his forces to Bolton, and there he stistained the as- sault of the overwhelming numbersof Prince Rupert and the Earl of Derby. The town was captured and many hundreds of his men were slain,and h e on) yeSca- ped himself by plunging on horseback amongst the Royalist soldier-, who mistook him for one of their own generals; until "he saw a fit time for him he took it, and with one man went his way towards Yorkshire." On Ist June, 1649, Vl° Housb ot Com- mons approved the appointment of Alexander Ri,gby Esq., as one ot the Barons of the Court: of Ex- chequer, but, not enjoying this honour long, he died at London on the 18th August, 1650. Having lain in state at Ely Place, Holborn, the remains were conveyed into Lancashire and buried in Pres-, ton Parish Church.

' CHAPTER- Xlll.—Continued. Titß LINK IS FOUND. Anne went tnat nay in. an Opposite nireerion,io TavipAeck. She folik an hour mid a half's journe;r to Exeter:to see Martin for the first time in erison.! Ile was..alreadY„ looking •very wan and 1;0110\v•eved. Prison life was almost 'maddening to a man et his proud and sensitive nature, his love of ont-doerilife, and the wild freedom of the moors. Ile was Ir,:u h' newly-caged bird r sometimes he felt ready to dash his brains out against the well. When he cold no longer forget his misery in reading, he spent hours in gazing at the morsel of sky lie conld sae from the little window of his cell. But he made no complaint, he was only -very silent, he was , disin- • dined to speak to anyone evenwhen he had the chance in his almost solitary confinement; so that the authorities Of the prikon,like a good many people!out- side, called Martin Derrick sullen and morose. , Stronger than-ever now was the always dominant expression of his face—stern and silent endurance of suffering < With bent brows and clenched teeth, he "set his face like a flint "to the outer world. But as Anne • entered, his compressed lips relaxed into a stuile, his eyes brightened, and he greeted her cheerfully. "i,f course," he said, in answer to her anxious questioning, "there's no denying it; a•man who has been used to be out of doors the greater . part of the day, and to tramp miles over the moors, does feel the confinement to one little room, and having nothing but a walled yard to walk in for an hour or. two, to be a pretty heavy punishment. But there's one thing to be said, I have plenty of leisure time for reading; and if ever I do come out of prison again, I shall come out a better-read man than I went in." It was well for Anne that she had an abundance of prosaic household work to do at Row-tor Farm_, where the solitude, whenever she had time to think about it, seemed toherquiteghastly. The lonely meals which she hurried through, Martin's vacant chair, the silence in the parlour during the long evenings, mu- broken by his voice,the blank everywhere ,in her daily life, with the dark and awlful thaught ever haunting the background, that perhaps he' Might never come back. "I think I should have gone mad," Anne said afterwards, "if I had not had plenty of things to do— things that had to be done if the house and the farm were to be kept together—for Martin's own sake." So it was that on that Saturday, Anne, careful house-wife as she was, decided that the whole lower floor of the farmhouse must be swept and-scrubbed. The entrance ball, the parlour, even Martin's smok- ing-room had been crowded with people on the day of the coroner's inquest. There was dust on the car- pets, prints of muddy feet on the flag-stones. Mrs. Lawson was as good as her word; she helped Mrs. Richards with the harder part of the work, and Anne herself did the rest. It so happened that about 11 o'clock that morn- ing Anne was in Martin's smoking room.. With careful, hiving hands, and eyes full of sadness, she was dusting and arranging his books andpapers,while 'Mrs. Lawson was down on her knees, rubbing the floor,_ which was of black oak, and had a :square of rather shabby red druggist in the centre. Anne had just been thinking how strange it seemed than Dick. Lawson's mother should be here, at Row-tor . Farm, working hard for Martin,when she was startled by a sudden exclamation— "Law, Miss Derrick, look here what I've found " Anne looked round. Mrs. Lawson kneeling on the floor in a corner of the MOM, held in her out-stretched hand, a morsel of something that shone like gold, surrounding something else which sparkled like a 'clew-drop. Anne started back, her ers wide open With wonder almost terror. " What is it? How did that come here ? " she said, half under her breath. Then she came forward, and eagerly, and yet, with a shudder, she took it, a ghastly treasure-trove, from Mrs. Lawson's band. ' It was part of a sleeve-link, such as men wear in their shirt-cuffs. There was a sparkling jewel— either A real diamond or a valuable bit of paste—in the centre, set in plain, massive, dead gold, and from It depended a tiny broken chain. Anne looked at it with horror, and yet with a wild thrill of hope. "Mrs. Lawson," she said, tn a quiet tone of conviction, "this belongs to the man, whoever he was,, who murdered my sister.,' Mrs. Lawson scrambled to her feet in great ex- e;tsment, "My dear life,, whatever makes you say that ? " •!I can't prove it, of course," replied Anne; "I have got to remember what ,a lot of people there have been about the house this last week. But let me see' —she pondered--" nobody came into this room at all' the day of the inquest, except the jurymen, when they were shut up to consider the verdict. Yes, there was Mr. Prior and Watkins that night. But there was not one of them would wear such a flashy sort of thing as this--farmers, small shopkeepers, and such like, and Mr. Prior least of all, such a plain, homely Sort ot a man as he is. Mrs. Lawson," and then Anne raised her head with a bright flash in her eyes, "this little thing that I bold in my hand. may save my brother's Fife, and we'll never forget that it was you who found it." "And there's another thing,' thought Anne,by-and- by when her work downstairs being finished, she went to her bedloom to lock up the sleeve-link in a ' box, and to think over all the bearings of the dis- covery which had been made. "There's another thing. I believe this clears James Stambridge. Haven't I heard poor Susan complain that he was so dowdy in his dross, and hadn't even a watch chain till she gave him one the other day. And if it's a real diamond, as I believe it' is, it must be worth a good bit of money, and quite out of the question to belong to Mr. Prior, or any of the neighbours." Everything seemed to point to the existence of an unknown, shadowy, yet terribly real third person as an actor in the tragedy of Susan's death. The murderer was neither Susan's brother Martin Derrick as the world said, nor Susan's lower, James Stambridge, as Anne had been inclined to fancy. " What do we really know about Susan?" thought Anne. "What do we know of her friends and her enemies, and all the secrets she may hairs had to keep, in the eight years' that she was away from home? Anne had not yet nerved herself to the painful task of looking through Susan's possessions; it seemed like a wrong to the dead woman, who was so much of a stranger in the house. But now the urgent necessity of trying to learn'a little more about Susan's past forced itself upon Anne's mind. Everything which once belonged to ,qusan must be i ransacked, n the hope of discovering a clue to her murderer. , Anne went upstairs to the little bedroom which had' been her sister's. Eagerly and yet with a certain shrinking, as if she were outraging the dead; she first opened a rosewood desk, inlaid with mother of pearl, which was on the top of an old-fashioned chest of drawers. It was unlocked, and it was nearly empty. Inside there was a black-edged envelope; containing memorial cards of the Derrickslather and ' mother; there was a much tarnished silver pencil-case; there was a faded daguerreotype in a gilt frame—a family group, Susan herself as a little child, Anne and Martin, boy and girl, all in prim attitudes and obsolete costumes. There were two small pencil , drawings of an ancient boarding-school type of art; and other relies which Susan little valued, but which- she had not liked to destroy. And amongst them there was something of more modern date—a letter written only three months ago. It was from Miss Evelyn ,the daughter of the deceased lady to whom Susan had been maid for the last seven years; it spoke 'of Susan in the kindest terms, and was, in fact, an ex-: cellent testimonial to her character. These were the sole contents of the desk, which was of the sim- plest construction, and contained no secret drawer, as Anne convinced herself. Next she turned to the dressing-table, where stood a rather handsome box made of olive wood. This was locked, but Anne found the key in a drawer of the quaint shield-shaped looking-glass. Within the box, reposing on dark-blue velvet, was a goodly array of brooches, bangles, and ear-rings. But there was nothing to interest Anne, though she carefully looked through Susan's treasures, with a wild fancy that amongst them she should find the other half of the broken sleeve link. • Anne opened one after another of the drawers in the chest and turned their contents on to the bed. It was a sorrowful sight to see all the new gowns and linen, the trousseau which the poor girl had pre- pared for her wedding. But amongst all Susan's possessions nothing threw any new light on her past history, and Anne carefully put away everything i again n its place, sand left the room With an over- whelming sense of disappointment and discourage- ment.

• CHAVTER XIV.

THE DIAMOND. The following Monday Anne Derrick went to Tavistock, trusting that in her deep mourning, with a thick crape veil- over her face, she might -escape recognition in the streets. With the precious sleeve- link in her purse, she presented herself at the office of tha lawyer Martin had employed—Mr. John Harrison. She had to wait a long time in his outer office, while he was engaged with another Client in hi,s sanctum. No one has ever undertaken any strenuous and important work who has not had the wear and tear of it more than doubled by these unavoidable sorts of trials to patience. At last the client—a downcast, careworn-looking farmer, trying to find some weapon to light a tyrannical land- lord—came forth; and Anne was shewn into Mr. Harrison's private room. He was a grizzled, dry-looking elderly man, who placed a chair by the fire for Anne with some politeness—hut she felt instinctively that she was un- welcome, and that there was little help or comfort for

her her. , "I want to say a few words to you about my brother, Mr. Harrison,' she began, struggling. with her feeling of discouragement. "We shall do the very best we can for him, Miss' Derrick; just as we did the last time." (Oh how those dreadful words, "the last time," kept on coming to every one's lips, thought Anne.) "But you must be aware that the circumstances are very different," and the lawyer knit his brows and compressed his lips with a gloomy air. "Of course they are, quite different. Last time he—he did it," said Anne in a low voice. "We are placed at a disadvantage when a cilent will not confide a little more in us than your brother

has done." "My brother has told you and everybody else everything he has to tell," said Anne proudly, her cheeks flushing. "Well, so you think, no doubt," replied Mr. Har- rison, slowly ; and then he rested his elbows on the arms of his chair, joined the tips of his fingers to- gether, and gazed abstractedly out of the opposite window. "Mr. Harrison," cried Anne, with a flash in her eyes, "there is plenty more to be found out, though not about my brother, and if it were to cost me my life, to say nothing of every penny I have in the world, I'll find the man who murdered my sister Susan." The lawyer gave a slight shrug of the shoulders. "I should strongly advise you, as a friend, Miss Derrick, not to meddle with the matter. It will bring you only pain and disappointment, depend upon it." Anne rose, bitterly indignant, but holding a strong control over herself. 'Then I'll wish you good morning, Mr. Harrison, with many apologies for having taken up your time to no purpose." • ' Mr. Harrison, as he rose to. open the door for her, suddenly awoke to the fact that Anne was very hand- some, if she was not very young; and he said in a much more kindly tone, "I assure you, you have my deepest sympathy,Miss Derrick (yes, she is really a line wonian), and we will do . the very best in our power for your brother (how did that morose fellow, with the d67il orf a temper he is supposed to own, come to have such a devoted sister ?)," and then, without a word of reply,Anne left the office and went out into the street, with the diamond sleeve-link safe in her pocket, and her secret untold. No, she would not tell this coldblooded lawyer who believed Martin to be a murderer, she would not tell him of the discovery she had made, until, alone and unaided,she had done her utmost to find the diamond's owner. "I may be able to set a trap for him which he will walk into, while he would be on his guard against the lawyers or the police." Her next step was to enter a jeweller's shop in the chief street of Tavistock. Will you kindly tell me if this isa real diamond?" she said to the master of the shop, who was quite a stranger to her. The jeweller took the diamond from her, and re- tired into an inner room. Presently he returned, with a look of increased interest and respect. "Yes, it is a diamond of the first water." " "And worth a good deal of money, I suppose?" " Well,it depends upon what you call a good deal," was the cautious reply. "Are you wishing to part with it," "No," answered Anne; "it does not belong to me. I wanted only to know' its value." "Well, at a rough guess, I should say from eighteen to twenty pounds. "Thank you very much," said Anne, and he hurried out of the shop. From thence she went to the Post-office, where she bought some stamps and postal orders. After that she went home. It was now, when Anne returned to Row-Tor Farm, that she became conscious how her nerves had been shaken by'! all she had suffered. She could not cuter her own doors without shuddering at the remembrance of the unknown man—the murderer— whom\ she had touched in the darkness. And tbe dreadful sight she had beheld when she went into the parlour, would, she thought, haunt her until the (lay of her own death. But this evening she had work to do which kept her thoughts employed. She _wrote half a dozen copies of the following

NVITas • • "Found, a valuable diamond. ;The owner can have it by sending an exact description of the setting, to Mrs. Lawson, Post-office, Tavistock." Anne had easily gained the widow's leave to use her name. "There isn't a thing you can ask of me that I wouldn't do to help you in your trouble, Miss Derrick," said she. Anne despatched the advertisement and a postal order to each of the local papers; she even sent it to the Times and the Daily Teltgraph. It was but a forlorn hope, she know; • the owner of the diamond uld probablyfar rather lose it than run the slightest riAt °flailing into a trap set by the police. ' These was nothing more to be done but to wait with patience for a day or two. Then Mrs. Lawson'. went to Tavistock, and returned with a letter, which she gave to Anne in triamph. "It's the only one that's come, Miss Derrick, but it may be: all you want." Anne tore open the letter with a wildly beating heart. She read it through ; then she handed it to Mrs. Lawson, whom she knew could be trusted with a secret. The letter was written in a lady-like hand, and ran as follows: " The writer is anxious to know if a diamond I which she believes has been lost by a friend of hers, is the same as the one which has been found by Mrs. Lawson. Would Mrs. Lawson be good enough to meet the writer at six o'clock to-morrow evening by The river-side under the old abl.ev walls at Tavistock; when a full description of the missing . diamond shall be given. The writer is a young lady, she Will wear a brown- ulster and felt hat." That was all. There was not the slightest clue to the writer, but the Plymouth post-mark on the envelope. Anne pondered for some time over this mysterious letter. "I am not at all sure," thought she, "that this is not a trap set for me. The place is not lonely in the day-time certainly, and Six o'clock is not late. But it will be quite dark by that time, and—the Tavy runs close by. For. all I can tell the young lady' may be a man in woman's clothes, who knows no more about the owner of the diamond than I do, but who answers my advertisement by trying to rob TM I'll go; run any risk for the chance of find- ing out something about the murderer. I'll go, but I'll leave the diamond at home." However, she was equally determined to do all she could to protect herself. She- felt that her life was especially valuable just now to Martin. Had that fatal revolver of her brother's been still at Row Tor Farm, she would have carried it with her, for she was quite at home with firearms, but the polio hail it in their possession. She took Richards with her . to Tavistock, and precisely as the church clock struck six they went together to the bridge which spans the river Tavyl4 the entrance of the town, a stone's threw from the Abbey and the noble, modem town hall. • "Richards," she said.to the old man, who would have been ready- to follow Martin through fire an, water, "I am going to meet some woman close here—a stranger to me, who may possibly tell in, something which will throw a little light upon th way in Which my sister met her death. But I inus speak to her alone. Will you wait on the bridge her, whilst I go a little way along the path by the river If you hear me call out to you, come to me as ouicL as you can." - "You b'aint running into any danger, be you, Miss ? "asked Richards, uneasily. "That remains to be seen," said Anne. She turned away from the old man, who stood sentinel where she had posted him, leaning over the parapet of time bridge,.\ straining his eves and ears to find out what was going to happen in the darkness a few yards away 1/
(To be continued)

div.p: BIG NUGGETS OF GOLD.

The luckiest "find" ever made in California Was made by a man named Finney, who "turned up" a solid lump of gold near Downieville. in 1866, that weighed five thou- sand ounces, worth 18-00 dols, per ounce; which would make the nugget worth £lB,OOO. This was the largest nugget of pure gold ever discovered. Heretofore the Australian nugget found in the Ballarat gold fields has been considered the largest. Itwas valued at £15,000. This man Finney, or "Old Virginia," as he was called, went to Washoe, California, and there he made the great silver discoveries, wheye the " Comstock " lode was located, and where Virginia City, which was named after him stands. He died in great poverty. Ho was cele- brat:ed for his wonderful head of hair, which was of a rich, dark brown in colour, full of golden tints, and which fell in heavy curls over his stalwart shoulders. He was 'very proud of his head covertng and always carried in his " outfit " a brush, comb, and small hand mirror, and whenever he made his " camp," while prospecting, would comb and dress his hair with great care. , When misfortune overtook him and he continued "playing in bad luck "—as he termed it—he began to neglect his hair, and it became frowsy, began to turn gray, and fall out, so that a few years before he died he was nearly bald, and his few remaining hairs were quite white. Had he added to his " outfit " Mrs. S. A. Allen's World's Hair Restorer, he might have retained his hair as long as he lived, for it never fails to strengthen and invigorate the hair, restore its colour, and render it soft, glossy and strong. It can be found at any chemist's or perfumer's in the world. It is the.best and most agreeable hair dress- ing known. Try it. •

FRANCE.—ASSASSINATION •PLOT:M. FERRY SHOTA.T.2IIIE NEViLMINISTRY: UNPROMISING PROSPECT. Pawns, SATURDAY EVENINCL--A determined attempt upon the life of M. Jul e% Ferry was made, this after- noon. in the precincts of the Chamber of Deputies. While the House was sitting, a man presented himself in the vestibule, to 'which the public are admitted. imme- diately preceding the Salle .des Pas Perdue. and told the official on duty that he wished to see M. Jules Ferry and X. Goblet. 'The message was duly delivered to the two deputies, and in a short time M. Ferry appeared. lie had scarcely entered the vestibule when the man who had asked to see him advanced, and, aim- ' ing a revolver point-blank at him, fired three times. Some of those present rushed forward to support M. Ferry. who was seen to be staggering from the effects of the shots, while others seized the would- be assassin, who would have fared badly at their hands if the officials had not vigorously intervened to rescue him- Meanwhile M. Ferry was assisted by his friends to the Infirmary in the Petals Bourbon. where his wounds were treated by Doctors Trelat and Raynal. In reply to the anxious inquiries made on Al sides. M. Ferry said, "It is nothing." The medical examination showed that M. Ferry had had a marvellous escape. One of the three bullets fired seemed to have missed its aim altogether, as no trace of it could be found. The course 'of the other two had been so stopped by the clothes that( 'they had only produced contused sores, without penes' trating the skim One had struck the chest and the other 'the right side, near to the lowest ribs. After the wounds 'had been dressed M. Ferry was able to walk home, with the aid of some friends, after receiving numerous ex'i pressions of sympathy from his colleagues in the 'Chamber. During this time the prisoner was 'being inter- legated and searched. He declared that he belonged -to aband of twenty persons who had resolved to act as he had done- A paper found on him indicated that his name had yesterday been drawn by lot, and that he teas therefore told off to go to-day to the Chatriber -"to execute summary justice." Tuns, Moretisr Nu:ram—The attempt on M. Terry will have political consequences. It has enlisted public -sympathy in M. Ferry's behalf. He has thus become -once more possible as a ruler. which was not the case a week ago.; One paper remarks with perfect truth that -if Aubertin had shot at him on the 2nd of• December. he and not M. Carnet Would have been by this time the occupier of the Elysee. M. Athalin, the •examinine .magistrate, has spent several hours to-day in ques- •tioning Aubertin, and hearing the declarations of numerous witnesses relative to the crime. M. Athalin is convinced that Aubertin 'must be -regarded as perfectly responsible for his acts, but- he is inquiring whether there was any particular , cause for Aubertin's state of excitement on the day of tbe crime. The sealed packet deposited by the prisoner 'with Madame Hervien was opened to-day by the police -commissary. It was found to contain the prisoner's will, bequeathing all his fortune, which, by-the-by, is 'only 65 centimes, to his partner, Madame Grainger. In this document Aubertin wrote--" I make my will be- cause probably I shall make the long journey -when I have accomplished is great act of justice—that is to say when"l have killed Ferry." Besides the will the packet also contained five long letters, all addressed to M. 'Ferry. Paws, MONDAY Arrernsoors.—M. Floquet appearing un- willing to undertake the responsibility of GOVernmAnt- rnaking,President Ca mot has again urged upon M. Tirard 'his request that that. gentleman woeld form a Ministry. PARIS, MONDAY NIGHT.—M. Cslllol has signed decrees for the following appointments :—M. Tirard, Premier and Finance Minister:M. Fleurens, Minister for Foreign Affairs; General Logerot, Minister of War; M. Fallieres, Minister of Justice: M. Sa.rrien, Minister of interior; M. 'Faye, Minister of Public Instruct-ion; M. Demahv, 'Minister of Marine: M. Loubet, Minister of Fut& Works; M. Dautresme. Minister of Commerce.; M. Viette, Minister of Agriculture. In to-day's sitting of the Chamber of Deputies. M. Delisse brought forward' a pro- posal for increasing the import duties on flour, and asked-that it should be referred to the Customs Commit- tee, which was approved, by the House. The Chamber also took into consideration and voted urgency for a pro- posal to raise the Customs duties on Italian products. 'MM. Timrd, Fallieres, • Faye, De Mahy, Loubet, and Dalltre.sme belong ' to the Union ,of the Left; and M.M. Sarrien and Viette to a rather more advanced group; while M. Flourens •General Logirot have no seats in Parliament. , MESSAGE FROM. PRESIDENT CARNOT, ' 'PARIS, TUESDAY APriaxoore.—At today's meeting of -the Chamber, the new Premier, M. Tirard, read a mes- -sage from the President of the Republic. M. Carnot -says-the first task which he has before him is to -bring about a spirit of concord and union amongst the various -sections of•the Republican party. He then proceeds to .enumerate certain reforms, the realisation of which will meassure the country and inaugurate a period of lasting, -peaceftil, and fruitful activity. The Chamber will thus give to Europe a most precious Tiedge of -the ardent desire of Tmnea to assist in the consolidation of general peace. M. Carnet appeals to the pritriotism of the Chamber -to support this policy of progress, appease- ment, and concord, so that France may be enable to pre- parei herself n peace to celebrate worthily the cen- tenary of "1789. The Presidential Message •*sras coldly Teceived. . PANIC ON STEAMER.—SAD LOSS OF LIFE. - -

VIMNA, MONDAVNIGHT.IIA Smyrna telegrrren received here to-day contains ch tails of a lamentable accident on board the Asia Minor Company's steamer Beßona. The -vessel, which had four hundred passengers, mostly Greeks, on board, was not very long out from Salonica, :and was near the island of Imbros, in the Archipelago, when a dreadful panic arose in consequence of an alarm of fire. The alarm was a false one, but before the fact 'could be brought home to the terrified passengers a general panic seized upon them, ands' rush was made for the boats. Before the captain and crew could inter- fere the struggling and terror-stricken crowd had scrambled into the boats and begun to lower them. In doing so one of the boats overturned, precipitating, its occupants. 47 in number, into the sea. To mall matters worse, a strong gale was blowing at the time and all at- tempts to rescue-the helpless victims in the water seem to have failed, the efforts of the crew having apparently 'been impeded bythe terror-stricken mob on board. The' whole of those who were in the capsized boat 'wore con- sequently drowned, while several persons were crushed to death in the struggle that took place for the boats. Eventually, by threats and persuasion, the officers of the steamer succeeded in-restoring calm among the terrified Tome sem

- • FREE TRADE IN SPAIN. MADRTD, MONDAY.—The Minister of Finance in the Senate, and Senor Sagasta in the Cengress,have declared that the Government would not assent to the creation of any tax on foreign cereals, flour, or cattle, as Spain in most years did not produce enough for home consump- tion. The proposals of Senor Canovas for stopping the progressive reduction of import duties and for termin- ating all treaties of commerce as soon as possible were likewise rejected by the Government in the Congress on the ground that official statistics showed how much Spain had gained by the reduction of tariffs and through the medium of treaties of commerce. The GoVernment intended to seek remedies for agricultural and industrial tdepression not in a Protectionist reaction; but in un cx- tensive reform of the system of taxation. THE FIGHTING IN THE SOUDAN. CAIRO, WEDNESDAY NIORT.— News has been received confirming the report of the attack on Suakim. Osman Digna has not reacked Tokar. The Shatu fort was at- tacked, but the enemy vr-as beaten off by the Egyptian cavalry and suffered heavily.

The Princess afterwards visited several public institutions, and re- turned to London in the evening:. • rot all kinds of doniestso sewing, Bagley and Wright s cotton Is the best. —A ,fct. ALLEGED MURDER OF A 13ROTIIER-IN-LAW.—At Whit- church, on Wednesday, Elijah Bowers Forrester, farmer, 4 was committed for trial on the charge of murdering his brother-in-law, Wm Powell. The most important fresh evidence given was that of a man named Newbrook, who said that about two months before Powell was I killed the prisoner told him he had bought a, double- barrelled gun to shoot that enemy of his—meaning the deceased. It VMS disclosed in evidence .that the gun was fired twice, and this is one of the Most important facts in the ca.se. THE DYNAMITE:I9. Thomas Gall= and Michael Harkins were again before Sir James Ingham at Bowl street, on Monday, on the charge of feloniously conspir- ing to-cause explosions, to the danger of life And loss of property. Several Witnesses having been called, Colonel Majendie, chief Inspector of Explosives, and Dr. Dupre gave evidence to the effect that a substance that had been handed to them by the police was dynamite of American Manufacture. Sir James Ingham expressed the opinion that there was a prima fame cam to go be- fore a jury, but formally remanded the prisoners for a week. Y0.1.11.1U5. Lardl,Bartington left town on Monday morning fot Hardwicke Hall, his country seat, where he will remain several days. Lord Randolph Churchill arrived at Hard- wicke Hall, Derbyshire, on Monday evening, on a. visit to Lord Hartington, who is entertaining a distinguished party. Mr. Balfour' Chief 'Secretary. for Ireland. was for- mally installed Rector of St Andrew's University on Saturday. In the course of his address be criticised the recent recommendation of Mr. Frederick Harrison, who had condemned general desultory reading. He thought Mr. Harrison had not adhered to that principle himself. and wag more in favour of Dr. Johnsen's practice to read almost anything that came in his way. The Central sews says a West Southwark elector, who wrote to Mr. Goschen, suggesting that lie should make his position clear on the question of Protection, received the following reply am directed by the Chancellor of the Exchequer to acknowledge your letter of December 3rd. In answer to it he begs to refer you to his speechat the Liberal Unionist banquet on Thursday last, in which he expressed. his conviction that there was no danger of the adoption by the Government of any fiscal principle wkich would threaten the alliance of the Liberal Unionist and Conservative parties.—l am, sir. yours faithfully, A. Muzfirn.”

At a meeting addressed by Mr. Stangeld, at Dunoon, on Monday, the following lett:a from Mr. Gladstone was read:—" If you have my friend Mr. Stansfeld to address you on Monday, I feel sure your meeting one require neither information nor stinsulns from we. or do the people of Scotland generally, or of Argyieshire in par- ticular, need much aid in order to perceive what shock- ing and painful discord is now created in the name of Union, as once the worst crimes were committed in the name of Liberty; or how sadly the state of Ireland had grown worse since the present Government came into office. The following telegram was received at the meeting from Lord Rosebery ; "1 sun sorry I received your letter too late to write. I wish all snocees to your meeting, and I am glad you have secured the inspiring assistance of Mr. Stansfeld."

In reply to Mr. Bradlaugh's application to Lord Salis- bury that his lordship as Prime Minister should signify his consent to a Select Committee in the terms of Mr. Bradlaugh's letter published on December 3, the follow- ing communication has been received :-441Ffatfield House, Hatfield, December 10, 1887.—Sirr—I am directed by the Marquis of Salisbury to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 7th inst. In reply lam to say that in re- spect to a purely personal matter Lord Salisbury cannot venture to anticipate the decision to Which the House of Commons may come on any motion which is made before it —I am, your obedient servant, R. T. GUNTON." Mr. Bradlaugh will, therefore, place a notice on the order book so soon as Parliament meets for the•appointment of's Select Committee, with power to .call ,for persona, books, and papers. '

MR. BRIGHT AND THE CRIMES ACT. An Irish voter in Mr. Bright's constituency having written to the right hon. gentleman, asking him how he reconciled his recent speeches and letters with a speech delivered in 1870, in which he said thvt it was the cus- tom of the Tory party to meet every demand for reform in Ireland with coercion, Mr. Bright has sent the follow- ing reply:--" Surely the extract you send me answers your question. What has Parliament been doing since lB7o—and more since 1881—but milting concessions and granting reform for Ireland? When reforms were not made I did not oppose the Acts giving strength to the Executive Government, add now when the great object of Parliament is to do full justice to Ireland. Tam the less likely to see a system of terror in operation over a large portion of the country and to refuse the legis- lation whieh the Government believes, and which I believe, to be necessary to repress it. You speak of:the drastic policy of the Government it fa much less drastic, than the policy of Mr. Gladstone's Government in 1881 and 1882, and if anyone denies this he is either ignorant of the Acts of those Tears or he is guilty of falsehood. In 1881 many hundreds of men were put in prison for months without trial, without evidence againet then., without the defence of council, and without any proof of having broken the law. No man is punished or imprisoned except after trial by two magistrates in an open court, when witnesses may be heard on his behalf and when counsel may be heard in Is defence. The ruffians who are exciting your sympathy are the stipporters of the terror which prevails, and theirpunish- nrent, so far as have seen any description of it, is much more mild than their offences warrant- I have written other letters in which I have explained the course I have taken. It would, seem that you have not seen or read them. This short reply to your note may give the in- formation you seek.'
GENERAL

Mr. Jus*T----'-'4Vice gay, tting inqd-hhancery Division ot the High Court of Justice on Saturday, made an order, on the petition of a large judgment creditor, for the ap- pointment of a receiver and manager for the Scar- borough and Whitby Railway Company. At noon on Monday, a fire broke out in one of a block of warehouses in Irlam-road, Bootle, owned by Alderman James Webster, Liverpool. The warehouses were stored with cotton, valued roughly at £BO,OOO. Three of the upper storeys Were completely destroyed, and the roof also fell in. The cotton continues to smoulder, and yes- terday a will fell in, some firemen narrowly escaping. The December Session of the Central Criminal Court was opened on Monday. The Recorder, in charging the Grand Jury, remarked with regret upon the numerous charges of murder, of which there are no fewer than six. Regarding the charge against the American stockbroker Doherty of shooting a friend named Groharn, be urged them to find a true bill to ensure an investigation .of the affair. The'body of a man was, on Saturday, found weltering in blood in the grounds of the Upper Welsh Harp, Hen- don. A doctor was sent for, and, on examination, found that he had been shot, and the positien of the bullet. wounds led him to surmise that the man had been foully murdered. No weapon was found near the plane. Thi) body was removed to a room at the Upper Welsh harp to await an inquest. ANOTHER FATAL ACCIDENT AT TITE FORTH BRIDGE.— An accident occurred at the Forth Bridge works at Inch- garvie, late on Saturday night, whereby a boy, 14 years of age, named Thomas Shannon, was killed. Shannote. who had been workieg as a rivet heater on the iuternel viaduct, had leaued against a packsheet cover on a rail, when when he fell to the pier beneath, a distance of 150 feet. He was killed instantaneously. THE REV. C. A. BERRY'S DIICISION.—The resolution of the Rev. C. A. Berry to remain in Enffland, sis announced on Monday, gives much satisfaction in this country and a corresponding disappointment in the United States. So great was the desire of the New York press to annonace Mr. Berry's expected acceptanoe, that the London representatives of two of the leading transatlantic newspapers last week made several jetvrneys down to Southport, where Mr. Berry has been PAVVYtHg• A serious explesioe occurred at the Yorkshire Trott and Steel Works, Penistone, belonging to Messrs. C. Cam- mell and Co., Sheffield, on Monday. The bottom of a des- semer steel converter full of molten metal fell out, and it exploded with great force, destroying buildings clone adjoining, setting the roof on fire, and seriously burning eight men and a boy. The severely in'tnred are Alfred Scrivner, John Mills, Allen Cartwright, Thomas Parker, Tames H.amer, Thomas Thew, Charles Meriden, and ,bb

Kay. On Monday. the Glasgow police reported that late eu Sunday, Janet Copekind, 24, committed suicide by swallowing strychnine in a druggist's shop in Argylle- street, where she was employed. She told her sweetheart that she had taken poison, and asked to be conveyed home. She died immediately after reaching her residence, in Raeburn-street. Her lover had remonstrated with her for being escorted•by a young Men on Saturday night. It is believed that she committed the rash act as a result of a quarrel. DESTRUCTION' OF A FACTORY BY FIRR—DAMAGE £40,00.1. Sunday afternoon, fire broke cut hi the Sarre fee- tory at Alva, Stirlingshire, belonging to Messrs. Ross and Son and before the fire brigade from Ali ,cotild reach the scene the building was completely de- stroyed. It was three storeys in height, and gay. employment to between 300 and 4GO workers. The which is covered by insurance, will atiesaint to abo:l4t .£40,000. The buildieg was of recent construction, and the machinery of the latest and newest description. The tause of the fire has not been ascertained.

THE PRICE TO SEE THE CHAMPION " BRaisEn."—Fitty guineas is said to be the price of a ticket to witness the illegal combat which according to reports, J. L. Sullivan (who " performed" the other day with so much acceptance " before the Prince of Wales) is pledged by signed articles to engage in with an Englishmen some- where within a thousand miles from London. Ot course the place of this promised prize-fight is not known 4 but one or two men willing to pay the above price and to risk arrest by the police have been understood to sey that it will take place within four walls, and not in the open air. -

RAID ON BOGUS CLUBS : CONFLICT WITH THE An encounter encounter took place on Sunday between the pace of Cardiff and the members of one of the numerous bogus clubs which have sprung up since the passing eff the Welsh Sunday Closing Act. The Wipe arranged to make a raid on a dozen of these establishments, and at. the majority no resistance was offered, but at a club which is frequented by dock labourers and coal trim- mers a violent conflict occurred. A foroe of 30 police freely used their truncheons, and the members of the club retaliated with bottles, glasses, ire. MAIM con- stables were injured, hut the members of the club were eventually glad to escape. THE DISASTER OFF DOVER.—R, Will be remembered that a few weeks ago the Dutch passenger steamer W. A. Sholten was sunk near Dover, through colliding with the Rosa Mary steamer, and that a number of the crew and passengers were rescued by the Sunderland stein-ter Ebro. On Monday information was received that the owner of the ill-fated vessel had presented Capt. Skipper. of the Ebro, with a gold watch and chain in recognition of his humane conduct, and awarded £2O to be divided amongst the crew of the vessel. It was also announced that the Dutch Lifeboat Society had voted a gold medal to Captain Skipper. I PRINCESS LOUISE AT NOTFINGHAM.—Princess Louise attended It meeting on Monday, presided over by the Bishop of Bouthwell, at Nottingham, in support of a movement for establishing reereative evening classes throughout the country in continuation of Board School education. Resolutions affirming the desirability of seizing upon children when their minds are most 'plastic and easily inoulded were moved bythe Bishop of Ripon and Mr. Samuel Smith, M.P., and spoken to by Mr. Cyri Flower, M.P., Mr. Henry s,mith Wright, M.P., and others. Princess Louise, who is tile guest of the Mayer of Not- tingham (Alderman Turney), met with almost cordial reception, and to-day, will open an exhibition of work done at evening classes. . GRF.LT Flan 111 YORKSIEUR.7.—P-150,030 DAMAGES. —Early on Monday, the extensive premises of the Driffield and East Riding .Linseed Cake Company were discovered to be on ire. The flames rapidly spread, and in a very, short tine° the whole of the six-storeyed build- ing was Involved. The mill was one of the largest in the kingdom, and occupied an entire block, facing three streets. The damage is estimated at not far short of £150,000, which is partly covered by insurance. A hand- some clock tower shared in the destruction. A large number of hands will be thrown out of employment, and great distress will probably result. The outbreak was 'discovered by the night-watchman in a mill on the south side of the block, but though the fire brigade quickly arrived they could only save a building containing large tank of 200 tons cf oil. The mill was lighted by electricity. •

FUNERAL OF .THE LATE LORD I/YONS AT ARUNDEL.— A special train left Victoria Station, London, on Saturday. for Arundel, conveying those who 070ie to he present at the funeral of the late Lord Lyons. Ceptain Byng represented the Queen Colonel Teesdale, the Prince of Wales; and Mr. Barrington, Lord Salis- bury. Among other gentlemen in the train were Sir Edward Malet, Sir Edward Mdrison (British Minister at Copenhagen), Count Ilviandt, Sir Julian Paunceferte, Sir Chas. Ferguson. the Rev. Father Bernard. of High- gate, the Rev. Father Vincent. and about fifty others. including representatives from nearly all the foreign embassies. The funeral took place at 11 30 a.m., service being held in the Fitzalan Chapel. The coffin, of polished oak with brass fittings, was placed in the centre of the chapel, and covered with a black velvet pall with a gold cross traversing it. On the coffin was pieced the de- ceased earl's coronet. The chapel was draped with black. Silver candelabras, along the sides of the building and behind the altar, supported lighted tapers. THE PRINCE OF WALES AND LONDON APPRRNTICEB. On Saturday the Exhibition of Apprentices' Work Avas. opened by the Prince of Wales in the People's Palace. Mile End-road, London. His Royal Iliehness announced that the Drapers' Company had addressed a letter to the Charity Commissioners offering £40,000 from their cor- porate funds, in addition to a donation of £20,000 more, for building the technical schools, provieed the Charity Commissioners would, out of the money at their disposal under the City of London Parochial Charities Act, sup- plement it by a sufficient sum to carry on the establish- ment with economy and yet with efficiency. To this a. favourable reply had been received. His Royal Highness also stated that the Ironmongers' Company had sug- gested that if a sufficient som could be obtained freak.] the source previously alluded to, they would be willing in some other part of London to co-operate in the founda- tion of en institution of the same character for providing technical, scientific, commercial, and artistic education. united with physical and social recreation. This appeal had also met with a favourable response. THE QUEEN AND THE NURSES : GIFT OF £70,000.— Communications from Windsor Castle and Grosvenor , House respecting the generous decision of the Queen to devote the Women's Jtibilee Offering of £70,000 for the benefit of nurses and nursing institutions have been pub- lished. From Windsor Castle, General Sir H. F. Ponsonby (Private secretary of the Queen) writes stating that the committee, of which the Duke of Westminster is at the head, "are working out a scheme for improving the con- dition of the nurses fcr the Sick poor." The Duke of Westminster communicates to the effect that the details of. the scheme dealing with the £70,000 have not yet been settled. Sir Andrew Clark was some time ago requested to submit for the consideration of the committee the claims of a proposed , pension fund for nurses and hospital officials, as some of its friends hoped that £20,000 might be secured to help to start that movement.. There are several charitable institutions providing for nurses whose claims have been also submitted to the committee. The Queen, however, expressly desires to show her sympathy with those of her subjects who are in the unfortunate position of being poor, for the letter of Sir Henry Fonsonby dis- tinctly stales that the scheme under consideration is for "improving the conditiOn of nurses for the sick poor."
