IRELAND. Alderman Winstanley, -Protestant Home 'Ruler, has been appointed by the Lord-Lieutenant to be High Sheriff Of Dublin for the ensuing year. Aid. Hooper, M.P., proprietor of the Cork Herald, was arrested on Saturday for unlawfully publishing reports of National League meetings. He was afterwards admitted to bail, to appear Tie!ore the magistrates on the 19th Inst. The same paper having made a charge of jury-packing against Crown officials, Mr. Justice Murphy stated at the Cork Assizes on Saturday that if such com- ments were repealed he would fine and imprison the editor. The -wife of a labourer, named Quinn, and their little child, about two years old, were burned to death early on Monday, in the house in which they were sleeping in New Lodge-road, Belfast. It is not known how the fire eriginated, but a neighbour hearing screams rushed into the burning house, and saved another child, four years of age. Thereof and upper floor fell in, and when the bodies were recovered two hours afterwards they were unrecognisable. One of the largest schemes of pea.ant proprietary yet carried out in Ireland unber the provisions of Lord Ash- bourne's Land Purchase Act has just been satisfactorily completed on the estates of the Duke of Abercorn in !County Tyrone and County Donegal. The total sum in- [volved amounte to over £300,000, and about 300 farmers become owners of their holdings at 20 years' purchase, 'based on the ordinary valuation. The negotiations be- tween the duke and his tenants were from the first con- ducted in a most friendly spirit The purchase will re- duce the area of the duke's estate by about one-third. Further S'utrages are reported from Kerry. As early as six o'clock in the evening a band of six Moonlighters, armed and disguised, entered the dwelling of a farmer ' named Kerin. They were at once set upon by two dogs. The leader of the party called upon Kerin to draw off the brutes if he did not wish to get shot. Kerin did as directed, but while he was dragging the animals to an outhouse both were shot dead by the Moonlighters, theirblood spurting into their owner's face. The ruffians then made Kerin go upon his knees and swear that he would not pay his rent rSome time ago an attack Vi AS made upon Kerin by an 'unarmed party, but upon that occasion he chased them across the country with the assistance of the dogs now shot. His brother-in-law is under police protection. owing to his having transgressed the rules of the League by taking an evicted farm for which the previous tenant refused to pay rent. Jr. the same locality, near the vil- lage of Knocknagoshel. a quantity of hay, the property of Mr. Kerry-Thompson, has been maliciously destroyed. Mr. Thompson refused to discontinue speaking to a boy- cotted schoolmaster. THE MURDER OF HEAD-CONSTABLE WHELEHAN. The trial of the wren persons indicted in connection with the Ballvvaughan affray was resumed at Wicklow on Saturday. Further evidence was given in support of the alibis set up in the eases of three of the men. and a priest spoke to the general good conduct of the prisoners. Mr. Loamy, M.P., then addressed the jury on behalf of the prisoners. He submitted that it had been incontest- ably proved that neither Tom Leary nor the two Murphrs were present at the attack. Sexton's house was attacked solely for the purpose of getting arms. They would have to disbelieve the evidence of several respectable witnesses if they believed Cullinan. Dr. Falconer also spoke for the defence. The jury found Dan Leary, Lawlor, Efehir, Curtis, and Tom Leary guilty, but could not agree on their verdict in reference to the two Murpheys. Tom , Leary was sentenced to tea years' penal servitude. and Lawlor, Hehir. Curtis, and Dan Leary to seven years each. The Attorney General for Ireland said that he would not again indict the two Murpheys until the next assizes. THE ALLEGED MANSLAUGHTER BY EMERGENCY MEN. On Monday, at Wicklow, the trials of the emergency men alleged to have been engaged in the affray on the 28th September at Coolgreaney, in which John Kinsella was shot, commenced before Mr. Justice O'Brien and a special jury. Altogether 17 men are accused of being connected with the affair. On Monday, John Idc.Cabe, Thos. Clinging, Thos. Macnulty, Moses Porter, Alex. Kinsbury, David Crawford, and John Harris were put on their trial on an indictment charging them with manslaughter. The whole of the 17 were subsequently charged with sic& Stephen Maher deposed that he was with about 20 peons in the yard of a man named Kavanagh, on 28th September, when 17 emergency men came to carry out a distress for rent They demanded the cattle in the yard, but Kavanagh refused to give them up. When one of the emergency men attempted to get in, Kinsella threatened him with a pitchfork. Several of the emer- gency men then fired, and Kinsella was shit dead. On Tnesday, a conflict of testimony arose as to who fired the first shot, but all agreed that numerous shots were fired. Evidence was then taken for the defence. John John- son, otherwise "Red Johnson," one of the emergency men, stated that he climbed on to the gate, but gut, down again on Kinsella making a thrust at him with a pitchfork. A movement was then made by the people inside the yard, and a clear space was left near the gate. Seeing this, witness climbed the gate again, with a man named Oaks, and the latter was struck by a stone thrown from inside the yard. People in the yard threw stones and 'fired shots before the emergency men fired. They also cried, "Come on, if you dare." fl'itness would not say positively that the shots from the yard killed Kinsella. None of the emer- gency men exchanged firearms after the affray. Santee' Seott corroborated Johnson's evidence. About forty people were in tho yard. Witness was knocked senseless with a blow of a stone, before any shots were fired. He had a five-chambered revolver, but he did nat fire till after Kinsella made a lunge with a fork at John- son. They brought away the cattle after the affray. The jury found a verdict of "Not guilty," and the prisoners were discharged.

div.head: CLANRICARDE CASE.
div.p: THE CLANRICARDE CASE.

An application was made to Chief Baron Palies and Mr. Justice Andrews in the Exchequer Division on Satur- day, on behalf of Lord Clanricarde, for a conditional order to change the verdict in the case of Joyce v. Clan- ricarde into one for the defendant, or, in the alternative, for .a new trial, on the grounds of the reception of illegal evidence, misdirection of the Chief Baron, that the ver- dict was against the weight of evidence, aud that the damages were excessive. The action was for libel, and was tried before the Chief Baron and a special jury, re- sulting in a verdict for the plaiatiff, damages £2,500. Theiapplication was granted. Sir Michael Hicks-Beach has published the fetters which passed between Lord Clanricarde and himself after the interview with Mr. Joyce. Sir Michael stat.es that with no other landlord did he go nearly so far in the way of " pressure" as he did with Lord Clanricarde; that his threat to his lordship was never carried out because the circumstances contemplated did not arise. andlitat the aid of the forces of the Crown were never ret Used to the Sheriff or other officer of the law. Reply- ing to one of Lord Clanricarde's letters, in October,lBs6, Sir Michael flicks-Beach said:—" You complain that I did not communicate directly with yourself, and at a considerably earlier date. If your lordship resided is Ireland I should certainly have sought an interview with you,•but I admit that I thought your nen. would be beakr acquainted than your lordship with the condition of a property which you have not even visited for years, and that I supposed that, in such circutistances, you would have acted on his advice in making; any necessary reductions to your tenants. In your opinion, the 'law and the Government will be crushed' if you now do this. In-my opinion you will be only following, thoueli late, an example set to you, not only by other great and j wealthy Trish landlord's, but by very many men who. though struggling and in difficulties, have felt bound by. their position, no matter how great the inconvenience to themselves and their families, to proceed with generositpand forbearance in the exaction of ill tir legal rights." _ _ .

LORD ROSEBETIT AT OLDHATC—Tho• Earl of .Rosebery delivered an address on Tuesday evening at a large gathering Af Liberals in the lotirOugh of Oldham in sup- port of a resolution declaring that the Irish policy of the Governmentis onpressiire, unjust, and dangerous to the. best Interests of the empire, and that, the only durable. solution of the Irish difficulty is to be found in a manly recognition of the right of the Irish people to manage their own internal affairs. He created much mirth by his satirical 'allusions to the "Olympian feasts" of the Liberal Dissentients which have recently been held in Dublin and London. Ho maintained that the party ' mist' cordially working with Mr. Gladstone represented, the old Liberal party, and had the title.deeds of that party. The Irish people were asking for the restoration ' of their ancientconstitutional legislature in Dublin, and he did not think the English or the Scotch democracies would be deaf to the appeal now being made to them by their Irish brethren. I I EARL urRANVILLE ON THR IRISH QUIISTION.—EarI Gran: vine, speaking at the dinner of the Eighty Club, London, on Tuesday night, referred to the Liberal Unionist meet- ing, and denied that it was in the • power of one Section of the Liberal party to destroy; the whole. He heartily agreed with the Dyike of Argyll's advice that harsh lan- guage should not be used towards Ireland, but that ad- vice came too late, and had been lost upon the Prime Minister, the Chancsllor of the Exchequer, and the Irish Secretary, who had referred to the Irish as Hottentots, rebels, and fraudulent bankrupts. The Liberals did not desire to leave the Liberal Unionists out of the party, but they conlcl not recede on the question Of giving Ire- land self-government so far as Irish questions were con- cerned. He did not believe any suspension of the Irish question was possible. He expressed doubt as to the duration of the Liberal Unionist organisation. As to their &Which: towards the Government,' the Liberals would support a necessary reform of umeedure, while being mindful of the rights of minorities, and would support the Government if .they.. se.t_theinselves against , the leolicy of Foir,Traders. They would not harass the Government in foreign! affairs; they would support and , improve any good bill for local government, but they must riot allow these questions to put aside the IriSh question. - • •

THE IRISH SECRETARY AT MANCHESTER. Mr. A. J. Balfour, the Chief Secretary for Ireland. addressed a meeting in the Manchester Free Trade Hall on Wednes- day night, largely composed of his constituents in East' Manchester. Admission was by ticket, and every per- son entering the hall was subjected t 4. iareful scrutiny. Extraordinary precautions were taki to prevent any Possible attack on Mr. Balfour, and about 250 policemen were on duty at or near the place of meeting. Mr. S. Chesters-Thompson presided, and on the platform, in !addition to a number of- prominent Conservatives, were several Liberal Unionists, Mr. Balfour dealt in his speech exclusively with Irish affairs, replying to recent criticisms of the Government policy by Sir George Tre- yelyin, Mr. Dillon, and others. He declared that there was no attempt to prevent criticism or to interfere with free speech in. Ireland so long as it was not likely to lead to crime, but when a man.incited the peasantry to break the law he ceased to be a politician and became a crimi- nal; and as a criminal he saould proceed against him. A resolution of confidence in Mr. Balfour was passed. At the terinination of the meeting a large crowd had assem- bled outside the barrier 'which led from the Free Trade Hall to the Town Hall, and lustily groaned as the right hon. gentleman drove through. His carriage was surrounded by a strong body of police, and there was no attempt at serious disturbance. For greater safety, Mr. Balfour was lodged in the Town Hall during the night. div.head: CHRISTMAS BOOKS, &c.
div.p: CHRISTMAS BOOKS, &c.

"Peter Parley's Annual for Boys and Girls" is here, and is as welcome as ever. It is published by Mr. Ben. George, London, has now reached the forty-seventh year of its existence, but the boys and girls who are favoured with the issue for 1888 will ,testify that it has lost nothing of its juvenile freshness and bouyanc.y. It is as to appearance—in its gorgeous binding, of scarlet arid blue, and gold—one of the hand- somest books published. The coloured title page is, too, aNvork of art, and gives an agreeable foretaste of the good things within. "Peter Parley" addressee his readers briefly, but to the point; and we cannot but_re- iterate his advice when he says that these who are won- dering how to keep 'boisterous boys and girls quiet -dur- ing the holidays should present them with a i copy of, his annual. The best that can be said of the stories s that they they are equal to their predecessors, which is another way of saying they are well written full of 'adventure, and therefore of absorbing interest. The titles are as follows :—" The Feud," "The Enemy of Man," "Only a Cad," "In Peril amongst Papiraus," and "Some fine old Puzzles." It should be added that the stories have been specially illustrated, , and , that the I, illustrations are numerous. Peter Parley" is therefore still " booming." , Messrs. llildesheimer & Faulkner, of 41, Irwin-street, London, have a world-wide fame for the beauty and variety of their Christmas cards and Christmas books. They spend large sums of money every year in order to secure artistic excellence of the highest order, and with it the variety which is ever charming. It has been a subject of discussion whether the sending 6f Christmas cards was Ot on the wane, but 80 long as there are so many things of beauty to tempt the eye we feel per- suaded that, with an increasing taste in. matters of art, buyers will never be wanting. Having for several years paid attention to novelties in Christmas cards, we were half inclined to think that invention must be well nigh exhausted; but Messrs. Hildesheimer and Faulkner come before the public this season fresher and stronger than ever. -The-newest thing, for those who do not mind spending is what is terinid 'thF-Fhotographic Opal Souvenir. It is just what its name suggests—a charm- ing photo. in opal, inn handsome substantial box, ready for sending by parcel post, It is fit up so that it will: Stand; and thus become a tasteful ornament. -Then there are innumerable sets of autograph Christmas and New Year cards—six in a box, with envelopes. The ides in this case is for the sender to place his or'her name on the,card with best wishes for a happy Christmas or New Year, as the case may be. It must be an extraordinary, and we may say a bad taste, that cannot be met, for we have cards in all shapes and designs—square. crqscent, oval; some fan and others palette-shaped. "Birds, flowers, weeds, grasses, bells, berries, yachts, .cottages, and mansions all do duty in one form or another by way of lending enchantment to eaeh view. There are, too, of course, double and single cards of all sizes, some beauti- fully coloured, and othera in tasteful monotint. If the purchaser has any difficulty, it will be that he is embar- rassed with so much that alarms him. Those, who re wanting something sacred will turn to the series of "Emmanuel" cardwwhich have been specially designed by such well known artists as Alice Havers, Alice Reeve, B. D. Sigmund, and C. G. Noakes. Some of the designs ate in colour, others are in black and white, and they are all well conceived, and well drawn. Last, but not least, we have a series of what may be called cards in book form, or, more strictly speaking, booklets. We cannot speak too highly of• this set, for they are as charming as they are cheap, nothing equal to them having previously been issued. All the illustra- tions are finely finished in monotint, and iS is not ,too much to say they are a high compliment te‘the writers whose works they illustrate. •The booklets have gilt edges, and are tied with pretty silk ribbons. Each is encloged in an illustrated envelope hearingan autograph greeting. Among the subjects we have Lord Houghton's poem" Good night tind good morning," "Sea poems" and" "River poems" by various authors, and several specially written Christmas poems by that versatile author, Mr. F. E.Weatherley. Coming to books proper, Messrs. Hildesheimer and Faulker are not less successful in this department. One of the most charming Christmas books ever printed is "Goldsmith's Deserted Village." It occupies forty-eight pages, and every pagel,,is illustrated, the artists who

Like the rest, this book is profusely illustra- ted ; some pictures are in colour and others in monotint by St. Clair Simmons and Ernest Wilson. It is sufficient fo say of it that it is in no wise inferior to the rest, but we must in especial mention the coloured picture of the-bonny little girl with the bonny little dogs, and that, too, of the —other little"--girl -who, candle in hand, is watching -for the old clock to strike the hour which signals the advent of a new year. Altogether it must be said of Messfs. Hildesheimer and Faulkner that they have excelled themiselves. • "Mignon's Husband," by the author of "Bootle's Baby,' is published by Messrs. F. V. White and Co., Lon-don, and has reached a fifth edition. It is capital reading • Bootle's Baby has grown into a charming young lady who has the usual experience in finding that the course of true love does not run smooth; but (also as usual) all comes right in the end. The various personages are so dealt, conceived and finely drawn, that the reader feels that they are people he 'has met or may meet. We cannot help noticing by-the-by that the name of Redfern crops up pretty often as the ladies' tailor; it looks like an advertisement. Dr. Parker is coming home to spend Christmas in - .

the bosom of the Tem-ple, a sadde`r, and probably a wiser man. He has himself confessed his visit to the United States a failure by the decisive step of cancelling all his engagements, and hurrying home nearly four months sooner than he had intended. He was to have stayed in the United States till April, but by the end of November had found the place too big for him, and yearned for the cosier comforts and closer companionship of the Temple. Things have gone wrong with him from first to last, culminating in the amazing indiscretion of his auctioneering proposal to interview Mr. Gladstone, disposing of his six columns to the highest bidder in the American Press. This was a procedure so in- credible, that it was only natural to doubt the authenticity of the letter which the " New York Herald" published over the al- leged Signature of Dr. Parker. But the Doc- tor has not denied its authenticity. It was a mean trick for the "Herald ' to publish a dama- ging letter of this kind, which was essentially of a private character. Pro'•ably, if Dr. Parker had made the offer of the despatch solely to the" Herald," it. would have been accepted. But, with childish in- geniousness, he announced in the triplicate letter he wrote to the ' Herald," the "World,' and the "New York Tribune," that he had made the offer to three papers, and was open to the highest bidder. It was bad of the " Herald " to betray him, but, it was worse still for a man in Dr. Parker's position to put himself in the loser of the traitor. The cor- respondence will be pleasant reading for Mr. Glad- stone, when he reft.cts over Ins friendly relations with Dr. Parker, of which the historical break- fast at the Doctor's house, last summer, was an inci- dent. Dr. railer says, doubtless truly enough, that he had no hankering after the succession of 31r. Beecher'a pulpit, and that he would not have occu- pied it had is been offered to him. Nevertheless it is pretty certain that he would have liked to have had the offer, and that he was passed over in favour of a younger and comparatively unkncwn man must have added gall to the bitterness of disap... pointment. There was a very interesting incident in connection with the eulogy service, of which par- ticulars have not yet reached the English papers. Admission to Plymouth Church on that oc- casion was by payment, it being under- stood that the proceeds were to go to- wards the cost of the Beecher memorial. The committee, rightly or wrongly, regarding Dr. Par- ker's service as gratuitous, looked forward to net- ting a sum of at least £.500 from this source.. Up to the present time they have not received a single cent. Major Pond, the gentleman who undertook the business transaction of Dr. Parker's lecture tour, included the Plymouth Church service within the range of his duties, and ran it on commercial pan- ciples, to the expressed astonishment of the com- mittee. Major Pond paid Dr. Parker £6O for his sermon, or the eulogy, as it is called in the United States. Major Pond paid all the other expenses and, according to latest advices from New. York, positively declined to render any account until the 10th of December, being last Saturday, the day on which Dr. Parker was to sail in the Etruria. AU this has created much ill-feeling in Brooklyn, and Dr. Parker is probably heartily glad to be out of the- business. He is to preach in the-City Temple on Christmas Day. In addition to the eulogy he preached on two Sundays in Plymouth Church, re- ceiving for each service a fee of £25, in addition to his hotel expenses. Mt. Stead has got up a little peformauce for Sun- day, which may result in further street disturb- ances and more broken heads. It is a pity that the vindication of the right of public meeting has fal- len under such auspices. In the meantime it is in- teresting to note what deep root recent manifesta- tions of police power have taken in London daily life. The favourite game of the school boys in the dinner hour now is to play Trafalgar Square. Every- where where boys gather in the vicinity of a'school house you shall see them slinging their coats, or their caps tied to-strings, beating each other about the head, and crying "Pass away Move on! Pass along." I notice that it is always the big boys who answt r for order, the victims of the batoning being the smallest and weakest in the school.

div.head: OUR LONDON LEITER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LEITER.

LONDON, THUREiDAY NIGHT. The news of the relapae of the Crown Prince Tines as a sudden and unexpected shock. The singular turn for the better which the malady took had created widely-spread confidence, not least em- phatic in the mind of the Crown Prince himself. Sir Morrell Mackenzie, speaking to me again on the subject at the end of last week, had somewhat modified the seepticism with which he originally viewed the improvement. He still feared it might be only a temporary effort, but was so far assured that he had definitely postponed his journey to San Remo till the 15th Of January. Yesterday he was I called off by an &Lim telegram from the Crown Princess, and will to-night be at the Prince's bed- side. Ever since the Crown Prince rode through the multitude gathered in the streets of London on Jubilee Day, h e has become aPopular favourite in Lon- don. He looked the very embodiment of sturdy health and manly form. At that time the terrible disease had not fully developed, and no one imagined that the stately massive guardsman in his white uniform would a few weeks later be hovering between life and death. When the news came, the millions who looked upon him in the Royal cavalcade recalled his bearing, and .began to take a keen personal interest in his condition. Since he bee-tithe an Object of con- centrated interest, much has been made known of his public life and his private character, which was formerly only dimly comprehended. All that is known of him is to his credit, antl every one now knows that in the event of his death not only would there be removed from a family circle a faith- ful husband and a kind father, but that a great nation would lose the prospect of a benignant ruler. Since the Crown Prince'iS again in imminent peril, with the almost nonagenarian Emperor tot- tering towards the grave, Prince William of Prussia, the next heir to the Throne, again engrosses atten- tion. It is taken for granted that he will, in the event of his ' father's succumbing to the disease that has attacked him, and the Emperor presently dying, come to the Throne. But it is well known to those having intimate relations with our own Court Circle, that the Queen's grandson is not a favourite with the • Germans. Prince Wil- liam of Prussia, the Heir Apparent in suc- cession to his father, the Crown Prince, is very unpopular. He is spoken of as ill-condi- tioned in his personal relations, and Jingo in his foreign policy. He is truly, ill-conditioned. But that is the direct result of a state of bodily health, in its way quite as deplorable as his father's. He is suffering from the development of the ' peculiar disease which carried off the late King of Prussia, after-rendering him insane for the last few years of his reign. He is the victim of a succession of abscesses formed in the ear, anti the physicians, who are his constant attendants, fight night and day against the prospect of inflammation of the brain setting in. This seems an inevitable result, and the only thing the doctors hope is to delay the inevit- able as long as possible. Apart from this painful infliction, the Prince hat; not since his boyhood been in robust health. His left, arm is withered, and as he goes about with pale face, bleared eyes, affd masses of discoloured cotton wool in his e rs, he is, it will be understood, not exactly the kind of material out of which Emperors are made He has ' a little foes year 0151 eon who, unhappily, according to present appearances, is within Measurable dis- tance of being proclaimed Emperor of Germany, with the attendant risks and inconveniences of pr.- longed regency. The political position at home has been consider- ably cleared bp within the past week. The diffi- culties surrounding the Liberal party have been much complicated by the uncertainty of their at- titude towards the Dissentients. There was up to within a recent date always a lingering hope that, after all, as Mr. Goschen says, they might repent and come back to the fold. Lord Hartington's latest deliverance has settled that paint for ever. When a statesman who has ranked as a Liberal hints at the possibility of his being able, in given circum- stances to support the Cameivative party in re-im- posing Protection,,he is hopelessly gone over. That is the position Lord Hartington has now formally assumed, and it is much better so. There need now be no further coquetting . with his lordship for the interesting but not numerically important body of gentlemen who accept his leadership. They may be regarded as having gone over bag And baggage to the Tory camp, and the Liberal party may resume

FOUNDED A.D. 1526. Heed Muter: The Bey. B. J. WILLCOCKS, M.A., Late Scholar at St. Catherine's College, Cambridge. • Second Muter The Rev. H. G. SMITH, M.A., Scholar of St. John's College, Cambridge ; And five Assfistaid Mmters.

The School contains two divisions. The work of the Lower Division comprises a regular course of instruction in English, French, the rudiments of Latin, elementary Mathematics and Science, with Reading, Writing, Arithmetic, Drawing, Drill, and Vocal Music, and all other elements of a sound modern education. In the Upper Division, the choice is offered of a thorough mercantile or high classical comae; German and Greek being optional subjects. Twelve Free Scholarships. Two Exhibitions to Oxford and Cambridge. The year is divided into throe Terms. Capitation Fees, everything Included, £4 and P.. 3 per term in the Upper and Lower Divisions respectively. , Entrance Fee, El.

THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 17, 1867.

- TEE Eighty Club did itself and Earl GRAN-. VILLE honour by inviting his Lordship to be their guest at a banquet which was held in London, on —Tuesday mght. bord GRANVILLE is a teran leader of the Liberal party, who has susta d the burden and/ the heat of the day for many o: long year in struggling against Tory stupidity in the House of Lords. It is hard to be fighting with all the odds constantly against you; but this is what Lord GRANvILLE has done with conspicuous sue- cess. His style for such an assembly as the House of Lords is perfect; he has a genial presence, and a polished wit which readily pierces the weak places of his opponents. Beating, or beaten, he is still the same. Those who are familiar with the despatches he wrote as Foreign Secretary in Mr. GLADSTONE'S Government will readily acknow- ledge that they are models in their way. Lord GRANVILLE is so uniformly courteous that there are people who think he was not a strong man as Foreign Secretary. But he has a timid of iron, which we like all the better for being covered by a silk glove. The speech which he made, on Tuesday, was in a characteristic vein. He showed himself

the pink of politeness to his opponents, but he did not fail to make known how and where they are in the wrong. How neatly he exposed the numerical weakness of the Liberal Unionists, when in Con- ference in London, by the remark that " he be- lieved the speakers derived encouiagement from the fact that they were addressing almost the whole of their party united in one building !" He quite agreed with the Duke of Auovu. as to the desirability of avoiding harsh language; but, he said, " the Duke's advice had been entirely lost upon the PRIME MINISTER, the CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER, and the CHIEF SECRETARY for IR.F4aND. They had compared the Irish to the Hottentots, called them rebels, and said they were a combination of fraudulent bankrupts; and Mr., Goscinor, almost in his last speech, described the elected governing bodies of Ireland as lunatics." Touching the Irish question, Lord GRAN VILLE said it was impossible for the Liberal party to recede from the position they had taken up as to granting Home Rule for Ireland. He went, indeed, so far i as to say that he did not believe that if Mr. GLAD- STONE himself were to join with Lord SALISBURY in tving to suspend that great question, that "air united efforts could succeed. This is the right view to take, and shows how thoroughly his Lordsh:i. has made himself familiar with the fact that the Liberal party, as a whole, are as much in earnest about Home Rule as are the Nationalists them- selves. The Liberal Unionists continue to cling to the delusion that, because Mr. GLADSTONE is at the head of the Home Rule move- ' ment, the agitation would collapse if he were out of the way; and it is for this reason, and this 'alone, that some of them have vowed that they will do all they can to keep the Tories in office. They know that Mr. dLADSTONE is an old man;' that, in the ordinary course of things, his leader- ship of the Liberal party cannot be of long dura- tion'; and they are determined if they can, to wear him out by incessant opposition and incessant irri- tation. This is a poor, mean policy, and it is founded upon an utter misconception of Mr. C4LLDSTONE'S personal influence. That influence is great undoubtedly, but it is great because it has its rots in the consciousness that he is actuated by just and noble motives; and that he appeals to the reason as well as the allegiance of his followers. He has a great mind, which moves quickly, and it thus happens that, in the first instmee, timid sort of people are startled when he points to the fresh fields to be conquer.d. But when they come to see as he sees, they are as eager as he to go for- w r 1. It was so when he intimated that the tithe had come to disestablish the Irish Church. There were supporters who looked upon the movement as a rash undertaking. Some of them went over

to the Tories, but the bulk of those who hesitated were found, in the end, helping the leader of the , Liberals to remove another stumbling block from , the path of progress. And so it is to-day; the dis- may at the daring of the proposal to grant Home Rule has given place with the masses to admira- tion, coupled with resolution to render all the aid they can in giving justice to Ireland. In `the ranks of the Liberal party there never was greater enthusiasm on any questimi. Mr. GLADSTONE is not required to get up steam; the steam is up; and all that is now needed is that the block shall be removed—that the way shall be cleared. Lord GRANVILLE sees this, and he wishes the Liberal Unionists to see it; for the sooner they realise that their opposition is hopeless, the sooner will they cease from troubling, and the sooner will Ire- land be at rest.

"How to road and what to road" was the sub- ject of the address which Mr. A. J. BALFOUR de- livered to the students on Saturday afternoon, as the new Rector of St. Andrew's University. Mr. BALFOUR is not to be counted great either as Irish Secretary or as University Rector, but he is much more acceptable in the latter capacity than in the former; and it is pleasant to find ourselves for once to a large extent in agreement with him. Mr. FREDERIC HARRISON, with his exalted and severe views of the duties of life, is in the habit of con- demning the omnivorous style of reading which is 80 prevalent to-day, and would have people strengthen their minds by reading only what the world recognises as masterpieaes of literature. Emerson has somewhere said that it is a good rule not to read any book that is not at least a year old. In the meantime it will have been deter- mined whether the book is worth reading at all. It was with some such idea of saving time that the great Napoleon stated that he sometimes al- lowed his letters to remain unopened for a fort- night. He found that by taking this course there were few letters that in the end required answer- ing. But with regard to reading, it is so much a matter of enjoyment, as well as instruction, that we agree with Mr. BALFOUR in thinking there is much to be said for miscellaneous reading. No two minds are alike, and what is food for one might be so much rubbish for another, if not so much poison. Nearly all our great writers and thinkers have been, at one time or another, great readers—not by any set rule as to subjects of study but by a process of natural selection. They had "a crop for all corns," and everything was turned to good account. It is not, of course, to be supposed from this that a person has only to go on reading voraciously, and without rule in order to become famous in the world of literature. He may become a great reader with- out becoming a great man; indeed, his case may be so b'ad as to give some warrant to the rude sar- casm of the farmer who pointed to his calf and said the more it ate the bigger calf it grew. Boys and girls require, of course, to have their studies directed; but, in these' days of keen competition in producing results, it. may safely be left to their teachers to see that they do not waste their school hours in swallowing mental food which they cannot possibly assimilate. But people who are up-grown may be wisely left to themselves as to what they shall read, except in so far as they seek instruc- tion with regard to sources of special knowledge or special lines of thought. It is something gained that they acquire the habit of reading, for they are thereby fitting _themselves for enjoyment of the highest and of the purest kind—enjoyment which holds its own when other pleasures pall, and which, unlike coarser gratifications, yields its charm in old age as well as in manhood and youth. We therefore say, let people read—systematically if they will, unsystematically if they like. The mind has a place for every fact; and sometimes, when least expected, the fact whicli has been stowed away, which, it may be, has beedforgotten for years, leaps forth and finds its place in the economy of nature.

The Rev. C. A. Bann, pastor of the Queen-st. Congregational Ohurch, Wolverhampton, has, after , all, declined the flattering invitation to succeed the late HENRY WARD BEECHER as minister of Ply- mouth Church. It would seem that the Press has been entirely out of it, and we, too, must confeis ourselves at fault in coming to the conclusion that the reverend gentleman would certainly accept the offer to occupy the first Congregational pulpit in the world—to say nothing of .an annual salary which is in itself a small fortune. But Mr. BERRY has shown himself above such considerations as personal ambition or love of lucre, and must be classed amongst those noble-minded men who, in a crisis of their fate, ask themselves earnestly and sincerely what is best to be done in the interests of their kind. Having settled that point, they cheerfully adhere to their decision whatever the sacrifice to themselves may be. And that the sacrifice in this instance is a great one—looking at the matter from an ordinary point of view—is be- yond question. We have reason to know that so far as salary is concerned, the sum that it was proposed to give Mr. BERRY was even larger than the amount generally named; while, as minister of Plymouth Church, his sermons would have been ensured a market in the reading world which would of itself be equivalent to an ordinary income. But beyond all this, the call was, we are told, "laden with a weight of spontaneous unanimity, and the urgency of a splendid enthusiasim," and it may therefore well be that Mr. BERRY has, as he puts it in his letter to his congregation, had a question to decide which has been " the occasion 4 long perplexity and ceaseless study." But he •has decided; he has resolved to remain in Eng- land; nd we trust it will be found that his deci- sion is for the best. His congregation have resolved to relieve him of work in connection with his pas- torate which may quite as well be done by other people, leaving him to devote his energies and talents to tasks of wider import. It is obvious that this call from beyond the Atlantic, declined though it be, will bring the pastor of the Queen- street Church into the very front rank of English ministers. From henceforward the Rev. A. C. BERRY will count as a more important factor when ecclesiastical or political questions are being dealt with in this country. Brother JONATHAN having discovered him, he cannot any longer be hid; and it is gratifying to know that if he is not destined to do a great work in America, he will, ,in all likelihood, do a larger work here as a con- sequence of the invitation to become the suc- cessor of the greatest preacher in the United • States.

" TOUCTI AND GO."
Lord Randolph Churchill has been the guest of Lord Hartingtbn, at Hardwick Hall. Righteous- ness and peace have -kissed each other; and the millennium is nigh.
There is another war scare on the continent, but nobody seems to know what it is about. . It is further evidence of the little wisdom with which the world is governed.

The discovery of gold in Wales seems likely to turn some people's heads, and fill promoters' pockets. There may, or may not, be a great deal of gold in the mines, but there is certainly a great deal in the imagination.

There is something of the old Adam still left in the Prince of Wales. He wont to patronise Sul- livan the other day; but it ended in the prize- fighter patronising the Prince. Sullivan looks on a Prince as small beer when he is about.

What learned nonsense is being talked about the possibility of Bacon being the author. of Shakespeare's plays! Some of these little-minded controversialists may be able to deal with a mole- hill, but they cannot understand a mountain. Let them go in for Bacon, if they will, at breakfast- time.

At a meeting; the other day of the Liverpool As- tronomical Society, Mr. W. H. Davies F.R.A.S., remarked upon the singular mistake which many people were making as to what was called the Star of Bethlehem. What they were now looking at as a wonderful re-appearance was in reality the planet Venus, which is now at its nearest approach to the earth.

• It would seem that the Vicar of Ashton is alto- gether in the wrong in thinking that he can pre- vent the clergyman of another district lecturing in his parish. He can prohibit his preaching or visiting ministerially, but his authority ends there. The Rev. W. Edmondson, of Parr, was therefore within his right in proposing to lecture in Ashton. This if; the view of the law which is taken by the Bishop of Worcester, and he is likely to be better informed than the Vicar of Ashton.

The Fair Trade nostrum is a drug in the politi- cal market. Lord Granville, on Tuesday, said the smugglers used to call their operations "fair trade." Mr. Goschen, on being appealed to, says he has already "expressed his conviction that there was no danger of the adoption by the Government of any fiscal principle which would threaten the alliance of the Liberal Unionists and the Conservative parties." This is cold comfort; it is enough to cause Mr. JohnbWhite, as the only enrolled member Of the League in Warrington, to send in his resignation.

The members of the Widnes Local Board appear to be tired of beating time in the matter of the nuisance arising out of the deposit of alkali waste. The subject was under discussion on Tuesday, and there was a disposition to bring matters to an issue. However' after duo consideration, it was decided to consult a solicitor as to the powers of the Board under the Public Health Act. There can be no question that they have power to inter- fere with anything ,that causes a-nuisanoe. It is bad enough to have foul fumes in the air without having foul waste under foot.

Mr. Pyne, M.P., seems to be enjoying himself by befooling the constaßles who have surrminded Lisfinny Castle with a view to arresting him. He disappeared on Tuesday, and left the police lament- ing. How he got away was a mystery, but—" oh, what a surprise I"—it was found yesterday that he had returned, without so much as giving the policemen a chance. The gentlemen in blue are looking very blue indeed, for they have come to the conclusion that Mr. Pyne is making use of an underground passage. It is very unkind of Mr. Pyne to laugh, so to speak, in the face of the law.

The "New York Herald" states that the Rev. Dr. Parker proposes, on his return to England, to .interview Mr. Gladstone with a view to sending an account to America which is to be paid for in solid cash. It says a proposal to make terms in advance was received in a note, to which Dr. Par- ker's private card was pinned. We suspect that Dr. Parker will be called upon to say ‘,‘ an enemy hath done this." An enemy, getting possession of his private card, might certainly write a note and attach the card. Dr. Parker has done foolish things at times; but we cannot think that he has made such a fool of himself.

There is a local story told of Dr. Parker which has the right ring with it. Perhaps some of our readers will be able to confirm it. Some years ago he was waited upon, in London, by a deputation from Warrington, with a view to inducing the great man to preach sermons for a special occa- sion. He was got at after considerable difficulty, and listened to their request; but when the name of the town was mentioned, he exclaimed—" Out of the question !—Warrington !—Why, I couldn't hang my hat up in Warrington!" .

William Tracy was brought before the Newton magistrates. on Saturday, for being drunk and dig- 1 orderly. It seems he has been there, and still would go; so the chairman put the question to him --" Why do you come here so often ?" "Because," I added William nodding his head at the constable, "it was the bc:bby that fetched me here." Just so; William would never have gone there so often if he had been left to please himself. It is to be hoped the chairman was satisfied with the infor- mation he obtained. Instead of fining William 5s and costs, he ought to have let him off for answer- ing so truthfully.

Lord Rosebery made a capital speech at Oldham on Tuesday night. We should advise those Liberal Oaionists to read it who have laid the flattering unction to their souls that his lordship was coming over to their side. They will see that in so far as he comes near them, it is to run them through with the bright sword of his wit. Besides being telling as to style, the speech was powerful in argu- ment. The Duke of Argyll will wish he had said nothing about Mr. Fox and Lord Grey. Lord Rosebeg has knocked his inaocurateostatements all to pieces.

Perhaps the happiest hit at the Duke's lecturing and hectoring manner was made by Lord Rosebery in the followiag terms. Ho said:—" How did the Duke end his speech? He ended it, as usual, with an eloquent peroration—he deals largely in eloquent perorations—(laughter)—and he called on Almighty God to save Ireland. But even there he presumed to offer his advice (renewed laugh- ter). The salvation of Ireland was to be accom- plished by the methods and under the guidance of the Duke of Argyll (laughter)." After this, one is tempted to say with especial emphasis—" God bless the Duke of Argyll!'

Lord Clanricarde fignred badly in the cburt when his agent got damages against him; but will he not make bad worse by trying to reverse the verdict? The letter just published, which was written by Sir Michael Hicks-Beach when he was Irish Secretary, shows that the Government had a Plan of Campaign as well as the Nationalists. It was perfectly allowable, it seems, for the Irish Secretary to put "the screw" on to compel a landlord to reduce his rents to a reasonable level; but when the Nationalists sought to attain the same end it was "intimidation and robbery." However, we must say that Sir Michael showed some regard for the tenants. Whether he was quite consistent or not is another matter.

THREATENING A CHESHIRE PA/MM.—Mr Brad- ford, a well-known Cheshire fanner, who resides near CTrappenhal I, has recently been the recipient of a threatening letter, signed "O'Donovan Rossa," and intimating to him the advisability of getting a coffin, as a bullet would probably be put into him. Mr Bradford, who is a member of the Daresbury Highway Board, employs a large number of Irish labourers. The letter was not sent by post, but was stuck on the end of a pitchfork, which was placed where it would be easily discovered in the farm yard. Edward Marsden presiding, Miss Mary Jones, of Llan- beris, was unanimously appointed assistant mistress of the Beard School, situate at Aston. There were nine applicants for the pest. RUNCORN STARR BOWKETI4 BUILDINO SOCIETY.—An ap- propriation in connection with the first established society was held at the offices .of Mr. V. Handley, onMonday. Mr. John Wilson was chairman; Messrs. W. Booth and W. Cartwright, scrutineers; and Master W. Littler, balloter. The first number' drawn was 552, and being over the registered number, another ballot had to be taken. The nunibers of two members who are in arrear were nextdrawn, but at the fourth attempt Mr, John Hedley, of Widnes, became entitled to £2OO for l years 'without interest. • FOOTPATH OBSTRUCTION AT WIDNES.—MY Samuel Reed, draper, Albert-road, was summoned before Mr F. W. Earle • and Mr J. C. Gamble, at the Widnes Petty Sessions, on 'Thursday, to answer a charge of obstructing the footpath.—P.C. Porter stated that about half-past four on the afternoon of Monday, the sth instant, the defendant had upon the footpath in front of his shop six bundles of cloth, three parcels, and a large box four feet long and feet wide. The defendant -had been previ- ously cautroned.P.S. McGregor corroborated.—Mr Reed said he had no wish to break the law. A railway lurry had left him 15 cwt. of goods, and these could not be got into a draper's shop in ten minutes.—A fine of 2s 6d and costs was imposed. • INDIGESTION CURED by one box of Howell's Golden Herb

DEATH OF AN OLD WIDNF.9 TRADESMAN.—Many of our readers will learn with feelings of regret of the death of Mr. John Timmins, of Macclesfield, Cheshire. - Timmins, who had attained the age of 69 years, was for a period of twelve years a tradesman in Widnes, taking up his residence there when the town was yet in its in- fancy. He carried on the business of a boot manufac- turer in the shop in Victoria-road, at present kept by his grandson, Mr. John T. Poole, and the building, which is now. in the centre of the town, was then at the extreme outskirt. Since leaving Widnes Mr. Timmins had lived the life of h retired gentleman at Macclesfield, and his mortal remains were interred•on Monday, amid numerous demonstrations of the respect and regard in which he was held. •
