DIPCUSSION AT RUNCORN ON SUNDAY OPTINING OF MU- SEUMS.—The members of the Bethesda Nutual Improve- ment Society have devoted three of their weekly meet- ings to the discussion,of the important question—" The Sunday opening of museums; is it requisiteor necessary?" On the first occasion the subject was introduced by Mr. Arthur Higgins, who argued in the affirmative, and Mr. T. Lydiate read a paper in the negative. At the next meeting Mr. Beck opened the debate with a denial of the necessity for opening museums, &c., on Sundays, and Mr. Aikenhead replied on the other side. At the meeting on Wednesday last another interesting discussion took place, and at the conclusion a vote was taken on the subject, with the result that 11 voted for the Sun- day opening, and 17 against. Several members did not vote. . .

• WIDNES COUNTY COURT.—The only case of interest brought before His Honour Judge Thompson, at Widnes County Court, yesterday, was one in which A: Solomon, hardware dealer, brought an action against J. Rimmer, butcher, Victoria-road, to recover £l5 damages alleged to have been sustained by a breach of the contract he had entered into with the defendant. It appeared that the defendant was the lessee of a shop in Waterloo-road from a gentleman named Mr. Wm. Lloyd, of Manchester, who was the owner of the premises. In June last the defen- dant sub-let the premises to the plaintiff at a rental of 12s. per week, which sum Was paid regularly. Five weeks after this arrangement Mr. Lloyd distrained upon the plaintiff's furniture worth £35 for a quarter's rent owing by the defendant.—Hence the claim, which was allowed with costs. _ .

SUICIDE BY POISONING.—On Monday, at the Golden Ball, Moss Bank, Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy, coroner, held an inquest on the body of John McCririe, 57 years of age, who had lived at 8, Chatham-street, and followed the occupation of a blacksmith. The deceased had been living apart from his wife for some time, and on Friday last he went to the house where Mrs. McCririe was residing and induced her to give him a blanket. It Via.. 4 believed that he pawned the article, for shortly afterwards he purchased a quantity of laudanum from the shop of Mr. Stead, chemist, of Widnes-road. He stated he wanted the drug for a horse belonging to his son. Later he saw his wife, and told her that he had taken "a fatal dose." She searched him pockets and found a bottle labelled with the name of "Laudanum." but he died before medical aid arrived.—A verdict of " Suicide " was returned. .

TNE TALx OF THE 'T I,lm-I:Lowell's Golden Herb Pills.— Advt. RUNCORN SCHOOL Boartn.—A special meeting of this Board was held on Saturday afternoon. Mr Pritchard presided, and there were present Mr Lake. Mr Beckett, and the clerk (Mr G. Moss). The Board interviewed three candidates for the two vacant positions of assistant master at Greenway-road Board School. On the motion of the Chairman, seconded by Mr Beckett, Mr Joseph Short, of St. Saviour's' Liverpool, was appointed. The meeting was adjourned to Tuesday evening, when Mr Pritchard was in the chair, and there were present Dr MacDougall, Messrs Lake. Frith, and Beckett, with Mr Moss (clerk). A second assistant master was appointed In the person of Mr R. H. Marsh, of Acrefair Board School, Ruabon. On the proposition of Mr Beckett, seconded by Mr Frith, and supported by Mr Lake, the Rev James Baptist Gustaldi, D.D., was unanimously ap- pointed a member of the Board in succession to the late Father Fennelley. MARRIAOR AT WIDNAS.—The marriage took place at the Parish Church, Widnes, on Wednesday afternoon, of Mr. Tom Laws, the well-known athlete, and Miss Annie Anderson, only daughter of Mr. John Anderson, of the Railway Hotel. The ceremony, which was wit- nessed by a great many persons, was performed at two o'clock by the Vicar (the Rev. J. Wright Williams). The bride was given away by her father, and the bridesmaids were Miss Laws, Miss Burgess, Miss Edwardson, Miss Kiddie, the Misses Penny, Miss A. Lomax, and Miss B. Anderson. Mr. G. Kiddio.officiated as best man. The wedding breakfast was spread in the Baths Assembly Room, and was partaken of by upwards of 200 guests. In the evening dancing was indulged in, to the strains of Mr. Powell's quadrille band, and was kept hp with vigour until six o'clock next morning. The presents were both numerous and costly, and include a solid silver five o'clock tea service, from the members of the Trades- men's Select Dancing Class.

RUNCORN Beaux BOARD.—The monthly meeting was held at the Cemetery office on Wednesday. Mr. W. H. Rogerson presided, and there were present Messrs. J. Handley, J.P., R. Morris, a Taylor, H. Coleburn, and W. F. Salkeld (secretary). The Secretary reported that the interments for eight months ending November 25th numbered 231, corresponding period last year 210, in- crease 21. The fees received during eight months end- ing November 25th amounted to £254 12s 2d, corres- ponding period last year £204 18s 6d, increage £49 19s 6d.—The report of the Finance Committee, adopted on the motion of Mr. Handley, seconded by Mr. Coleburn, stated that the fees received during the past month amounted to £4O 10s 2d, and after paying wages the balance, £2B 15s 2d, was paid into bank. The committee had arranged with Miss Smith, of Whitley, for a renewal of her loan of £750 at 31 per cent for five years; and ac- counts amounting to £l7 12s 3d were passed for pay- ment.. It was also resolved to pay on loans interest amounting to £3l 8s 7d. ,There was no other busines of public interest. WE WILL RETURN the purchase money if one box of Howell's Golden Herb Pills does not cure you.—Advt.

WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD AT WORK.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Mr. G. IL Denby, clerk to the Widnes School Board, prosecuted a number of persons for not sending their children regularly to school. The usual penalty of 5s was imposed in each -case. Martin Curley, son of Thomas Curley. was committed to St. George's Industrial School, Liverpool. INQUBST AT RUNCORN. Yesterday, Mr. Worsley, the coroner, held an inquest upon the infant son of Thos. . Horton, 138, Gilbert-street. Dr. McDougall had made a post-mortem examination of the infant, which was only three days old, and stated that it had been prematurely born, and its respiration had been imperfect. A verdict according to this evidence was returned.—The Coroner strongly condemned the house in which the parents of the child lived, which was a cellar dwelling. &MGR ASSAULT ON A WIDNES CONSTAIILE.—At Whines Police Court, on Monday, Robert Murphy, a young man, was charged with assaulting and resisting P.C. Almond whilst in the ex2cution of his duty. At ten minutes past ten, on Sunday, the constable was passing through an entry leading into Tithebarn-street, Appleton, when he saw the prisoner standing in the shadow. He told him to move into the light or sonic person would fall over him, whereupon the prisoner struck the constable a savage blow on the face, blackening one of his eyes and bursting his nose. A severe struggle ensued, and ultimately the prisoner was with difficulty got to the Police Station. The prisouer afterwards told the ,con- stable that had he met him on Saturday he would have had something heavier than his fist.—The bench said the assault was of the most unprovoked character, and sen- tenced the prisoner to two months' hard labour. FaLcesiss AT WIDNRS.—On Monday, at Widnes Police Court, Mary Connolley, of Victoria-st. was charged with stealing a brush, worth is.. the property of Arthur Tra- vers, butcher, Anne-street, West. The prisoner was ' Seen to take .the brush away from the door of the prose- cutor's shop, and information being given to Mr. Tra- vers, he pursued and caught the thief. A fine of 10s., or ' seven days' hard labour was imposed.—James Moran, a young man of 32, Orford-street, was charged with stealing a bag of chaff, value Is. the property of Luke 'Kelly, marine store dealer, Midwc:od-street. The priso- ner stated that he believed that his mother hail paid for the chaff, and that the prosecutor had refused to let her have it.—The prisoner was informed that he had a law- ful remedy if that were the case, and he was fined 10s. orseven days' hard labour.—Frank Bayliss, of Penrith, and James. Bancroft, of Altrincham, were charged with having on Friday last, stolen a quantity of horse hair, value 10d., the property of William Williamson, farmer and milk dealer, Moorfield-road. The Bench considered there was a doubt in the case, and discharged the priso- ners. ,

A BRZTAL HUSBAND AT RIINCORN.-At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Peter Knight, a carpenter, who lives in King—street, was summoned to answer a charge of assaulting his wife Annie.—Mr. F. A. Lake, appeared for Mrs. Knight, and stated that the parties have been married for upwards of 12 years. During that period the husband's attentions had consisted chiefly of brutalities and abuse and neglect, and on an average he had assaulted her three times a week. On the 7th inst. the defendant went home about half-past six in the evening and complained that the fire was not bright, and that his tea was not ready, and wished to know why his dinner had not been of better quality. His wife retorted that it was because he did not work for it, whereupon the defendant struck her upon the head, and elevating _a three-legged stool, he threatened to kill her . . . . . . .

if she did not quit his sight. Mrs. Knight ran from the house and had since lived with her family at the home of her sister.—Mrs. Knight cocroborated the statement, and stated that during the past seven months her husband had only worked for two months, and her relatives has had to keep him and the family.—The defendant said his wife was always aggravating him, and that he only gave her a slight tap on the face.—The Bench described the defendant's conduct as disgraceful and imposed a fine of 40s. and casts I,os 6d., or in default two months hard labour. He was ordered to be bound over to keep the pace for six months in his own recog- nizances.

ASSAULT ON A WIDOW AT Wmcas.—,At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Honora Riley summoned John Campbell for assaulting her. Mr. Swift, of St. Helens, who appeared for the complainant, said she was a widow with five children, and carried on a small shop in Wellington. Since the death of her husband, several years ago, she had kept lodgers, and amongst her lodgers were two brothers of the defendant. The defendant was annoyed because he thought that one of his brothers was courting the complainant, and on Saturday night he went into the house of a neighbour, named Mrs. Tobin, where the complainant was. He told her that if what he heard was going on, was true, he would kill his brother, and followed up his words by striking her a number, of blows upon the side of the head. She fell to the ground, and while she was lying there he kicked her, and she became partially inierible. He after- wards went into her house and caused a disturbance.— Several witnesses confirmed this statement, and Mr. Knowles, solicitor, contended that the defendant was acting in the interests of morality by preventing his young brother from marrying this woman of advanced years. It was alleged that the complainant had thrown a 21b. weight at the defendant, the missile coming in contact with his head.—Mr. Earle (chairman) said be- cause a young man was courting a woman old enough to be his mother was no reason why the defendant should assault this woman, and he would have to pay a fine of 30s and costs, 14s, Jr go to gaol fora month.
. - - MYSTERIOUS DISAPPEARANCE ON A. BOATNIAN The mysterious disappearance of a flat captain, named A.:•-berton, of Sankey Bridges, has been re- .. . .

ported to the police, but tip *to the-present nothing has been heard or seen of the missing man. It ap- pears that Atherton took a cargo to Widnes, and docked in the Widnes basin. Here he unshipped, and took on a fresh cargo. Everything was ready t-) sail by Wednesday, and it was intended to sail that night, but Atherton did not turn up. Inquiries were made, when it was found that he had not been seen since early on Wednesday morning. As he was regular in his business habits, it is surmised he has fallen into the basin and been drowned. The basin WAS emptied, but no vestige of the man was to be seen, and it is now supposed he must have fallen into the river. He has a wife and eight chil- dren, who depend upon him for support. GAS INQUIRY AT MANCIIIiSTILIL—The "Gas World" says :—As a result of the statements made in the "Gas World" by Mr. Alderman King, of Manches- ter, arrangements have been Made for an investiga- tion with regard to the quality and illuminating power of the Salford gas. To a meeting of the Town Council on Wednesday the Gas Committee reported that Mr. .J. Paterson, engineer and mana- ger of the gas department of the Warrington Cor- poration, had been engaged to test the quality and illuminating power of the gas manufactured at the three stations in the borough, and thab Mr. Alder- man King had consented to allow tests to be made .at the same time at his mill in Salford, and other- wise to assist in the inquiry in any way in his power. It ishoped that the tests made by ' such a competent expert as Mr. Paterson will have the effect of settling the point in dispute.

div.head: RUNCORN BIGAMY CASE.
div.p: A RUNCORN BIGAMY CASE.

At the Leigh Police Court, on Monday, a woman named Alice Clarkson, of Atherton, was charged on remand under a warrant with having committed bigamy at Atherton by contracting marriage with a Man named James Dickinson, an operative spinner, her first husband, John Hulse, of Winsford, being alive. From the evidence adduced it appeared that Clarkson was married in May. 1857, to Hulse, at Runcorn Parish Church. About two years ago she married for the second time, at Bolton, a man named Clarkson, who had since died. William Rose Bury, a waterman, of Man- chester, stated he was present at the first marriage of Clarkson, but after that he saw Hulse on very few occa- sion t as they passed in their boats on the canal, and pre- vious to being called as a witness in the case he had not seen him or defendant for 28 years. The prosecutor, : James Dickinson, said he became acquainted with Clark- son about 12 months since, and during their courtship, which extended over that period, she represented herself [as a widow. She said she had been married twice before, ' but both husbands were (lead. He married her at Ather- ton Church in February last. It was stated by a woman named Caroline Murray, residing in 'Bolton, where:de- fendant formerly lived, that she had a conversation with Clarkson about two years ago, in the course of which she said that Hulse was living at Runcorn. At the close of the evidence, the Bench committed Clarkson to the Liverpool Assizes for trial.

WIDNES LOCAL BOARD. The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on Tuesday. Mr. F. H. Gossage presided, and there were present Messrs. Carey, W. W. Gocsage, D Wright, J. 31idw0od. R. Cook, F. Heyes. G. Taylor H. Onskell, jun., J. Houghton, S. Sadler, T. Handley J. T. Allen (clerk), T. lligginsort (surveyor), and I Carr (gas engineer). RENT FOR AN OUTLET. A letter was read from the office of the Duchy of Lan- caster intimating that the Board would have to pay an annual rent of £1 in respect of the proposed outfall sewer in the river Mersey. • INFECTIOUS DISEASES. A letter was read from Mr. S. H. Hartley, clerk to the Prescot Board of Guardians, who, in reply to inquiries respecting the treatment of pauper cases, said he was directed to suggest for the consideration pf the Local Board the propriety of not making a charge for the maintenance of persons in the Widneslnfectious Diseases Hospital where the persons were too poor to pay. The Rural Sanitary Authority would doubtless pursue this course if other local authorities did the same.—The Chair- man said the cest should come out of the rates of the Guardians, and not from rates levied by the Board.— The letter was referred to the General Purposes Com- mittee.

GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE. The minutes of this committee contained the report of the engineer, who stated that he would direct their at- tention to the damage the gas and water mains and ser- vices have sustained through the sewering operations

whi6h are now in progress. In Lugsdale-road a 3-inch water main, running alongside the trench, broke off through being insufficiently supported, and a consider- able length of it fell into the hole. This occurred on a Sunday, and consequently a large quantity of water was wastod,before a man could be found to shut it off. In Victoria-road an ltinch gas service crossing the sewer trench was left unsupported, and when the ground set- tied, assisted by the steam roller, the pipe, almost a new one, was broken. The gas escaped, and passing through the newly filled in earth, made its way into the sewer and up through the gullies to the cellars of the neigh- bouring property. The mean rainfall for the month had been 1.085 inches, and the water in stock on November 30th was 6,378,846 gallons.—The minutes were approved on the motion of Mr. Gaskell.

div.head: HIGHWAY 177130.
div.p: HIGHWAY 177130.

_ The Highway Committee recommended that the Sur- veyor bc instructed to prepare plans and estimates for the paving, &c., of the back passage behind Parr's Bank.. It was also recommended that three lamps be fixed in Milton-road—The minutes were adopted.
THE HEALTH OF THE TOWN AND THE WASTE HEAP NUISANCE.

The Medical Officer of Health reported to the Health Committee that during November there had been 85 1 births and 70 deaths, being at the rate respectively of 34 and 28 per 1,000. Nineteen deaths occurred amongst children under one year, and 17 amongst children be- tween one and five years. Zyrnotic diseases caused six Ideaths.—The Nuisance Inspector reported that there had been six fatal cases of zymotic diseases ; enteric fever and diarrhcea, one each; and measles, four; Several cases of typhus and typhoid fever and one case of small Ipox had bsen report d during the month; all these were pauper cases, and the Union officers were attending. Disinfection and isolation had been attended to. The small pox patient was convalescent, and was discharged on the 2ad inst. After considering the letter of the Local Government Board with respect to waste heaps, which has appeared in these columns, the committee re- commended that the depositors of alkali waste be re- questa-1 to provide the necessary drainage, and to cover the waste with soil or cinders to the depth of at least 14 Inches, and that they be allowed two weeks in which to make the necessary arrangements.—Mr. Cook moved, and Mr. Houghton seconded, the adoption of the min- utes.—Mr. Ueyes moved an amendment that if deposi- tors fail to do so within the time named. be Messf:lpen- heim and Malkin instructed to take legal proceedings to restrain such offensive deposits. Mr. Heyes said there was not a person with a nose on his face that could not contradict the statements that the nuisance had been abated. He did not perceive any diminution whatever, and it was time the. Board took action.—Mr. Wright seconded the amendment.—Mr. Gaskell pointed out that the nuisance was caused by the oxidation of the waste, and said that cinders would be worthless in preventing tbis process taking place. Soil would be infinitely superior to cinders. The inspectint -contended that at present the best practicable means were being adopted for the purpose of preventing a nuisance. Under these 'circumstances Mr. Liaskell -considered that the best course for the Board to adopt was to ascertain from Messrs. Oppenheim and Malkin, their exact legal posi- tion with regard to the matter, and then have an inter- view with the depositors of waste. He believed the Board had power under the Public Health Acc to prevent Ithe deposit of waste where it was o be injurious to health, and certainly alongside a public railway sta- tion, and near domestic dwellings, was not a fit place.— Ultimately the committee's recommendation and Mr. Heyes's amendment were withdrawn, and Mr. Gaskell's suggestion was adopted.
FINANCE COMMITTEE.
On the recommendation of the Finance Committee accounts amounting to £4,798 Os 8d" were passed for payment. The proceedings then terminated.

WOUNDED WITH A CAlsr AT WIDNES. At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, before Mr F. W. Earle and Mr. J. C. Gamble, a labourer, named , Thomas Price, who lives in Regent-street, Runcorn, was charged on remand with unlawfully wounding Michael Lever, of 42, Princess-street, Runcorn.— Lever is a labourer at the works of the Alkali Company. and on Saturday evening, the 26th November, he went into West Dank Vaults, Church-street, in company with a man named Walter Davies. The prisoner and a man named Pendlebury were together there. Pendlebury had several canaries in a paper bag, and in a conversation respecting the birds, Lever expressed the opinion that they were no good, and that they would not live until Pendlebury got home. The prisoner thereupon threa- tened to give Lever a slap in the mouth." Lever then left the house, but had not proceeded far when he heard the prisoner behind him ask "What do you mean." He turned round, when the prisoner struck him on the head twice with a.brea.kfast can, and he fell to the ground. He was taken home by Walter Davies, and was confined to bed for a week. He had suffered great pain, and was now in a very weak state. These facts were corrobora- ted by several witnesses, and Dr. Nealan said he had at- tended the injured man, who was suffering from a con- tused wound on the left side of the head, and penetrating to the bone. An artery of the scalp was divided, and he had lost a considerable quantity of blood. He fainted twice whiLst the wound was being dressed. He was not out of danger until 6th Dectenber, and was now-so weak that he could not go to work for a week. When taken in eustody by P.S. Clarkson, the prisoner said "lam not guilty. It was done accidentally. It was done in swinging my arm round- to get away from him."—The prisoner was committed to take las trial at the ridxt Liverpool Assizes. Mr. Lake, solicitor, Runcorn, who appeared for the prisoner, applied for bail, and prisoner was allowed at liberty, himself in £5O and two sureties of £25.

RUNCORN PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH. FAREWELL TO THE PASTOR. In connection with St. John's Presbyterian Church an interesting yet somewhat melancholy event, took place on Monday evening. Owing to the delicate health of himself and family the Rev. Evan Williams had resolved to seek . renewed vigor. and fresh fields of labour in the sunnier clime of Australia, and the congregation amongst whom he had laboured and made himself beloved, assembled to bid him farewell and God speed. The proceedings commenced in the recognised old English fashion of a tea party in the schoolroom, which had been appro- priately.decorated by the willing harids of Messrs. R. Harrop, F. Hewitt, Leyland, J. Dobson, T. Dobson, and J. Gunning. The arrangements for the tea had been successfully carried out by Mrs. Kirkham and Mrs. Fred Jones, and the good things provided were agreeably dis- pensed by Mrs. Williams, Miss Humphreys, Miss Taylor, Miss 'Raynor. Mrs. Warburton, Mrs. Robinson, Mrs. Hayes, Mrs. Booth, Miss Kunsan' Mrs. Harrop, Mrs. D. Jones, Mrs. M. Thomas, MM. R. Evans, Miss Dodd, and Miss Jepson. Subsequently an adjournment was made to the Chapel; and amongst the large audience were numerous members of other religious denominations in the town. The platform was also a very representative one, Mr. James Pritchard, the chairman, being suppor- ted lw the following local ministers :—The Revs. G. Wood and A. P. Watson (Wesleyans), J. D. Thomas (Congregationalist), and E. Hall (Methodist Free Church). From a distance were the Revs. J. Thomas 8.4. Liverpool ; E. Jermain, Wrexham; and J. Thomas, Thomas, Liverpool: there were also on the platform the departing pastor, Mr. John Humpreys, (Nottingham), and Mr. James Kirkham. After . the devotional ex- ercises, the chairman delivered a speeds in which he said the severance between pastor and people was oc- casioned by domestic afilic.tion. He was happy to say that no difference had arisen between pastor and people. Mr. Williams' ministry in that church was still appre- ciated to the same extent that it had been during the last 20 years (Hear, hear) and so far as he knew Mr. Williams was quite contented and happy in that sphere of labour.. (Hear, hear). To both pastor and people the severance was a painful one, and had arisen from causes to which they were bound to submit. The Rev. E. Jermain then spoke in a suitable strain and assured Mr. Willliams that he was leaving with their best wishes, and that those ho left behind would rejoice to hear of his usefulness and prosperity when he arrived on the other side of the world. The Rev. J. D. Thomas made a few encouraging re- marks, and said that for the past nine years Mr. Wil- liams had been a good neighbour of his ; he had always regarded him as a kind and genial brother. (Applause). They had been accustomed to exchange pulpits once or twice in each year and he had always found that his ministry was appreciated by his (the speaker's) people. (Applause). He wished Mr. Williams and family a pleasant and safe voyage across the ocean, and that he would have few storms and plenty of sunshine. He did not for a moment doubt that the success which had at- tended Mr. Williams' ministry in Runcorn would attend his ministry in Australia. (Applause). Amid the plaudits of the audience, the Chairman then presented Mr. Williams with a first class passage ticket for himself and family on the Orient line of Mail Steamers from London to Australia. The cost had been con- tributed by Mr. Niatheieson (Widnes), Mr. McKeehnie (Mayor of St. Helens), Mr. " Shaw, Mr. Gibson, Mr. Humphreys, Mr. John Pritchard, and him- self, the Chairman. (Applause.) On behalf of the the congregation, the Chairman also presented Mr. Williams with a beautiful illuminated address and a purse containing £3O. (Applause.) Mr. James Kirkham read the address as follows "To the Rey. Evan Williams. Dear slr.—The church at Run- corn, of which you have been the pastor for ;inwards of 20 years, desire to express by this address our earnest, sympathy Yiltliyou in this time of trial, in having through family affliction to seek a more genial elitnate, anr/ to assure you it is with feelings of deepest regret that we are obliged to acquiesce in the necessity that has arisen for your severance from the field of labour you have so long and worthily occupied. We gratefully acknowledge the faithfnlness of your ministry and fidelity to the Gospel of Jesus Christ, and that your teaching has been so richly exemplified in a oonsistent and pious life. which has borne fruit in the amity, peace, and goodwill which have characterized, without, intermission, the church over which you have presided for so many years. We feel that this expression of sympathy and regret is your jugt due, especially when we remember the earnestness and real you have always displayed in promoting any good work in connection with your own and other churches; and this has not been confined to purely religious matters, but has embraced other branches of labour calculated to advance the social and moral well-being of the various classes of your fellow-townsmen. We

_ desire to assure you that prayer without ceasing shall be offered to our heavenly Father, that the removal to another land may prove conducive to the health of yourself and be- loved family, and in your distant place you may ever realize that God is with you, guiding you by His counsel, and direct- ing you by His providence, an'd that every step you take may be ordered of the Lord is the eartfest prayer of the Church you leave behind in Runcorn. And though we may never be privileged to behold your face in the flesh, we trust that as the result of your 20 years' ministrations many will meet you in heaven and become bright jewels in the crown you will then be ready to cast at the feet of our Saviour, whom you taught so many to know and love. Signed on behalf of the members of the Church, W. B. GIBSON, Jaarts Paircaann, FRANCIS HEWITT, ROBERT BAITER ; JOHN EDWARD WARBUR- TON, secretary." The Rev. John Thomas, 8.A., of Liverpool, acting for the Lancashire Presbytery, then presented a purse containing £4O and an illuminated address, to Mr. 'Williams. The address read as follows : "Our dear friend and brother.—On behalf of the Lancashire Presbytery and other friends connected with the Presbyterian Church of Wales, we beg your acceptance of this address, to- gether with the accompanying purse of money, as a token of oar esteem and good wishes on the occasion ot your leaving this country for Australia. We deeply regret that your re- moval from amongst us has become necessary owing to the health of your children, and we sympathise with you in this heavy affliction most patiently borne. Our present prayer is that yourself and dear partner in life, and your children, may be preserved during your voyage, and that the change of climate may be attended with great physical benefits to you all, For 23 years you have been an ordained minister of our church, and for 21 years you have been the faithful devoted pastor at St John's, and during that period the church under your care has been fruitful in every good word and work. We desire to place on record our appreciation of your high moral character, your courtesy and gentlemanly bearing in all your dealings with your brethren, and your reauiness to assist in every good work. During the past year you have occupied with dignity and acceptance the position of Moderator of the Lan- cashire Presbytery. In this capacity you have been a wise counsellor; you have shown tact and judgment in the con- duct of business. We trust that the same kindly feeling and affection which surrounded you here may be enjoyed by you and yours in even greater abundance in your new sphere of labour, and that a door of usefulness may be opened for you in the ministry of the Gospel. We are, dear brother, yours in Christian sympathy, OWEN THOMAS, D.D., OWEN JONES, D.A, J. THOMAS, 8.A., Liverpool; Jolts' WILLIAMS, Chester; THOMAS P/lENNAII, moderator; EDWARD JERMAIN, secretary; EDWARD JONES, treasurer; EDWARD.!. BadtddY., Chester." _ _ _

—Tii-e-ftWEIT-o-nes made a few observation's on the per- sonal worth of Mr. Williams, and Mr. E. Jones, BA., of Liverpool, also spoke to the address. The Rev. Evan WiLliams,who appeared to be consider- ably affected, then returned thanks for the unexampled and undeserved kindness shown to him by all concerned that evening. While here his family had passed through trouble and sorrow, and had it not been for the sympathy and prayers of those about them, he was sure he should not have been there that evening. He thanked the speakers very heartily for their Christian sympathy and for their kind words, and also the congregation for the manner in which they had treated him. (Applause.) He did not think that there were better people in the world than the people of Runcorn—more true, more honest, more liberal than the people of Runcorn. (Applause.) The members of the congregation had shown great kindness and sympathy with him and his family in their trials, and he was pleased to refer to the kindness dis- played by the Rechabites, who had presented him with a beautifully-framed motto of the Order, and who had promised that somebody should meet him when he ar- rived in Australia. (Applause.) One could not help but recall things that had taken place during the past 20 or 21 years. Then there were about 37 communicants, and it was encouraging to think that there were exalt 100 communicants at present in connection with that church, young people full 'of zeal, full of life, and full of energy, willing to lay themselves &ern to the service of the Master. (Applause.) He believed they were, with- out exception, teetotallers. (Applause.) They would be able to carry out the various meetings until some one took his place who would carry on the work far more successfully and effectually than be had been able to carry it on. Again, he askea them to accept his warmest thanks for their kindness, and the kind words which had been spoken, and which would remain engraven on his heart during his lifetime, and he did not think he should forgot them when he passed away-. (Applause.) Suitable speeches were afterwards delivered by the Revs. E. Hall. G. Wood, A. P. Watson, and J. Calvin Thomas, and Mr. Humphreys. It should be stated that the addresses, which were handsomely framed, were written and illuminated by Mr. James Orr Marples. The emblem of the Order of Rechabites, to which Mr. Williams referred, bore an inscription, stating that it was presented by the members of the Union Tent, No. 215, 1.0. R., as a token of their respect and esteem, and of their appreciation of the service he had rendered in connection with Rechabitism.

div.head: STREET GAMES AT RUNCORN.
div.p: STREET GAMES AT RUNCORN.

Before Mr. John Brundrit and Major Harlahurst, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Frederick Griffiths (17), Geo. Gatley (14), and Geo. Albert Williamson (9), were charged with playing a game named "Tick" in Bridge-street on the Ist inst. to the annoyance of the passengers thereon. P.S. Woolley and P.C. Potts proved the case.—The former said he had received numerous complaints from the tradesmen of the nuisance caused by boys like the defendants. Superintendent Hollings- worth said it was annoying to the police to have to summon these boys, and it must be annoying to the Bench to hear them, but complaints were con- tinually coming into the office that people could not move about the town without being almost knocked down by boys in their rough games.--Mr. trundrit said the boys had no right to play in the public streets, and they knew it; and future offen- ders would be seriously dealt with.--Williamson was dischargesl, and the other defendants were each ordered to pay costs. ss. 6d.—Ralph Clay (14), pleaded guilty to having, on the 3rd December, un- lawfully thrown stones in Greenway-road.—P.S. Woolley proved the case.—Mr. Brundrit said the practice of stone-throwing was very dangerous.—A fine of 6d. and costs, Ss. 6d.. was imposed.

div.head: MR. J. T. BRUNNER, M.P., AT CHEETHAM
div.p: MR. J. T. BRUNNER, M.P., AT CHEETHAM
HILL:

A meeting of the Cheetham Hill Liberals was held at the Victoria Hall, on Wednesday evening, and was addressed by Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P. There was a good attendance. Mr. J. W. Southern occu- pied the 'hair, and he was supported by Mr. J. Brooks, Dr. H. J. Roby, Mr. E. J. Broadfleld, Mr. R. P. Hewit, Mr. B. L. Green, Mr. B. J. Robinson, Mr. J. Holliday, Mr. lAlex. Porter, and Mr. J. R. Hatch (hon. sec.) The Chairman, in his opening remarks, - said that he was pleased to preside at a meeting upon the Irish ques- tion, when one of the number present had experi- enced and had gone through some of the rough work that was at present going on in Ireland—he referred to Mr. Brunner—(cheers)—who was fully alive to all the wants of the Irish people. They were face to fa ue with things in Ireland which was a disgrace to Ireland, Eng- land, or any other civilised country. The Coercion Act was to put down "Moonlighters," sedition, and crime, and not to imprison such men as Mr. O'Brien, M.P., and his steadfast followers. (Cheers.) Mr. BRUNNER, M.P., in addressing the meeting, met with a cordial reception. He said that as the represen- tative of the Northwich division he was pleased to ad- dress the present meeting. Without flattering, himself, he said that he had been returned for a noble constituen- cy, not opposed only by a Coercionist, but by the son of one of the most influential landlords of Cheshire. (Hear, . .

hear.) Apart from all that,he was present to give the Manchester people a few of his experiences in -Ireland. With regard to the riots at Mitchelstown he laid the whole of the blame on the Government political reporter, who caused a disturbance by his appearance at the meet- ing. Enough had already been said of that incident, and it was useless for him to dwell upon that disgraceful act any more. Mr. O'Brien had been thrust into prison, and in a very few days hence he (Mr. Brunner) expected that Mr. Dillon, M.P.—(hear, hear). would also be COM- mitted to goal for a somewhat similar crime. Mr. Dil- lon and he had stood together during the Mitchelstown riots, and he witnessed his friend rush between the police and the mob to rescue and Are his imperilled countrymen from the bayonets of the Irish constabu- lary. .(Hear, hear.) Mr. Brunner then dwelt upon the distress which existed on the estate of Lord Clanricarde, and said that Mr. Balfour was an able agent after Lord Clanricazdes stamp. Mr. 13alfou'r was always ready to put people into gaol, and seemed to be at home in that sort of work. It was a sad day for Ireland and England whmi Sir M. 1 Hicks-Beach stepped out of the Tory Government, and Mr. Balfour stepped into the vacancy. (Hear, hear.) In ' conclusion, Mr. Brunner asked the meeting to give their support to the inventor of the finest Home Rule scheme that was ever brought before the country--(cheers)— which would without doubt 'bring forth peace, pros- perity, plenty, and content both to Ireland and to Eng- land. (Cheers.) Dr. H. J. Ron Y moved the following resolution : " That this meeting protests against the action of the: Government in suppressing public meetings in Ireland by armed force, in treating as criminals many high- minded and patriotic men, and in depriving Irishmen of their constitutional rights. It expresses also its strong sympathy with the numerous distressed Irish tenants who. unable to pay their e7.-erbitant rents, have been cruelly deprived of the home.iteads Created by their own labour, and it declares its opinion that the continuance of the coercive policy of the Government is calculated inevit- ably to destroy all hope of restoring law and order, and. to postpone indefinitely the peace and prosperity of Ire- land. _ _ _
Mr. E. J. BROADFIELD seconded the resolution, which was (varied unanimously. The proceedings then terminated.

A LIVERPOOL STEAMER IN COLLISION.—The Liverpool steamer Barden Tower reached Middlesborough on Thursday, and reported having been in collision with the J. M. Charnley, of Barrow, off Flamborough Head, on Wednesday morning. The latter vessel sank with the captain, mate, and able seaman.

div.p: A COLONEL SAVED.
Mow A MEMBER OF HER MAJESTY'S SERVICE
ESCAPED DESTRUCTION.

An all-wise Providence provides a climate in each quarter of the globe particularly suited to the in- habitants of that section. and a change from one to another usually causes disorders of the internal or- ganism that must be carefully watched, else the re- sult will be the contracting of a fatal disease. No worse change is made by an Englishman or Scotch- man than to go from his native country to one like India, where the sun shines down with tropical heat for ten months in the year, and where every method of living is so entirely different from what has been the habit at horn'. It is then that the change is felt most, and aggravated forms of local diseases are the result. The liver and kidneys are the most sensitive organs to these sudden changes, and in them nearly all diseases have their origin. India being in reality a possession of ours, naturally many of our people have interests there, and are obliged to reside for many years in that country of enervating and debilitating climate. How many have returned home, after a few years' residence in the East, total wrecks of their former physical selves? How many, in fact, have returned only to be buried in the soil of their native lands? It is to these and their friends that we "bring glad tidings of great joy ;" for one poor sufferer, after years of residence in India, coming home without health or hope, has been enaided to return, with his physical and mental powers restored, and with a knowledge of how to avoid future ?troubles of a similar char- acter. A reporter a few days ago called in at Mrs: J. B. Gillander', View Place Rouse, and during the course of conversation the case in point was referred to, and as it proved both interesting and valuable, we only deem it a duty to give the facts as much publicity as possible. Lieut.-Col. 3. W. Hindle, of Her Majesty's service, sta- tioned in India, came home in November, 1883, suffering from kidney and urinarydiseases, thoroughly unfitted for service. Mrs. Gillander states that he remained in her housetinderphysician's treatment until Jnly, 1884, but that he received no benefit whatever ; in fact, when they all went to the country, Colonel Hindle was unable to walk, and had to be carried from place to place. The shampooing treatment was tried, with temporary relief, but no lasting benefit. She then advised him to try War- ner's SAFE Cure. After taking three bottles an improve- ment was noticeable in his condition. Continuing the treatment his improvement was so great that in "July, 1885,he went before the Army Medical Examiningßoard, with the hope that he was sufficiently recovered to be al- lowed to rejoin his regiment. He failed to pass the ex- amination, but had his leave of absence extended tvo years. He continued the use of the SAFE Cure urftil January, 1887, when he again went before the Examin- ing Board, passed, and at once left for India to join his regiment, six months beforehis leave of absence expired, taking with him a quantity of the SAFE Cure, to use after his arrival. Col. Hindle told Mrs. Gillander that he be- lieved he owed his life to the use of Warner's SAFE Cure. Mrs. Gillander states that she herself has used the medi- cine for dyspepsia and general debility with the greatest benefit. In substantiation of what is given above, the following letter from Col. Hindle is given. The Colonel Hughes re- ferred to 14 his old commander, now retired and living at Plymouth. "32, Fountain Ball Road, Queen's CIOSS, "Aberdeen, IV,ES " Febrtuzry hu $B7. "Colonel Hughes was so amazed at what he calls the marvellous cure' in my case, that he has promised to try Warner's SAFE Cure himself. I mean to make every one try it. I hear that General Rutherford, when he heard that I had passed the Medical Board, has been telling (hem all at the club here what a wonderful effect the SAFE Cure has had on me. I stood all my long journeys without the slightest fatigue. J. W. MEDLE, Lieut.-Col." the OAP of Colonel Hindle is not an isolated one, al- though a severe and stubborn one; still, there are thousands of similar cases that have been cured by this medicine when the patient observed the directions strictly, as did the Colonel. The remedy can be had of all chemists at 4s 8d per bottle, or direct of the manufac- turers, H. H. Warner & Co., 47, Farringdon-street, Lon- don, B.C.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Alderman Chandley. DRUNIENNESS.—James Barker, farmer, Lymm, was fined 10s. and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment, for hav- ing been drunk on Knutsford-road, on Saturday morning whilst in charge of a horse and cart. Mosoay.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Sutton), Alder- man Davies, and Councillors Greening and J. Pierpoint. DRUNEENNESS.—For this offence Thomas Knox, Cath- erine Eason, James Foy, and Sarah Burke were each fined ss. and costa. ASSAULT. Thomas Miskell, wiredrawer, for having been drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-street, on Saturday night, and having assaulted P.C. Jonston, Nl-0.8 fined 20s. and costs. DYSTITIVRING TEN PBACE.— Thomas Kelly, John and James McCrone were mil ordered to find a surety for their future good behaviour, they having been found guilty of having disturbed the peace. DI-mous DRIVING. —John Duckworth and Thomas Cooper were each fined 5s and costs for this offence, committed in Buttermarket-street on the 4th inst. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE PAOSACITTIONS. Mr. George Riley, School Attendance Officer, prosecuted the follow- ing persons for neglecting to send their children to school, and the fines mentioned were imposed :—Seth Travers. Howley-lane (third time), John Stringer, labourer, Old-road, Latchford; Walter Tolley, forgeman Rank-quay; Joseph Thomson, forgeman, Watkin-st. ; John Sl‘Cean, forgeman, Friars' Green; Thomas Wright, Glasshouse-row, Bank Qua-, ss. each; and Sarah Davies, Foundry-street, 2s. 6d. TUESDAY.—Before Councillor Francomb. BEGOING.—Thomas Rigby was sent .to prison for seven days for this offence. WHDHESDAY.—Before Mr. John Fairclough. BEGOLVO.—Micheel Costello and John Hewitt, who were brought up on charges of begging, were discharged with a caution. FRlDAY.—Befere Mr. John White and Dr. Gornall. DRUNICENNESS.—For having been drunk in Bridge- street on the night previous, a man named Robert Cross- ley was fined ss, including costs. MAINTENANCE.—An order was made upon Joseph Grice for him to contribute is ed per week towards the main- tenance of his mother. CauaLTY To A Cow .—James Shaw was charged on a summons with having ill-treated a co*, on the 29th ult., at Warrington Fair. Inspector Stambridge, of the Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, gave evidence to the effect that on the morning of the day in question he saw defendant in the fair in charge of a number of cows. Defendant had in his hand a stick, with which he was beating the cows, and he struck one of them over the head and nose six or seven times. De- fendant, who, as an excuse, said that he was drunk at the tune of the occurrence, was fined 5s and costs.

Lymy PETTY SESSIONS. FRlDAY.—Before Messrs. P. Stubs, C. Lister, and W. Long. CHARGE AGAINST A POLICEMAN.—WiIIiaM Foden, a police officer, stationed at Heatley, was summoned to answer a charge of being the father of the illegitimate child of Annie Elizabeth Walton, a single young woman. Mr. P. Davies appeared for the complainant,andMr.W.H. J. Jenkins for defendant.—Mr. Davies stated that he had been consulted in this case only within the last few days, and he at once advised the complainant to take out sub- poenas for necessary witnesses. It had been found, however, that she had not had time to take out these sub-poenas. He, therefore, asked that the case might be adjourned.—After some consideration, it was decided to adjourn the hearing of the case till next Friday. The question of costs of the adjournment which was raisad was left over. CHARGE AGAINST A PITSLICAN.—Thomas Marsh, .land,- lord of the Bridgewater Arms Inn, Lymm, was charged with having, at one o'clock on the morning of Saturday, the 26th November, unlawfully sold intoxicating liquor during the time the premises ought to have been closed. Charles H. Marsh and James Marsh were charged with having been on the premises on the occasion referred to. Sergeant McHale said that at one o'clock on the morning referred to, he Was passing the Bridgewater Arms when his attention was attracted to the house by geeing a light in the bar. He watched for a short time and heard sev- eral people inside. He heard one ot the men say "Fill these glasses" and he afterwards heard money jingle. He heard other remarks which seemed to be directions to bring liquor. Sergeant Harrington and P.C. Ardem , also gave evidence. Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins, who defended said that on the night in question the three defendants, who are brothers, were settling up sernil monetary trans- actions and this accounted for the jingling Of the money, but there wa.s no liquor paid for after 11 o'clock.—The bench dismissed the case at the same time 'remarking that the. police were perfectly jn.stified in bringing it for- ward. DRUNKENNESS. William Brown, for having been drunk and disorderly on the 13th November, was ordered to pay the costs. 4s ed. POACHING.—James Harrison was charged with having trespassed in search of game on the land of Mr. Joseph Taylor on the 3rd December. It was stated that the de- fendant came across the river Mersey, in a boat, from the Lancashire side, and he was seen to take a rabbit from a snare, and also that several other snares were found on the land. He was fined 30s and costs, or, in default, one month's imprisonment. STEALING CARDS.—Edward Brazendale; a lad, was charged with having stolen a pack of playing cards from the shop of Mr. T. Ardem, of Lymm. He pleaded guilty, and was ordered to receive 12 stroke with a birch rod.

ALLEGED THEFT OF A •TIORSE.—A lad named John NT, Fielding was charged with having stolen a horse and t valued at 50s, from a stable at Agden Bridge, on the 14th November. The horse, it appeared, belonged to William Wood, of Stockton Heath, and after it had been stolen it was found in a knacker's yard at Newton Heath. At the latter place the'horse had been sold by a man, and Fielding, on being apprehended, said he had been given a shilling for leading the animal. On the application of the police the case was adjourned.

WIDNF.S POLICE COURT. SATURDAY.—BefOTO Mr. J. Brock. A VAGRANT.—Henry Smith a tramp, was sentenced to seven days' hard labour for begging. MONDAY.—Before Mr. J. Brock and Mr. T. S. Timmis. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—i7Or the offence of drunken- ness, the following were fined :—Patrick Towey, David Jones, David Plant, Peter Keogh, William Glynn, Geo. Swindles, and John Cullen.—Catherine Owens, of Vic- toria-street, pleaded guilty to having been drunk and re- fusing to quit.thc King's • Arms, Anne-street West, on Saturday, and she was fined lOs and Osts, or 14 days in ' default.—For creating a breach of the peace in Lunts Heath-road, Farnworth, on the 30th ult., Martha Brad- shaw was bound over to be of good behaviour.
WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. Tnnasnar.-1-Before Mr. E. H. Earle and Mr. J. C. Gamble.

VAGRANCY.—For begging in Albert-rd. on the previous day, John Wood, a tramp, was committed to gaol for seven days. DRUSEENNESS.—Thomas Smith, John Lynch, Catherine Lyncn (25th appearance). John Moss, and Edward Ford were each fined for the offencelof drunkenness. WOULD BE AT THE WEDDING.—Martin Glynn, a young man, was charged with being drunk in Victoria-road on the previous night, at half-past eleven. The prisoner, it appeared, was attempting to force himself into the Baths Assembly Room, where a wedding was being celebrated. A fine of Ss and costs ;.vas imposed. •
RUNCORN rErry SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. John Brundrit and Major Hazlehurst.

DArmic AND DISOIDERTY:;I;;;Fay was fined 10s. and costs for having, on the 27th November, in Fryer-street, used obscene and profane language.—Mary Conway, 18 years of age, was fined 10s. and costs, 15s„ for hay- ing been drunk and disorderly in Salkeld-square on the Ist December. FELONY.--Jonathan Greaves, a rough-looking charac- ter, was remanded on a charge of having;on Saturday night, stolen two pairs of braces, the property of Wm. Blythe, tailor And outfitter, Bridge-street. The prisoner was caught in the act by a man named William Furneval.

(Sr. lIRLENS.)—The return fixtures of these clubs was played en the ground of the latter on Saturday, when the Rees again proved victorious, winning by two goals, one try, and seven minors to True Blues nil. WARRINGTON WANDRREIRS V. FRODSIIAII.—Thi3 match wa.s played on the ground of the former on Saturday in rather dull weather. Both teams failed to put their full strength in the field, and an agreeable game remained drawn, Frodsham haying scored 2 minors to the Wan-

derers one. Sr. 'HELENS RECREATION (3rd) T. HALEI3ANIE This match was played at Halebank on Saturday. Two 25's having been agreed upon, the Recs. started the ball. In the first half Halebank scored five minors, and in,the second half two goals and one try; Halebank winning by two goals, one try, and five minors to nil. The decisions of the referee gave great dissatisfaction to the visitors. RUNCORN FREE WANDERERS IST TEAM Y. WRSTON Ponrr IST TEAM.—This match was played on the ground of the latter, on Saturday, and resulted as follows : Wanderers 2 goals, 12 minors, to 3 minors. The home team played a capital game, and for the visitors Moly- neaux, Davenport, Price, Jones, and Hughes were the pick of the forwards. All the backs played a fine game. ST. FIELENS REC.'S "A" v. WIDNES Sr. MART'S IST. —Played on the ground of the former, before 1,000 spec- tators, and after a fast and pleasant game resulted in a win for the Rec's by two tries and three minors to one minor. The teams were very evenly matched forward, St. Mary's having the best of the scrummages, but were overpowered in the loose; it was in the back play that the home team excelled. Young Gerrard played a good game, and secured both tries. Potter showed that he is fast developing into a first-rate player. RuNcoaN 2NI) TEAM Y. NEW BRIGHTON OLYMPIC.— The return match was played at Runcorn, before a moderate number of spectators. The visitors arrived late, it being twenty minutes to four before Brazendale started the ball from centre, and, owing to a feeble re- turn by Hockey, the home players pressed, and several touchdowns were conceded. Darkness having set in, the play was not discernible, the score at the firush being —Runcorn two goals, four tries, six minors, to Olympic nothing. Brazendale, Riley, land Lunt played well for Runcorn; and Venabl, Jones, Morton, and Edwards were most noticeable for the visitors. ' MANCHESTER RANGERS v. WIDNE.S,—Thig match was played at Platt-lane, Manchester, on Saturday. Hammet started the leather for the home team, and Barker re- turned with is run anoLkick into touch. Play was then worked into the home-half, when Farrel passed to Mor- ris, who made a good bid for goal, but a dead ball was the only result. The 'Rangers soon equalized by regis- tering a touchdown, and soon after added another. Par- lane brought the hall out of a scrimmage and passed to Hamnett, who dribbled dangerously near to the Widnes line, where he was tackled. A. Hamnett made a good drop at goal, but it failed, and the ball was brought in- to play again. On crossing over Smith restarted, and Parlane returned to centre. Plumpten had the ball passed to him from a scrimmage in the home 25, and thoughtlessly kicked forward, registering a touchdown,. and losing a golden chance. The same player shortly after added another minor point by a good shot at goal. The game ended in a victory for Widnes by one try and four minors to three minors. Teams: Widnes—S. Bing- ham, back; S. Morris, J. Parkinson, F..Plumpton, and R. Barker, three-quarter backs ; T. Wilkinson and E. Farrell, half-backs; W. Kiddie, J. Hardman T. Pen- nington, J. Gandy, W. Barber, G. Woods, .I:Sampson. and J. H. Smith (captain), forwards. Manchester Ran- gers—A. Dickson, back; H. Radcliffe' A. Hamlet, and W. G. Sabin, three-quarter backs ; W. Parlane and S. S. Taylor, half-backs; Herbert Ha,sleham, H. Hamnet, g, Pollard, E. Mee, J. Jones' E. 0. Barrow, A. M`Dougall, J. Bradshaw, and Harry Hasleham, forwards. WIDNES RECREATION Y. SCOT-LANE (WIGAN.)--These clubs met in the semi-final of the West Lancashire Junior Cup Competition on Saturday, on the ground of the St. Helens Club, the Recreation winning by five points to two—a try and a minor to two mixers. The game was very rough throughout, and very little science was dis- played by either side. Scot-lane had the advantage of the incline in the first half, and at the outset pressed, a good run and judicious punt by Orrell causing the ball to be scrimmaged within the Recreation 25, Bradshaw, however, retaliating with a strong run and kick. Some severe loose scrimmaging gave Scot-lane an advantage, M'Cririe stopping a combined rush of his opposing for- wards in a daring manner. The Rees' forwards dribbled up the hill, and, aided by Bradshaw,Grundy, and Smith, the leather was taken over the line and a minor registered, Scot-lane disputing the poipt. The Wigan representatives went off with a dash and had the best of the struggle for a time, ultimately compelling Widnes to touch down. Scot-lane, although playing up hill in the second half, did most of the pressing, the Recreation conceding another minor. A scrimmage within five yards of the Widnes line gave the blues a fine chance of getting over, but Meadows, preferring to kick instead of feeding his threequarters, let it slip, and from a line out the Recreation rushed the leather to the opposite 25. Here the Widnes forwards, having the best of a scrimmage, the ball was taken over the line and a try allowed, Scot- lane again disputing: the decision of Mr. Varley, whose position was anything but a sinecure. Nothing further was scored after this, the game ending as above. Teams: —Widnes Recreation: D. M'Cririe (captain), back; W. 13racIshaw, R. G. Grundy, and R. Broome, threequarter backs; J. A. Smith and H. Barker, half backs; R. Robinson, T. Dickeson T. Waiting, J. Johnson, H. Daintith, J. Tomkies, S. Massey R. Charles, and H. Hewitt. forwards. Scot-lane: H. Eccleston, back; J. Fisher, T. Orrell, and A. Taylor, threequarter backs; D. Banks and R. Meadows, half backs; P. Turner, M. Phillips' J. Haslam, T. Peel's, J. T. Houghton, J. Roberts, R. Daniels, T. Haydock, and M. Telly, for- wards. MANN-INGHAM v. RUNCORN.—The return match between these clubs was played on Saturday, at Valley Parade, Bradford. Runcorn kicked off, and Fawcett returned, the first scrimmage being formed in the centre. *After a line-out, Fawcett got the ball at his toes, and kicked to the Runcorn 25, where Birmingham picked up and passed to Fawcett, who took a drop at goal, but the kick

was charged down, and a minor resulted. Neyrtmaafter the drop-out, had a free kick, but. nothing came of it. After Manninghani had notched a minor, the ball was passed out wide to Newton, who, dodging his men, dropped a magnificent goal, this point being got within eight minutes of the start. Some oven play then took place, and Speakman got hold at the line-out, and made a very fast run, but when a try seemed certain he slipped a few yards from the line andfell. Directly after, Man- 'ningham saved by touching down. Half-time was called with play in the visitors' half, the score being—Man- ningham, one goal and three minors, to one minor. On restarting, Faweetakicked off, the ball being returned by Faulkner to the centre, where some very even scrimmag- ing ensued. Runcorn were then hard pressed, and had to seek relief by touching down. The weather became very dark and misty at this stage, and it was with diffi- culty that individual play could be distinguished. Ilia miniaham passed to Fawcett at the centre, and the latter puttin„e on top speed, made a grand run close to the lino, whore 'he passed to Newton, but the latter was collared before he could get in. H. Hughes brought ' the ball away for Runcorn in'grand style, and reached the Man- ningham half. It was now the home team's turn to act on the defensive, and tho ball was passed out to Speak- man, who, however, repassed in the wrong direction, and a good chance of *coring was lost. Later on Speak- man gained possession, and ran in behind the Manning- ham posts. This easy place was missed by Wood, and time was then called' an even, fast, and interesting game being won by the home team by one goal and four minors to one try and two minors. Teams —.Runcorn:e T. Woods, back' ' . Speakman, Davies, and R. Wainwright. three-quarter baek; • H. Hughes and H. Andrews, half backs; Clarke, Lewis, Barns, Bowyer, Faulkner, W. Hughes, Gatiew, Riley, and Broady, forwards. 'Mau- ninghasn : Refasten, beck; Newton Fawcett, and Ayr- ton, three-quarter backs; Birmingham and Pocock, half backs; Calvert. Gill, Holmes, H. Jovrett, lioxon, Milner, Midgley, F. Wilkinson, and Waite, forwards. WARRINGTON T. SWINTON (" A " Teatea This specially-arranged exture was played on the Wildorspool ground on Saturday, in line weather. Great interest was taken in the match, and a large number of specta- tors assembled to witness the contest. The home team were very much weakened owing to the absence of several of their best players, whilst the visitors brought with them the best team they could get together. The home captain won the toss, and Scheles kicked off for the visitors at 3 p.m. prompt. Evans failed to make any return, and the first scrimmage was formed in the Warrington 25. The visitors had the best of two scrim- mages, but Whittle each time saved before they could get far. Thornley and Eyes each broke away from succes- sive line-outs, but Roberts got pea:melon from a scrim- mage, and kicked into touch in the Warrington half. Evans next attempted to get away, but he was held by Whitehead. Antrobus got away and kicked to the Swinton 25, and from a line-out Isherwood put in a fine dribble, Buxton saying grandly. The visitors, headed by Scholes and Hope, dribbled to centre, where Walsh passed to Sharpies, who kicked to Warburton, this player gaining a free kick, the hell going into touch near midfield. The Swintoniane worked the ball to the home line, Warburton saving well. The visitors pressed, and the home team were forced to concede a minor. Jolley dropped out, the ball going into touch near the centre. Antrobus next passed to Evans, who put in a splendid screw kick to the Swinton 25. Hudson got away with a nice run, but he was brought down by Bibby. Antro- bus again passed to Evans, who kicked, and following up prevented Whitehead from returning. Jonas put in a good kick into touch, and Antrobus next passed to Evans, who re-passed to Warburton, this player making a splendid long drop at goal, the ball going dead. Half- time was called with the score standing one minor point each. On change of ends Whittle re-started, play rest- ing in neutral ground. Antrobus passed to Warburton' who kicked well, and Eyes following up collared Roberts with the ball in hia hands. Whittle next passed across the scrimmage to Autrobus, this player mak- ing a dashing run, being brought down by Sharpies. Beans next put in a kick, and following; up stopped Whitehead from returning. Long kicks botvreen Whitehead and Jolley took place the ball eventually going into touch, and from the line- out Sharpies got hold and put in a lone kick, another minor point accruing to the visitors. 'Jolley dropped out, Eyes preventing Sharpies from returning,. Good passing titter:ea Whittle, Evans, and Bibby was wit- nessed, the latter playa l.rtli helf! by Sharpies. Creel= and Eyes next headed a dribble to the visitors' full back, who got possession and kicked to Evans, this player gaining a free kick and followed up, preventing any return being made. Whittle now passed to Antro- bee, who transferred the ball to Evans, the latter player making a good kick into touch in the visitors' 25. Moly- neux got nicely away from the line-out and passed to Thornley, and he to Unsworth, but the last-named player was hold by Sharplee. The Swinton men worked the ball out of danger and Roberta put in a long kick, which Jolley failed to return, Bibby having to kick dead. Jolley dropped out, Roberts returning to Thorn- ley, who put in a good punt. Whittle next passed to Antrobus, who throw to Evans. this player making a splendid kick into touch near tho visitors' line. War- nngton pressed their opponents, but could not score, and the visitors worked the ball out of danger. Whittle next kicked to Wilson who was held near the line. On time being called the score stood—Warrington. 2 minor points ' • Swinton, 3 minor points. Teams :—Warrington: Full back, Jolly; three-quarter backs, Bibby, Evans, and Warburton; half backs, Whittle (captain) and An- trobus • forwards, Molyneux, Craghan, Eyes, Donohue, Isherwood, Jones, Thornley, Bate, and Unsworth. Swims- ton: Full back, Wilson; three-quarter backs, Roberts, Whitehead, Buxton;and Sharplee; half backs, Walsh and Hudson; forwards. Scholes (captain), Rope, laothwell, Worsley, Hallam, Hall, Hardman, and Evans. • WARRINGTON V. DEWSBURY. The first-named team journeyed into Yorkshire on Saturday, to fulfil their first fixture with the representa- tives of thefamous " shoddy " town: The Warringtonians hed made an early journey, arriving at Dewsbury at 12- 15, but owing to the severe frost of previous evening, it was doubtful whether the match would take place, but an inspection of the ground having been made, it was decided to play, with the ultimate result that Warrington gained the victory by one goal to ene try and three minors. The Dewsbury team was without Lockwood, whilst from ,the Warrington ranks Fair 'Turner and Massey were absent. The first-named player was away through indisposition,and his position was taken by E. Bandies, who justified his selection by playing in first- class style. Appleton filled the vacancy at three- quarters, and Put in some useful work. At the adver- tised time, the teams made their appearetem on the Crown Flats enclosure, and the visitors were accorded a hearty reception, their pleasing appearance gaining a host of admirers. Garforth, having beat Barnes in the choice of ends decided to take advantage of the slope and the ;light wind which prevailed, and Bandies .was deputed to commence hostilities, the ball being returned to midfield. The first to make a movement was Redfern 0, Yorkshire county man and North of England player) who got in a neat dribble to the Warrington goal. Barnes repulsed this effort by a timely kick to Scholfield. who piloted hack to Appleton, the latter making a feeble return. Gradually the leather was removed from the proximity of the Warrington lines, but the Yorkshirei mon again threatened to be dangerous, Bandies being to , the fore. Each side had successively the best of it, but from A pack in midfield Warren effected a grand run I well into the Dewsbury quarter, Richards, however, nmei jug the ball back, a pass forward alrnest let the home team in. The Warringtonians, by spiended combined play, soon afterwards relieved the pressure, and after some loose play, Naylor made his mark in a favourable position. Stadden took the place, and the ball struck the uprights—hard lines for Dewsbury.' Jolley then got in a strong run,, but again the home team forced tha game on the Warrington lines, Berms only finding re- lief in conceding a minor. The drop out found play in neutral ground, and Povey distinguished himself by a neat dribble, to the Yorkshire goal. Speakman was next conspicuous by saving a rush of the Dewsbury forwards in grand style, and after pretty exchange kicking by Barnes, Hopkins, Rickards, and Nevins, the latter being col- lared close to the Warrington lino, Jolley strongly tack- lede Hopkins, who appeared certain' to score. 'he War- rington forwards played up with meowed vi ur, fore- most amongst others being Bandies, Rigby, and W. Dil- lon, and transferred play to the half-way flag. From a scrimmage formed here; Warren made a splendid pass to Barnes, who ran and put in a huge punt. Jolley, seeing an opportunity, razed up and secured possession; and eluding the opposing backs gained a meritorious try after a brilliant run from half-way. , Speakman was en- trusted with the place, and a grand goal was the remit. The ball was again set in motion from the centre, and Warren looked Like scoring after a brilliant run being. pushed in touch close to the goal line. Jolley made off, but his career was checked by Garforth. /the visiting team again threatened danger, but nothing else was scored from now till the call of half-time, the game then standing as follows—Warrington one goal; Dewsbury one minor. Garforth restarted, and the first to make a movement was'Barnes, who put in a tricky'run to mid- field, winding up this brilliant effort by punting to the 'Dewsbury twenty-five flag. The home backs now put in some neat passing, but Appleton safely held Rickards before he became too dangerous. The Dewsbury men now toox play to the Warringttnt quarter, but their efforts were neutralised by a sterling run by Davies, who transferred to Rigby, but Naylot was safe. Stadden forced the game on the Warrington lines, and Nevins saved be conceding a minor. Warren saved a rush at mid-fiela, and from theaucceeding pack Stadden passed 'to Iropldns, who was safely held by Jolley. Hopkins pit in a good kick, and no return being made, a scrim- mage was formed on the visitors' lineS. Stadden passed to,Naylor, that player rounded his opponents and gained a try after a brilliant run. Stadden tot* the place but failed to notch the premier point. Soon after re-start- ing, Rigby and W. Dillon were conspicuous by a smart dribble to neutral ground, and give and take play fol- lowed. It was fast becoming dark and the players were scarcely discernible, but a drop et goal by Stadden al- most reached its destination, a minor only resulting. The play from new up to the call- of time calls for no special comment,' each side striving hard to obtain another major point, but without avail, ' and after seventy minutes' pleasant* and interesting play, War- rington retired victorious by -one goal -to one try and three minors.

To beat a club of the standing of Dewsbury adds to the reputation the Warringtonians have already gained, and Saturday's victory ought to encourage them to try " freih field.a and pastures new." Barnes, Jolley, and Warren played in dashing style, Jolley's try being the result of splendid combination by the above-men- ' tioned trio. The forward diviaion ail worked willingly and unselfishly, and if special mention ought to be mad* none are more deserving than Yowl, Rigby, Davies, and Bandies. On behalf of the Dowsbury side Stadden, Hullah, Naylor, Bouthateti, Garforth de- serve notice. The following were the teams -- Warrington: Full back, Navies; three-gnarter backs, J...Jolley, T. Barnes (captain), and A. Appleton; half-backs, J. E. Warren and W. Speakman; forwards, H. Ashton, W. Dillon, T. Davies, R. Littlevrood, Wi Hayes, W. Fovey, E. Randles, E. Dillon, and J. Rigby. Dewsbury—Full back., Sohol- field ; throe-quarter backs, Naylor, Hopkins, and Rick- . ' ards half-backs, Staditin and Hullah; forwards, Gar- forth (captain), Stewart, Lorrytnan, Randall, Gee, Beck, Boothman, Redfern. and .Jackson. Referee, Mr. Jack- son, Wakefield Trinity. After the conclusion of,the match, the Warringtoniane were hospitably entertalled 'by the Dewsbury Club, and after spending a short but pleasant time with their new opponents, the Warringtonians returned home, having thoroughly enjoyed their fi6t visit to the county of many acres.

NOTEfc•ler THE WAY. The West Laneashiie Cup Competition has now passed all but ins final stage. On Saturday the semi-finals were played between Widnes Recreation y. Scott Lane (Wigan) on the St. Helens Recreation ground, when the Widnes- ion., won by a try and a minor te two minors; and Woodman Revers v. rootstock, whose encounter took place on the Wigan Rovers' ground, and ended in favour of the Woodman Rovers by two tries and four minors to a try. It has bean decided that the two winning clefts should meet in the final round on Bank Holiday, the 28th inst., on the Warrington football ground. The following team has been selected to represent West Lancashire in tho match with Westmoreland county on the 2nd January, viz.:—J. Pilkington (Aspull), back; J. Stevie' (Wigan) (captain), F. Shaw (Tyldasley), and W. Lund (St. Helens Recreation), three-quarter backs; D. Hulme (A-spull) and J. Pilkington (St. Helens Recreation) half backs; T. Hughes (Widnes), Holmes (Litherland), E. Wardle, Atkinson (Wigan), R. Littlewoocl (Warring- ton). J. Pyke (St. Helens Recreation), R. Lawson (Leigh), J. Lowe (Wigan Rovers), and J. Hampson (Tyldesley), forwards. Reserves Bingham (Wid- nes,. back; J. Roberts (Leigh), Plumpton and Parkinson (Widnes), throe-quarter backs ; W. Speakman (Warring- ton) and J. Mitchinson (Wigan), half back.; T. Heeketh (Aspull), D. McLaughlin (St. Helens), J. Hardman (Widnes), and J. Rigby (Warrington), forwards. The match with Cumberland has been declared off, as the Union found & difficulty in finding players willing to undertake so long a journey at the holiday (eason. The North v. South metal is fixed to take place to-day at Whalley Range. The following is the team•choscri to , represent North :--11. B. Tristam (Durham), back; F. T. Ritchie (Yorkshire), P. Robertshaw (Yorkshire), and J. Valantine (Lancashire),,, three-quarter backs • F. Boner (Yorkshire) captain and I. Mills (Lancashire), half backs; C. I ' nderton, H. Eagles, R. Seddon (Lancashire), C. Mather, Bedford, Ward, L. Hickson (Yorkshire), Cowen (Cheshire), and Cox (Durham), forwards. Re- serves :—Haslam (Ybrkshire); back ; J: Robertson (Lan- cashire), Morrison, (Northumberland), and Ash (York- shire), three-quarter backs; J. H. Potter (Yorkshire), half back; Elliott (Northumberland), Lowrie (York- shire), and Yierad (Durham), forwards. It was not generally expected that Warrington first team, which is just now weakened through the illness or injury of some of its beat players, would be able to hold , its own with Dewsbury on the York.shiremen's own ground, and consequently the admirers of the " wire- drawers " wore all the hotter pleased on learning that the pleasantly and keenly fought game of Saturday had been won after all, thanks to smart running by Jolley, and smart goal-kicking by Speakman. It it cannot be said that Warrington "A" tom aro still victorious, it can at least be send that they are still undefeated. Swinton evidently meant to pull down the colours of the home team on Saturday if they could, but in this intention they wore frustrated. Although the Sarintonians played four three-quarters, they did not go In so much for open play as might have boot expected, and, in fact, the game consisted too much of packed scrimmages to be of the highest interest. The home team was handicapped through the absence of some of its usual members ; had these been present it is more than likely that the result would have been the adding of another to their unbroken record of successes. Widnes scored their seventh successive win on Satur- day. They were "all out," however, to defeat Man- chester Rangers by a try, but it must be admitted that they did not display their accustomed form. The team chosen to represent West Lancashire against Westmore- land Is far from giving satisfaction. It cannot be argued with any show of reason that the best fifteen has been selected, and certainly the chemical town has not re- ceived justice at the hands of the committee. Farrel, who is one of the best half backs in the county, ought decidedly to have a place. The Runcorn club did not nominate; hence the name of a Cheshire player does not appear in the list. If to know that a game is lost by the most cruel mis- fortune is any consolation to the defeated, Runcorn had that consolation on Saturday, when Manningham ac- counted for them to the tune of a dropped goal to a try. Even many of the spectators acknowledged that by hard work and brilliant passing Runcorn had fairly earned a victory, but luck was entirely against them. On one occasion Speakman had eluded all his opponents, and was within a few yards of the lino when he slipped and 'fell, and a sure try was lost. Bowyer, a second team recruit, had also a clear course before him, but he did not uphold his reputation as a • • flyer," for be was overhauled and collared as though he had been standing still. Then the captain, after & smart piece of play, almost got in at the corner flag; but the culminating point in the misfortunes was reached when Speakman, having ground right under the post,Woods failed.at a remarkably easy place. How- ever, Manningham did their best to make their visitors forget their sorrow by genial hospitality afterwards, and the Runcorn team greatly enjoyed their first visit to Yorkshire this season.

ELOPEMENT AND ROBBERY IN DERBY -
SHIRE.
THE RUNAWAYS CAPTURED IN WARRINGTON.

A sudden, and to the parties most concerned a very unpleasant, ending was on Sunday put to the romance of an eloping couple who had taken up their quarters in Warrington. From what can be gathered, it appears that some time ago a man named Samuel Birks, a puddler by trade, who is about nine and twenty years of age, went to lodge at the house of William Wainwright; at Newbold Moor. Derbyshire. All went en well for a time, but it is said that it began to be observed that the lod- ger and Mrs Wainwright seemed to entertain some regard for each other, and, finally, what suspicions had been aroused were confirmed by the sudden disappearance of the t•o. As, however, they did not go away empty-handed, but took with them about two pounds worth of goods, principally cloth- ing, they rendered themselves amenable to the law, and the matter was in. du* course placed in the hands of the police. On Saturday Inspector Spinks, of the Warrington Borough Police Force, had occa- sion to call at a houSe on Town Hill, where, as it happened. the runaway &mplw were lodging, under she name of Smith. Soon after the:inspector had

a his call "Mr. anti Mrs Smith " left. their lod- gings, and the same day Inspector Hollingworth, of the Derby County Police, armed at Warrington, and );av,e to the .local police a descripiton of the eloping couple that heNvas in search of. This led to a visit to the house at Town Hill, where they had been lodging, when it was discovered that they had hurriedly left. Further search was made, and early on Stuithy morning Mrs Wainwright and her lover were found in lodgings at a house in Catherine-et., off Bewsey-road. Inspector Spinks at once pro- seeded to " interview " them, and' on his reacting out to them the warrant they admitted the offence with which they were charged. Mrs Wainwright; who is the mother of six children, emphatically stated that she wohld never live with her husband again, because, she said, "I love Sam (the lodger) better." She further 4eclared that she would "face death" for him, and, if he was sent to prison, that she would have him in the end, and would go through fire and water for him. After the arrest the runaway couple were handed over to Inspector Hollingworth, who took them back to Derbyshire. The stolen property, it may be added, was re- covered. ,
