SPEECH DAY. Thursday was Speech Day at this institution, and in the afternoon the prizes were distributed to the , successful students by Lord Winmarleigh, in the presence of a large gathering, of friends of the pupils, and of the local clergy and gentry. Before the terminal ceremony of the year's work of the school took place, a luncheon was served, at which the following ladies and gentlemen were present: —Lord Witimarleigh, The Hon. Ennio/. Wilson- Patten, Rev. E. X WillcOcks (head master).: Rev. H. G. Stnithi(second master), Mrs. 'Smith,. Mrs. Lyon, Mr. P. Stubs, Mr. and Mrs. W. Beamont, ,Mr. and

Mrs. John itylands, Mr. and Mrs. W. C. Jones, Mrs. Quekett, Mr. C. Taylor (Hong Kong), Miss Barton (Southport), Miss Smith, Mr. Shurrock, Mr. ' Hollowell, Mr. Thompson, and Mr. W. S. Woods, masters. At the prize distribution there were also present, amongst others: Dr. and Mrs. Gomall, Ser- gnat-Major and Mrs. FennellY, Rey. and Mrs. Canon Whitley. Mr. and Mrs. Gandy, Mr. and Mrs. Milling, Mr. and Mrs. Kenyon; Mr. 'and Miss Moore, Mr. and Mrs. Garnett, Mr. and Mrs. Eddowes, the Misses Oar-

land, Rey. and Mrs. J. J. Langha ,ro, Mr. Chas. Made- ley, Mr.. and ' Mrs. Dirties, Rey. S., Mrs., and Miss Wilkinson, Rev. 1 G. D. Wray, the Hon. and Rev. F. C. Cross, Miss Hood, Rev. 11. W. and Mrs. Williams, Major and . Mrs. _ . _ _._

• - Eitchts, Major kud. Mrs. O'Leary, Re-v. C. C. Elcum, Murd•ch. Dr, Mid !fn. Adams, Mr. C. H. McFall, Rev. gC. S. Stanhope, Canon and Mrs. Dodd, Mr. and Mrs. Garland, 'Rev. and Mrs. Phillips, Alderman and Mrs. Bur- gess. At the commencement of the proceedings the Rev. R. S. WILLCOCKS, M.A. the headmaster, who was cordially received, said that school had been for th o last three years a special centre for the Oxford Local Examinations, and the majority of the boys in the two highest forms were examined entirely by means of the printed papers used in these examinations, so that from the results attained the work of the school could be ap-

proximately compared with others of their own clais. Seventeen of the boys four seniors and thirteen juniors, had beon successfulthisyear in passing this examination, and had obtained certificates. It was interesting to note that of the four senior candidates three were dis- tinguished in the aggregate of language,s,three in religious knowledge, and two In mathematics. One boy .was ' second on the whole list in languages, third in religious knowledge, and tenth in mathematics. The total num- ber of distributions for both senior and junior candidates was sixteen. Five of the older boys in the sixth form were not entered for -the Oxford locals; as they had other examinations before them: They had all done honour and credit, bath to themselves and the schoel. A. S. Kidd, who was the head boy during the past year, had been suceessful in gaining in open competition—the Oliver Heywood scholarship of £soh a year—for two years, at the Owen's College, Manchester. G. T. Brun- arett, J. Henley, and F. C. Scotson had passed then- trance examination in arts (medical),or theMa:triculation Examination of the Victoria University, and were all three placed in the first class. .T. C. Fisher also passed, direct from the school, the examination known as " respon- sions" at Oxford, area has been admitted a member of Brasenose College. The other successes during the year in public exaimnations had been J. R. Preston, W. R. Fisher, and A. L. Knapman, medical preliminary, and J. E. 0. Johnson, law preliminary. Early in the year two of the boys were selected out of a very large number of candidates, after open competitive examinations, for Her Majertys service, namely, R. P. Jackson, as a cadet at the Royal Military Academy, Sandhurst, and J. C. Dewhurst, as an engineer student for tho Royal Navy, The reports on the schpol by the examiners appointedhy the Oxford Board were laid before the governing body at their last meeting, and met with their warmest approba- tion. He was requested to convey to the assistant mas; tars, by whose 'hearty co-operation with him their suc- cesses had been attained, and also •to the boys; tho congratulations ' and approval of the governors. The necessity of improving the school build- ings had been long recognised by the governors as imperative. Plan lad 'specifications were submitted to the Charity Commissioners in London for their ap- proval, and after some delay the work was commenced in the summer holidays. The three class rooms bad been enlarged, and the cloak-room accommodation increas ed and improved. Special attention had also been paid to the better lighting, heating, and ventilation of the rooms, and the newest appliances had been adopted with satisfactory results. They could now accommodate 150 boys, and the average number during the past year had been 125. He then asked Lord Winmarleigh to distribute the prizes and certificates. Such a tried and valued friend to Warrington as Lord Winmarleigh needed, he said, no introduction, and he was sure he was but echo- ing the sentiments of all present when he gave his Lord- ship a hearty welcome. (Cheers.) ' Lord Wissiatiteron, who met with a warm reception, said fie parents of the children Must have derived great encouragement from the belief that their children were not only being well educated, but were preparing them- selves for the new station in life to which they aspired on leaving that schgol, and the inhabitants of Warring- ton must derive pleasure from the Head Master's re- marks, because they must see that the school in which they all had taken so much pride for years past, was not only not losing ground, but was fairly gaining ground in the competition it had to stand with the rest of the edu- cational world. (Hear, hear.) When he looked hack to the earliest years in which he was connected with the school it was perfeCtly wonderful to him to note the great progress that had been mad? in the instruction which the pupils of the school received. He dared say ' his friend Mr. Benmont might recollect an old master of the school, Mr Boardman, in the early part of the cen tury. Well, he thought if Mr. Boardman had been asked to take the list of subjects be held in his hand into his schoolroom and asked any of his pupils to enter upon any one of them he could not have found a single one who could have gone beyond the most common classical language of that day, and he thought if he (Mr. Board- man) had been called upon to produce a scheme such as his friend Mr. Willcocks had done that day, exemplifying the statistics of the school, he would have almost fainted away (laughter.) They had now come to the end of fifty years of Her Majesty's reign, .and he saw that the liter- ary world were occupied in giving a history of the pro- gress made during thosefiftyyeara. .He'did not imagine it possible to name athrone subject in which greater pro- gress had been made than inithe education of every class of society. To begia with the elementary schools, toga through the private schools, the grammar schools' the great public schools and even the Universities it had been nothing leas than a positive revolution diet had taken place hi instruction. He recollected that when he went:to school; at-the terminal celebration they had a breaking-up supper, as, he thought they had now: but in his school da.vs it was accompanied with, good Latin song, wilh ' chorus to it, „With which they finished up their half year's labours. It was received with the greatest acolammation by .not only the school that he was at, but several others, and it was a proof that in those early days the same spirit in- spired the youth of that day which** had no doubt in- spired every one of those whom he saw in the gallery opposite him—that after a half-year's hard work and strict scholastic discipline they were not sorry to have recourse to a little home rule—(laughter)—and he did not believe that if Lord Salisbury Lord Hartington, or Mr. Goschen were present, and Salisbury, they felt so in- spired, they would find any fault With them for it. (Laughter.) As Chairman of the Governors of the

Schools, he expressed the great pleasure that he was sure it would be to his co-workers when he reported to them; at-the next meeting, the observations that had been made by the head master as to the prosperous state of the school. They must recollect that it was the duty of the Governors of the School to promote its interests, and to take care that a system of education was prac- tised in it which would enable the students to take part •in any profession, any 'branch of art, scienee, or commerce, or manufactures, in lwhich they might be engaged in after-life. They also hoped that his friend Mr:, Willeocks' and those with whom he was associated, would conduct the school in such a manner that the pupils should be not only dis- tinguished by their talents but by their conduct here- after. They had it in their power to asst very mate- rially in raising the character of the school,, not only by their talents, but by showing in after life that no person brought up at the Warrington Gratin/tar School could be guilty Of any dishonourable or dishonest action in life. They had only to look in Warrington now, amongst the most distinguished inhabitants of it, and they found that there was not one of them, as far as he knew, that did not do credit to the school in which he had received his eduction. He concluded by wishing them all a Happy New Year. (Applause.)

MISSIONARY MEETING AT WARRINGTON. A meeting in aid of foreign missionary work was held in Buwsey-road Wesleyan Chapel, Warrington, on Monday evening, when several addresses were given, and on the Sunday preceding serMons were preached in the chapel for the same cause; in the morning, by the Rev. E. H. Jackson, and in the evening by the Rev. „William Brookes. At the meeting the chair was occupied by Mr. William Barlow, who was supported on the platform, by the Revs. G. E. Young, W. Brookes, k. H. Jackson, and John Yonge. The CH.unms.x said that he had for long taken a deep interest in 'foreign missionary work, which was a great and gloriov work. They were following out the well-known motto of their founder when he said—" The world is my parish." They them- selves participated greatly in the blessings of the gospel, and they Were anxious that those who had not haard the Saviour's blessing should have that great privilege. Sometimes they met 'people who were sceptical. as to the -success of the missions. They said that too much money, and too many use- ful lives, were expended on them, when in our own towns, and at our own doors, they were surrounded with so much that 'required their attention. He i quite believed n home missionary work, but held that while they did the one they must not neglect the Other. (Applause.) . The Rev. Wm. littooms then gave particulars from the annual report of the society. Although the highest hopes of the workers, he said, had not been realised, there had been considerable progreas made with the work. Their mission operations were directed through the Mission House in London, and extended to many parts Of the earth. They had been trying to do something in Ireland, but had not got on very well there. It was a priest-ridden country, and he was afraid that much of the distress that obtained there to-day was largely owing to that fact. . They had Missions also in Germany and Austria. A considerable increase was reported in the Germ= mis- sion stations, and good work was being done in Austria. The society's operations had also been successful in Italy, Ceylon, India, and China, and efforts were being made to push the missions in Africa. The income, of the society for the year was £128,908 us lid, and the ex- penditure £134,992 13s sd, leaving a deficiency on the year Of-0,086 Is id, which, added to that of the pre- vious year, showed a total deficiency of £10,788 19s 11d. , Warrington circuit had contributed during the year the sum of £225 18s 7d, .and of that amount -ZlO5 13s 10d was raised in Warrington. (Applause.) - The Rev. G. E. YOU.NG expressed his deep interest in foreign missionary work. They did not set home mission work against foreign mission work; they believed both ' Ware necessary, and they could not discharge their obli- gations to Christ unless they tried to spread the know- 'ledge of Him. He believed that those men who were. carrying out the missionary work were \ good men and true, and he did 'not believe 'in those who had tried to shake public faith in them. (Hear, hear.) - They did not believe in going back, their motto was" Onward," and he trusted that that would be the motto of everyone in that circuit with regard to either home or foreign work.' (Applause.) The Rev. Jamas LEWIS (of- 'Bowdon) said that so long as they could point to the blessed rei4ults of their mission wprk, they need not waste time in answering those who were opposed to it. The work was practically only about one hundred years old, and when he thought of what had been accomplished since, notwithstanding many gigantic difficulties, he came to this conclusion— that when the history of Christian' missions during this -century came to be written, it would tell of triumphs more grand and .more glorious than any witnessed by the Church of Christ in any century of its history, not even excluding the century of Pentacostal days. (Hear', hear.). The Christian religion was enshrined in the affec- tions of the people who ruled the world, and Jesus Christ was indeed King of Kings. No statistics which any . society could produce would represent a tithe of the work done in India. and it was also prospering in Africa and other distant countries. The great Voltaire had declared that before the begin- ning of the nineteenth century Christianity would have ' disappeared fretri off the face of the earth. (Laughter.) They remembered what Mr. Hosea Biglew said, !' Never prophe.sy unless you know." (Laughter.) They hadgot rather far on into the nineteenth century new, andit was possible that Christianity mlit last six months longer. (Applause.) The Rev. JOHN* YONGE, who was received with ap- plause, said hemeed not sly a single word to commend mission work to them, foOhe supposed there was not a singip sceptic, present. SHOCKING BURNING ACCIDENT AT SANKEY.

A shocking law-fling accident that resulted in the death of a woman named Alice Kilshaw (66), a widow' who lived at Ivy House Farm, Cow-lane, Great Sankey, formed the subject of a coro- ner's inquiry at the Chapel House Inn, Great Sankey, on Wednesday afternoon. It appears from what can be gathered of the sad affair that the deceased was left alone in the • house on Sunday evening, her son John, who had gone to church, be- ing the last to leave her. After his departure she locked the door, and at that time there was a fire in the sitting-room and a paraffin lamp burning on the table. Nothing further is known of what took place until about half-past eight o'clock. when the servant, named Moss, aged 15, who had been on a visit to her relatives, returned. She was unable to gain admission, and on looking through the window she Observed 4 larger light than usual, and, convinced that something was wrong, ran to a neighbour's house, a distance of a quarter of a mile. The woman of the house (Mrs.Fairclough) returned with her, but as neither Were able to effect an entrance into the house, they pro- ceeded to the house of Mr. 'Henry Bate, farmer. Mr. Bate accompanied by Mrs. Fairclough and the girl Moss, proceeded immediately to • Ivy House, which they reached about halt-past nine o'clock. The girl was got through a window, and she then unfastened the door and the house was entered. The dead body of the deceased was found lying across the fender, and it was in a terri- bly charred eendition—the right arm, the right leg, and the lovrer part of her body being frightfully burnt. A chair on which Mrs. Kilshaw was supposed to have sat was on one side. of the fire, and her spectacles were placed on a Bible on a table beside her. It is supposed that she had been. seized with 4,fit, and, falling against the fire her clothes had become ignited. At the inquest, which was held by Deputy Coroner Husband, the following evidence was taken :—john Lu- shaw, farmer, Ivy Holll4o, Dow-lane, Great Sankey on of • the deceased), deposed that the farm' was m his mother's name. She resided at Ivy House, and was 86 years of age. Ho loft home on Su . day night about six o'clock, to f,:o to church. His mother was alone in the house,- and she then appeared as well as usual. It was sometimes her habit ,to lock herself in the house until either witness or the servant returned. When he got
back to tho hou.so he found his mother was dead,.—Emina

Jane Moss (16) servant to the deceased, said that she left Dry House on Sunday afternoon, and Mrs. Kilshaw was then quite will. Witness returned to the house about half-past eight _o'clock in the evening, and found the door locked. The deceased generally locked the door when left- alone.. Witness knocked, .but heard only a noise from the fire. She looked through the window and , saw the fire blazing, and she also thought she saw the deeessed lying on the hearth. Witness ran for Mrs. Pair- dough, a neighbour, and tried to get in, but did net em- ceed. Then they went for Mr. Henry Bate, and he helped witness through a window. Witness unlocked the door and let Mrs. Fairelough and Mr. Bate in. The house was then full of smoke. Mr. Bate and witness went into the sitting-room, and they found the body of the deceased in front of the fire, dead, and badly burnt. am:wer to Sergeant Devlin, who appeared on behalf of the police, witness said that deceased complained of a pain in her side that Morning.. She we.; not subject to fits.-=Henry Bate, Sankey Green,. deposed togcring With the previous witness, about nine o'clock on Bund97 night, to Ivy House. • Witness helped her through a win- dow and she opened the door. On entering , ,the sitting- room, ha found the deceased lying on the fender, quite dead. The lower part of her body was badly,bignt, seine portions being quite black. The head and upper `portion of her body were scarcely burned at all. Wit- ness did not think deceased had moved after falling, as she lay face downwards.—By the Foreman of the Jury . I formed the opinion deceased's dress had been caught on the " buffet ' of the fender.. By another the . De- ceased.was still burning when I Went into sitting- room.—The jury returned a verdict of " Accidental death."

div.p: OUR OUTRAGED LITTLE PUPPY DOGS. By " Mica." . ' Good-bye to all our peace of mind, • Good-bye to all hilarity, . Good-bye to even common sense, And sentiment and charity., Oh! what a mighty fuss there is, Oh! what a state .our laws are in, Wtien even little puppy dogs , Are often without cause run in. • Oh l Justice must be mad or drunk, Or drunk or mad, I don't know which, • It seems in such a bursting state— About RS full as any vetch. It scarcely can itself contain, It's over-fed like prize show•hogs, And vents it's callous choleric rage On harmless little puppy dogs. Ah, woe, it is a doleful tale ; , • It is too much, it is too bad, To think that at this time of year - Our pnpy dogs should all be mad! And 'tis a. cause of jwholesonie"grief— .. Each little dog should, oh! be a . k Sad victim to that dread disease That's known as hydrophobia! And monstrous muzzles- they must wear, , So that they may not bite us, oh! - Which; ta& epitomise their ba,rk, i. . That they may not affright us, oh! And now When carnal -puppy dogs Are-weaned, and would be guzzling • • Our tender flesh, 'tis wise that we ' Should straightway be them muzzling. Our "peelers" brave upon'their beats, • , Wi ; tt staff in hand so steady are, f ; , And e er are on the alert, , For " peelers" always ready are To capture anything that's loose— A pint or two of "feurpenny," And always very zealons are . To take it into custody. But latterly the " peelers' " hearts Are thumping hard in rapture, oh! A gallant member of the force • Had made a splendid capture, oh! Whirst on his beat with thoughtful face, And looks, enough to puwale one Oh! joy! he saw a puppy dog Thathad'nt got a muzzle on! It was a little dog," at large," As small a dog as you might see, , But "peelers" very cautious are: - And very cautious too was he. • He crept upon it unawares, As stealthily as any mouse, And heedless of all danger bore It bravely to the Station-house. Three days it yelled, three nights it howled, No owner ever came for it, And on the fourth they council held • And found to-live it was'nt fit: The dog was mad 7—of course it was: . Who would'nt be if they were served - In such an inconsistent way, • And treatment got they ne'er deserved? "To make assurance doubly st.iie " ,• They doubly charged the blunderbuss, - Then led the unwilling captive forth— He shivered hard, poor little cuss! • Oh! horror, let me close the scene, .. I cannot on much further go— • ', They let sunshine into that pup, And did a bloody murder, oh! ! ! 'Oh ! little dogs, and bigger dogs— Beware; beware; I say to you ; • Be sure and keep your muzzles on, , Or else the day you'll surely rue! For oh, our polimmen watchful are, And mighty cute and sly are you, . If you escape their vigilance-- • When once they've " sot " their eye on you Widnes, Dec. 13th, 1887.

div.head: 'TRAGIC WRECK OF A RUNCORN FLAT.
div.p: 'TRAGIC WRECK OF A RUNCORN FLAT.

Under the title of "A romance in Biology" in the. " Liverpool Mercury," en*Monday, R.M. writes an interesting account of the life led by the young married couple who are in charge of the Biologicat station on Puffin Island. He thus refers to the wreck of a Runcorn fiat. One day last month, two old men had come to be 'the guests of the newly-married couple. These were old rabbit catchers, sent by the landlord of the island to catch the "vermin "which infest the place. 'On that morning a strange looking cloud came 'creeping down the Welsh hills which lie across the Menai Straits from the island home. As the cloud seared the' sea line it burst forth in a tierce wind, which swept across the Straits, carrying before it -many of the helpless craft which were lying quietly -at anchor on the. Welsh coast. Some hoisted sail and bore away to safety or to destruction afar off ; but one unfortunate vessel, the Myra, of Runcorn, was blown helplessly across to where the sea broke in flying spume on the rocks of Puffin Island. The ,crew of the vessel consisted of two men and a boy of 15, the captain's son. One cable had parted at the anchorage, and the other anchor bad been •clragged for miles along the-sandy bottom. On the -edge of a sandbank, on the margin of the channel -which separlited the fated vessel from the rocky shore, a pause was made; the anchor hela for a few minutes, and the crew tried te raise a sail so as to adventure through the deep channel which cuts 'off Puffin Island from Anglesea. The keeper of the -island and the two rabbit catchers crawled along on hands and knees, clinging to grass and rock and thorny bush, to see if the vessel would escape; but, -alas, the anchor dragged again, and the vessel was lifted up on the waves and thrown helpless on the -web amid the boiling surf. With such force was she thrown down that a great moss-grown boulder of limestone, weighing many tons, was driven through her kelson, transfixing the hapless vessel as though she had been made of paper for a child's 'toy. One man got a rope cast round a jagged rock, which was only a few yards away, and'sec tired a peri- lous foothold. The boy was crossing the rope to reach the same place, when a larger wave than usual broke over the vessel, and dashed against the cliffs, bringing down many tons of the overhanging rocks with a thunderous noise. The boy was lost in the seething whirl of waters, and the father's bitter cry, "Oh. my poor boy," was all that reached the keeper's ears as he lay on the cliffs above The old rabbit catchers lowered the keeper over the cliff, and he managed to rescue the two men before the tide rose to overwhelm them, but the boy had been swept away. The sad party of cold, wet men reached the house of the young bride before noon. and she provided for the shipwrecked ones as well as possible. As the afternoon wore On, and the tide retreated, they found the battered body of the youthful sailor on the rocks below the house, and it was tenderly cared for by the bereaved father. They did not carry the little fellow to his home at Runcorn, nor did they bury him on the island, for the love of consecrated ground is strong in English hearts. They carried him across the deep " race " to Penmen churchyard, and buried him there, in one of the sleepiest old burying places ever seen. Many a poor, friendless, homeless sailor is buried in s nameless grace in that quiet spot. The church looks as though it might have been built during some recent century; but it stands beside, seeming to form part of, an ivy-covered ruin which dates back to the misty days of long, long ago. A pic- turesque old tower forms part of a kind of farm- :yard, and a bright-faced Welsh boy, looking out of the heavily-mullioned, ruinous, ivy-covered old towel, seemed strangely out of place in theae modern days. The graveyard is filled with lichen- 'covered old tombstones, and tottering relics of an- cient memorial stones; while the grass grows thick -and rank over all, suggesting the change in this earthly tabernacle which nurtures the green grass over the Fri-ayes. As the fat Welsh sheep cropped theluxuriant herbage in this country charchyard where the little sailor boy was laid to rest, one could but think of the words of that strong, true, 'though little understood, poet of these later days, who sang to his love of the transmutation of these eartbly bodies;— So when men bury us beneath the yew. Thy crimson-stained mouth arose will be, And thy soft eyes lush bluebells dimmed with dew; And when the white narcissus wantonly • "Kisses the wind, its playmate, some faint joy. Will thrill our dust, and we will be _again fond maid and 139 y.

BUFFALO BILL PISTOLS, dm. NOAH'S ARKS, with room for all! Small ones for 15 ani- mals; large ones, ON WHEELS, for 200 and 300. Hosts of Little Things for Little Girls and Boys with Little Purses. Boxes of Animal Carving, with Wood and Instruments complete. Fur Squirrels cracking nuts—the hardest nut to crack is SPRING-lIBEL JACK. Word-Making and Word Taking. 1,000 ordinary 2s. 64. boxes at Is. each. STORY BOOKS, the envy of Curators of FAIRY-LAND LIBRA- RIES. Halos of mystery surround Christmas Trees, and CHRIST- MAS-TREE ORNAMENTS kindle in every eye the light of happy memories; BOXES containing three Ilozen for Is. 941. BOXES containing twelve Sixpenny Articles 3.94. Nearly all large toys in miniature Windmills, Clothed Monkeys. Fur Par- rots Birds' Nests, Cupids. Caricature Figures, Animals in Wood, Clint, and India-rubber. In this Fair are MUSICAL PIGS, RABBITS—what right have we to eat them more than they have to eat us ° Horses on Wheels. COWS with voices and movable ears. WELSH GOATS that never pay tithes. RUSSIAN BEARS, fierce and angry at loss of prestige In Europe. THE LECTURE ON RITUALISM. Sir,—ln your report of my speech at Runcorn, on Thursday, there is a slight omission which most materi- ally alters the thing. Apparently a number of parsons came to interrupt, and Mr. Key asked if I believed in Apostolic succession. Your report says "Yes." What I said was "yes. only in so far as St. Peter's nolsle con: fession." I would refer Mr. Key to the great Isaac Bar- row's (D.D.) work on this sub]ect with which lam in. harmony.—Yours very respectfully, ROBERT FOULKES.

RUNCORN EDUCATIONAL MATTERS. Sir,—A great many remarks have beim inculo about the appointment of Mr. Moulton as Master of the boys' Board school in preference to Mr. Fletcher. I cannot but look at the matter in this way,— Mr. Moulton is known to his suppor- ters as a thoroughly good teacher, and one who has for years had to do with the class of boys that attend this school. Runcorn is his home and he would not be likely to look out for a better situation so soon as some others. Mr. Fletcher appears to be fitting himself for a position quite different from the one in question. He would probably be working hard with his Own studies, and would consider this poet a mere stepping st me to a better one, interesting himself little in either the place or the people. I think the Board did quite, right intlie appointment they mado.--Yours faithfully,!' JOHN SIMPSON.
Runcorn, December 7th, 1887._

- CORPORATION MUDDLING AT WARRINGTON. Sir,—l should like to ask what has become of the great Ratepayers' Association that was started with such a flourish of trumpets some short time ago. Why are they napping wh si such an important ekperiment is to be tried as a five-acre stone yard with the usual extras that generally fall to the lot f experimenting commit- tees ? (I mean the last fad of the Paving and Sewerage Committee of the Warrington Town Council). The present experimental Town Council want a little supervision. We have nearly every committee with a fad of some sort, all tending to the spending of the hard earned money of the ratepayers. We have the experi- ments at Longford and the collecting depots of the Sanitary committee. The total expense that property owners have been put to in converting these properties, and the amount spent by the committee out of the rates, would be something enormous if it could only be arrived at. There arc fads of the Street Improvement commit- tee such as Scotland-road and Bridge-St. speculations the general dodging about of the street lamps which never seem to be settled to the satisfaction of the committee; the Town Hall Parks and Bath commit- tee, with the pulling down of the Park Wall at a cost of—first £lO and then £400; the patching up the Baths at an outlay estimated to cost £2,000. Happily this committee has at la.st a drag put on them, and their ex- periments are waiting for, further development. The Markets committee by the elaborate blocking up of the new market in the centre by a so-called office, to the tune of several hundreds, seem to have a general desire to render valueless the original market structure. The Museum Committee have had their crochets, but thanks to the wisdom of an Act of Parliament that allows them only so much to spend, they try to cut the coat according to the cloth; but still they have over run the piper, and sadly want a philanthropist to die and leave them several thousands of pounds. Then there is the Gas Committee with the Longford mistake which to make a success has to be carried on at the expense of the original Mersey- street works, and that portion is to stand idle when the present plant wears out. The General Purposes Com- mittee has a fad for open spaces; for.instance the land in Howley, for which the Corporation pay £4O a year. The only benefit the town receives is to use it as a phce to deposit loads of snovr upon; it was so used last winter. - And now the Paving and Sewerage Committee are to have a brand new stone yard, which is to cast the rate- payers, as estimated by Councillor Wright, some £3,500. This, when correctly allowed far, will be nearer £5,000.; but what are a few thousand pounds to a little sleightsif- hand in hood-winking the ratepayers? The great ad- vantage supposed to be gained in carting materials from Bank Quay to the present stone yard will be more than counteracted by river dues, Ste. that can belevied from Bank Quay to the new site. This land has been offered to the Town Council before, and owing to its low situa- tion. Sze., it was refused by the Sanitary Committee; but now the Paving and Seworage Coratnittle, thanks to a little influence, can see a gold mine in it. Councillor Wright estimates that £1,250 will be all that is required' to be spent in finishing this site. I wonder what man that intended to pay his way would put a river wall for 200 yards is a substantial manner; wall round the five I acres with a 15in. wall (as the bye-laws require), Bft. to 12ft. high, with gates, &c.; culvert the present brook from llowley-lane to the river, putting in the necessary flood trap I suppose this is the reason the Sanitary Com- mittee advisethe purchase),raise the whole or thegreater portion of the land two or three feet; make sufficient roads through it, as no ens would attempt to have a steam roller passing up and down a quagmire, which the Reid would soon become ; build sheds, &c., and buy a steam crane and its usual sundries for the sum stated by Councillor Wright? I understand Alderman Davies is chairman of that committee. Why was not that astute gentleman in his place to put the bright side of the ques- tion? Was he ashamed of the bargain, as instead of costing £5O per annum extra, it looks like being nearer £l5O rr annum? Alderman Crosfield advises one town councillor to see the bright side of everything, as, for in- stance, his report of the Sanitark Committee. I wonder what sort of a bright side he would see if he had to pay the two rates due during the next month, with the limited means of some of the rappayers ? On some future occasion I may have a little more to say.— Yours, &c.,
JOSEPH DARBY.
Warrington, December 14, 1887.

THE FREE LIBRARY QUESTION AT WAR- RINGTON. Sir,—The letters on this subject signed "A Ratepayer," which have appeared in your columns, may be taken as an indication that there are still some not satisfied with the new arrangements. Indeed, I happen to know on the best authority the system of book-lending on hire just inaugurated is far from being generally appreciated. The gentlemen composing the Library Committee in the exercise of a wisdom more apparent to themselves than to outsiders, may possibly think they have made a large I concession. There are those, and not a few, who differ from them. A Free Lending Library was asked for, and is it for a moment to be supposed that the alteration in the method of collecting subscriptions, coupled with an advance of terms to non-ratepayers, will be accepted as satisfaction in full of their claim ? It would be a great mistake to consider the question settled. Shelved it may fle for a time, that isall ; it cannot be allowed to rest where it is. A temporary lull in the agitation is to be expected, but it must and assuredly will be renewed and continued till the perfectly reasonable demand for a Free Library is fully granted. The question of a Free Library for Warrington will have to be made a ratepayers' question. I am convinced that in no other way will a satisfactory solution be ar- rived at. The late Mayor, while professing all possible friendliness to the project, managed by a little judicious manceuvering, and an exhibitien of enormous respect for formal procedure, to delay an expression of the real opinion of himself and his followers till too late to be used on the last first of November. But there is another first of November in front of us, and it is highly pro- bable that by the arrival of this period, public opinion amongst the ratepayers of the borough will have ripened to the point of action. We may put to the credit of the recent agitation the , fact that it has revealed who are the true friends of the movement, and who are its foes, profession counting for nothing. I doubt not, sir, that in some odd corner of your note-book you have a record of a few facts of this kind, which, if need be, would be forthcoming about the middle of next October. Let me say, in passing, that I am not an outland out admirer of the happy family ar- rangement which seems to prevail in the Warrington Town Council, by which certain men, hanging on to the coat tails of others, are dragged in altogether irrespective of their capacity or fitness. In short, Mr. Editor, though my close acquaintance with the town dates scarcely fur- ther tack than your own, the conviction has been forced upon me that we have too few contested municipal elec- tions. The voice of the electors generally is not heard often enough or loud enough. Pleasant and economical and all the rest of it, it may be to avoid bitter and excited municipal contests, but I hold that worse things may befall a community. Therefore, I say to all who desire to have 'h Free Library, remember the first of November, and get ready for it in good time. Your correspondent complains, and justly, of the distinction made between those who have to take a penny and a guarantee to the Library before they can get out a book, and those who go with a yearly or quarterly sub- scription, and no guarantee to obtain the same privilege. I object to the unenviable distinction so persistently kept up between Warrington and most surrounding towns with respect to a Free Library. I have nothing to say against the guarantee, but I emphatically object to both the penny and the subscription. Further. as regards the doubling of the amount of sub- scription to non-ratepayers, and to those outside the borough, the compromise is a miserable one. It is a recognition that the Library Committee felt they were unable th justify their former position. But, having ad- mitted so much, they should have gone the whole length and refused any longer to lend out books at less than the ordinary charges made by subscription libraries. The people in question bear no part of the expense of pur- chasing the books, and purely as a question of right,they are not entitled to the use of them at all. While these have books, the ratepayers, whose money buys them, are deprived of their use. This looks very Brie injustice. What would be thought if the system were to be extend- ed to other commodities? Suppose, for example—if it were legal, which it is not—some wise Committee of our Town Council were, out of the rates, to set up livery stables and let out horses and carriages on hire, a small charge being made to those who found the capital to start the business, and who pay the working expenses year , by year, and a higher charge, but still only about half regular prices, to outsiders. There would be as much

sense and justice in this kind of business as in the zued§l of proceeding at the library. The result of all the recent agitation so far is not.lireat in itself, but it is valuable for what it heralds. The old system, which it has been sought to pull down, has stood some hammering. But having given the long-undisturbed rusty screw one turn, the remaining work will be easier, and perseverance will ultimately be rewarded by com- plete success.—Yours truly, ABRA CADABRA. December 6th, 1847.

A MISERABLE HOVEL AT RUNCORN. - At Runcorn Petty Sessions,"hu Monday, before Mr. J. Brundrit and Major Ilazlehurst, a labourer named John Critchley was charged under a warrant with having unlawfully and wilfully neglected to provide adequate food and clothing for his three children, whereby the health of the children was likely to be seriously injured.—Mr. W. H. Linaker prosecuted on behalf of the Board of Guardians, and pointed out that the prisoner hail rendored himself liable to fix months' imprisunment.—George Ward, the re- lieving officer, deposed that on the 2nd instant he ' visited the house of the prisoner in Water-street, and he found three children there, whose ahes ranged from eight years to four. Both the children and the house were in the most dirty and negh3cted condition. The children had had no breakfast, and the only'food there was for dinner was a Ptmss of crust about the size of his fist, which had been given by a neighbour. Beyond a bench, measuring live feet six inches by two feet six inches, and an old preserve jar, there was no furniture or utensils in the house. The only preparations for sleeping was a handful of filthy straw placed in the corner of one of the upper rooms, and this WM used by the eldest son of prisoner, a youth about 16 years of age. The bench was used as a ,bed by the prisoner and the three young children. The bodies of the children were in a dreadful state, and were scarcely covered with clothing. Thu youngest child was in a dreadful state. He (Mr. Ward) provided a dinner for the children, and subsequently removed them to the Workhouse. He ascertained that up to a few weeks ago the prisoner was in receipt of 24s per week at the works of Messrs. Wigg Brothers and Steele. but recently, through his bad conduct, his wages had been reduced to 16s per week.--Dr. Me- ' Dougall. the medical officer, described the filthy condition of the hovel and of the children.' added, however, that the children did not appear as if they were starving. The condition in which the children were was likely to injure their health. —lnspector Millington gave corroborative testi- mony.—The prisoner, whose only excuse was that lie was only in receipt of 16s per week, was sentenced to two months' imprisonment with hard labour.

THE FRE',AILING DISTRESS.—WHERE IS THE REMEDY? Sir,—lt appears that the present Tory Government are at- tempting to find a 'solution of the above urgent question by way of their old political panacea, i.e., force. The policeman's baton, and if "law and order ?" Tiernan& it, rifle bullets are the rewards which Lord Salisbury's minions bestow upon those of the unemployed and des- titute who venture to demonstrate their wretchedness rather than starve to death. Officialdom rightly suspects that to have thousands of half-starved people paradingthe streets of the wealthiest capital in the world may induce neighbouring nations to draw unfavourable cbmparisoa. And, besides, the wealthy class have a natural dislike to be brought face to face with the grim subjects of their greed and tyranny. So our rulers resolve not to find a cure for the prevailing inordinate distress, but under the cloak of "law and order" they attempt to drive this discontent under the surface—as the Tones always do—and then say that there is no dis- content or inordinate distress in the country. One often hears the clap-trap remark made by the enemiesof the people and by some ignorant working-men too, that the late Trafalgar-square demonstrations had nothing to do with the unemployed, but were chiefly got up by the Socialists. This is in my opinion all bosh, for where there is a great deal of smoke a fire is not so far off. But we have no need to go to London in order to find thousands of bona-fide working-men starving for want of work. It is to be seen daily on the roads in / Cheshire and Lancashire, whereas, at Lastham, hundreds under the fa/se hope that they are wanted at the Slip Canal works are turned away weekly. The misery and destitution by which England—and I may say the world—is at present devastated differ in kind from any known in the history of the past. Formerly the toilers suffered because they lacked the means of production. Now they starve because they produce more than the classes oan consume. This being so, it comas to pass that the worker every year receives relatively a less share of his own produce. In 1867 wages in Great Britain wore forty per cent, of the national income. Now they are only about twenty per cent. But this would not effect so. much were the rich able to donsiune their incomes, but they connot do so. What do they do with the surplus ? • Why, for the most tart they put it out at -rent or interest to the extent of I nearly two hundred' millions per annum, and thus all fthe toilers become the slaves of the drones of what is called aockty. Rent is the parent of interest. I say make the soil public property, and the capitalists will no longer be able to accumulate vast fortunes without having to work one hour for it. They would have to consumelbeiricapital like the ant and the bee. I know that I may be accused of advocating Mr. Henry George's theory on "Land Nationalization." Be it so, for lam of opinion that the existing system of land monopolization in England Is at the root of a great many evils, from which to-day her
MR. BRUNNER AT RUNCORN.

people suffer. The dangerous none-producing classes are steadily on the increase. From 1871 to 1881 the farmers, market- gardeners, and agricultural labourers of England and , Wales decreased by 149,701, and this is still going on. Landlordism is laving waste, not merely Ireland, but England and Scotland as well. It is like a huge upas tree which spread.s its branches over the land, and the only way to get rid of its npxious influence is to cut it

down. - Workingmen of England should always bear in mind that in helping Ireland's cause, they are virtually help- ing their own. For the settlement of the Irish land question, which is certain soon te be upon us—in spits of all Mr. Balfour's efforts to stop it—will, it is pretty evident, determine the issue between collectiveism and individualism for some time to come. And for this very reason the aristocracy which comprise the landlord class are resorting to every brutality in -their efforts to retain their hold on Ireland. They would be. no doubt, only too glad to stir up civil war, if they could so that they might have an excuse to resort to Captain Plunket's or- der of the day—" Do not hesitate to shoot them." The alienation of the people from the soil, or in other words, landlordism, accounts for nearly the whole of the enor- mons Skate debts of England, aye, and of Europe. War is the offspring of landlordism, and State debts are ' the outcome of war. It is not very long since the i favourite toast of "Country Squires' was "A longwar and a short crop." But they dare not say this to-day-s- -thinks to the Ballot, , Ono often hears teem those who support landlordism the argument adduced that the condition of the poor is as bad, or even worse, in those countries where the land for the most part is held by the people, than what it is in England; and I am not prepared to dispute it. 1 But as an argument, it will not stand a moment's reflec- I than, because in countries like Prince and Germany, 1 where peasant proprietors are as thick as blackberries in autumn, the people have to contend with the huge in- cubus of militarpsm on one hand, aid of Protection on the other;iv the former crippling their agricultural re- sources , drafting the peasantry to serve for seven years under a system which yields nothing in return; the latter restticting their commerce by' heavy tariffs. 'With free trade in land, I believe a vast change for the better vrould be brought about in the condition of the people of England. But while the gaunt spectre of want stalks through the land, a certain class will be content to join heartily in the old Tory refrain of : Let law and learning, arts and commerce, die; But spare us still---' Our Old Nobility." . The season of festivity will soon be here, when the sound of gaiety e,nd mirth will be heard from the halls and houses of the wealthy. But this alas, will jar dis- cordantly on the ears of a vast number this Christmas. I am, sir, yours, ere. rbrum.
Kingsley, Cheshire, Dec. 6th, 1887.

THE MANCHMER SHIP CANAL. WARRINGTON. About 50 new" tip" waggons that have arrived at Latchford Station, from Manchester, are as rapidly as possible being forwarded to Acton Grange. The new railway siding from Latchford Station to the canal is now in full working order. Materials still continue to arrive at Latchford sta- tin. At Acton Grange the work is proceeding at a rapfld rate, operations which were originally confined to a field on one side of Bell-house lane having now been extended to the field on the opposite side. It is stated that negotiations are being completed for the purchase by the Ship Canal Company of Arplev fields, the principal owners of which are Mr. T. H. Lyon, Lord Winmarleigh, and Mr. Legh. of Lyme. We understand that Mr. Squires will continue his supervision of the Warrington section of the canal.

RUNCORN. During the past week the neighbourhood of Old Quay has presented an animated aspect. The pro- cess of making the canal has not yet commenced, but every preparation is being made for a start. The chief work carried on is the discharging and loading of timber. In addition to the enormous quantity that has been brought up the river in flats. a steamer of large tonnage is being discharged of labout 500 tons of sleepers, and timber is being con- tinually dispatched up the canal to Manchester and other places en route. Mr. Thomas Kirkham, Run- corn, has secured a contract for erecting four wooden bridges across the Old Quay Canal at certain points, so that there may he means of communicaton be- tween each side of the canal during the carrying out of the great undertaking. IMAM. - -

During the week three locomotives, two portable engines, two large cranes, and other material have arrived at Irlam Station siding, on the Cheshire Lines Railway, ready for use in the construction of the canal. The superintendent of this section, to- gether with a large staff of officials, have taken up i their residences n the district, and are engaged making the arrangements preparatory to commenc- ing the work. Preparations for the deviation of the Cheshire Lines Railway at a point just below Irlam Station, where the line crosses the river, have al- ready been made, and the actual work, it is anticipa- ted, will not be more than eight or ten days before commencing. The staple industry of these districts —fustian cutting—is in a very depressed condition, and many able-bodied men now hope to find em- ployment. Implements have also arrived at Petri- croft goods yard for use in the works t Barton. Surveys are being made at Irlam for the construe- flea of a ballast line Which will run from the east side of the Irlam railway station on the Cheshire Lines Railway on to Warburton Bridge, where it is in- tended the Ship Canal works will commence in that district. By this line the contractors will be en- abled to convey their plant and material to the banks of the Irwell. Large quantities of bricks and other material are being carted to Hollins Green. where huts are being erected for the accommodation of the navvies who will be employed on the works. At present. not many hands are employed: and in all probability it will not be any different until the New Year.

„ SPEECII LAST NIGHT. Last night, a hastily-convened public Meeting of the electors was held in Bethesda Lecture Hall, for the purpose of bearing speeches from Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., be member for the division, and Mr. T. E. Ellis, M.P. for Merionethshire. Mr. Brunner, on Saturday last, returned from a briet holiday in Italy, and it was decided that he Would renew his acquaintance with his Runcorn consti- .tuents before visiting other parts of the division. In the absence of Mr. Frith, the chair was occupied by Mr. S. C. Beckett, and he was supported On the platform by Mr. Brunner, Mr. Ellis, Mr. John Brun- ner, junr., Mr. Kniveton, Mr. Clegg, and Mr. Handley (secretary to the Divisional Assodiation). The Chairman said they were all agreed that the sooner the Irish question was settledandthe better. He deplored very much the method the Government had adopted at the present time, and if they thought they would settle this important question by putting the Irish members in prison they were making the greatest blunder any Go- vernment ever made. (Applause.) Mr. Kniveton, in a vigorous speech, moved the follow- ing resolution: "That this meeting strongly denounces , the arbitrary, exasperating, and impolitic methods of governing our fellow subjects in Ireland; expresses its warmest sympathy with the trusted Irish leaders 130 W in prison; and emphatically pro- tests against the interference of the present Go- vernment with the freedom of the press and the right of free speech in England and Ireland—(hear, hear) —being of opinion that freedom of the Press, and the right of public meeting are the surest safeguards of our ' • just liberties, the firmest supports of just government, and the best guarantees of national contentment.” (Ap- plallse.) The key. E.'Hall, in seconding the resolution, an- , nounced that it was his first appearance on a political 1 platform. Mr. J. T. Brunner, M.P., supported the resolution. He said they could not expect from him an account , his stewardship, because he had only been in Parliament for about. a fortnight. (Laughter.) _But he wanted them to realise that he was elected not only as the oppo- nent of coercion, but as the' opponent of the representative of one of the largest land owners in Eng- land. The coming political struggle would be "the struggleof the workers against the idlers. (Applause.) Alluding to the Irish question, he said during the past twelve months he had seen not only Ireland, but a good many countries on God's earth, and he told them that, without exaggeration, he had seen no country in which it was more clearly evident that the people were opposed to the Government, and that the Government were op:- pressing the people, than in Ireland. (Hear, hear.) From the moment that he landed in Kingstown, until ' the moment he left again, he was under the surveillance of the police. (Laughter.) Outside Ireland, the I only place where lie had never seen a soli- tary policeman was in the City of Rome. He did not believe that the police were necessary to-day in Ireland, if they would only treat their countrymen in the spirit that animated their friend Mr. Hall. (Ap- ?louse). Mr. Brunner entered into a minute description I gf.the ,Mitchelstown affray, and said his visit to Ireland ma shown him that the people were on. the side of Home Rule. (Applause). The Irish-peOple were brand- ded by the Tories as liars and thieves, andwereabsolutely unfit to be trusted with their own affairs; but if we would only permit the Irish people to give play to that Christian sentiment which resided in their breasts, and we would withhold our hands, Christianity and peace would gain. (Applause). Sir Michael Hicks-Beach when in Irelanil prevented as much as possible , all cruelty ;on the part of the landlords to the tenants; but Mr. Balfour took to the work of eviction as if he loved it. (Laughter.) He (Mr. Brun- ner) was of opinion that if it had not been for the action of the Tory•party. in passing the Coercion Act that the landlords and tenants would have come to a friendly agreement before now. (Applause.) Mr. Brunner declared that the people of Ireland were treated with in- justice by the magistrates of that country, and that the Tory Government when the law Was on their side backed the law, and when the law, was against them they flouted the law. (Applause.) Mr. Brunner gave instances; and invited their attention to the actions of the Irish noble- 'man, Clanricarde. (Applause.) What was the value to society of a man who did nothing in this world but re- ceive rent; who never did a stroke of work from year's end to year's end for his living? It was the duty of all, whether Liberals or Tories, for every honest man, to protest against the folly and cruelty that was being car- ried out in Ireland. There was, in his opinion, no, other way of doing so than by adopting Liberal principle.s and following Liberal policy; Liberal princi- ples had been described as the spirit incarnate of right- eousness and mercy. Do you to them as you wish they should do unto you. (Applause.) Mr. T. E. Ellis. M.P., also supported the resolution, which was afterwards carried with enthusiasm.

SMALLPDX. AT SANKBY 'MMES.—We understand flint so far there have been three cases of smallpox at Sankey Bridges, which, have come within the knowledge of the rural sanitary officers. In each case, fortunately, the disease is of a mild type, and two of the patients are convalescent. BATEPA.YSII.B MEETING AT CADIBUSAD.—A special meeting of the ratepayers of the hamlet of Cadis- head was held•in the Wesleyan Day Schools on Saturday. Mr. W. Owen presided. The secretary. Mr. S. Barnett, explained that as the surveyor (Mr. John Howarth) was dead, it was requisite to elect someone to act as surveyor until March, 1888. Mr. A. Toft moved, and Mr. J. E. Winstanley seconded, a motion to the effect that Mr. George Rogers, being a ratepayer in the hamlet, and qualified to act, an 4 also being an executor under the late surveyor, be appointed to act as surveyor until the date named. The motion was carried. This was all the busi- ness. Cnorr HORTICULTURAL SOCIBTY.—A tea party, followed by a dance, was held at the Board School on Saturday evening, in aid of the funds of the above society. There was a large attendance. After tea Mr. F. W. Ball, chairman of the society, addressed those present, and thanked them on behalf of the contmittee, officers, and members, for their kind patronage, and hoped they would spend a pleasant evening, although the room was rather crowded. Dancing was engaged in until shortly before eleven o'clock, Mr. Burgess, of Newton, supplying the music. Apples and oranges were also distributed during the evening, and songs were given at in- tervals. SALE OF WORK AT LATCHFORD.—OrI Saturday afternoon a sale of work in aid of parochial and mission work was held in Christ Church Schoolroom. The sale was formally opened by Mrs Beamont, and amongst others present were Lady Greenall and the Misses Greene'', the Rev. B. B. Prescott, Mr. Bea- mont, Mr. J. White, Mr. B. Melville, &c. The stalls were well filled, 'and the room was decorated with Chinese lanterns and various ornamental devices. div.head: OUR FINANCIAL LETTER.
div.p: OUR FINANCIAL LETTER.

[FROM OUR OWN CORRESPONDENT.] 23, Old Broad-street, B.C. The fortnightly settlement which concluded on Thurs- day was apparently a very heavy one, but on the whole it has terminated very satisfactory, and prices Sr. i strong. As an example n values between the last set- tlement and the one just concluded, the following in- crease in prices in Home Rails exhibits the confidence that is returned and the support accorded to the finan- cial matters. On November 28th, the making-up price of the London and North-We.stern Railway was 164 k; this settlement it is 1824. London and Brighton:4 were 1154; this settlement 120*. Great Northern's last set- tlement 100 j; this 107. This hp:re:a:se in values applies not only to the lines cited above, but to nearly every railway stock in tke kingdom, and since thNi a still fur- ther rise has taken place in many of the liading stocks. In fact, the market has become perfectly jubilant. The immediate cause is attributed to the favourable outlook of the market, and the ease in money which is likely to prevail. The chief support is still bein evsn to mining invest- ments, copper companies leading the way. The readers of this journal at the beginning of October were advised of the low price at which Rio Tinto's then stood, and: the opinion was expressed that they were worth buying. With the gradual rise of these shares we have continued to suggest the profit that was to be made. Those who acted on this advice are to-day in the enviable position of having Increased their investments threefold; Rio Pinto's are quoted at over 21. In gold mining shares we directed attention last June to Moodie's, which were then dealt in at I.ls. To-day Moodie's can only be obtained for £3, with every prospect of their going still further. Last month Don Pedro's could be bought for lOs ; to-day they can only be obtained for 20s, and it is fully ex- pectol that before a month is past these shares will be worth £2 each. As a result of the buoyant feetinc, which pervades the market, the promoter has been induced to rush to the public with a hope of securing, at any rate, a small por- tion of the surplus capital which has been lying-idle for such a long time. Companies of all kinds, good, bad, and indifferent, are offered to the investor, from gold mines to bone boilers. Of the former, there are so many established gold mining companies in working order, the shares of whick can still be picked up cheaply, that we are strongly of opinion that speculators would stand a much better chance of making a profit in buying these than, in taking shares in new ventures, the future of which is an unknown quantity. A company at present before the public deserves more attention than the majerity of trading companies recently brought out. This is Henry IC. Terry and Co., the im- porters of the well known Richmond Gem and other well known makes of cigarettes. There is quite a rush for shares in this company.

Lone CHUIWIIILL AT STOCICPORT.—Lord Randolph Churchill addremed a meeting at Stockport on Thursday ' night. In the course qf his speech ho referred to the position of the Unionist party and the Irish question. Dealing with the legislative future, be said the Dartford programme had yet to be commenced, and he believed that neat session wonld be marked, by large reductions in public expenditure. Notwithstanding what had hap- pened a few months ago, he believed the Government were a government determined on economising, that the 7 would bring forward statesmanlike measures of legislation, and Would carefully avoid, foreign entangle- ments. div.head: CONCERT AT STOCKTON HEATH.
div.p: CONCERT AT STOCKTON HEATH.

On Thursday evening a concert was given under distinguished patronage in the Schoolroom, Stockton Heath, by the St. Thomas's Church Choir. The limited space was filled to overflowing, the audience including a large number of the gentry of the neigh- bourhood. A fashionable gathering and some tasteful Christmas decorations thus gave a cheerful and even

brilliant aspect to the roiim. The vocalists were Miss Annie Bellwood, Miss Slater, and Messrs. E. Reddish, W. Greenhouse, and C. G. McDowell. •In addition, the local in'tkrumentalists 'forming the now well-known orchestra conducted by Mr. T J. Down, gave their services, and proved not an inconsider- able. attraction. Miss Bellwood sang two of F. Cowen's choicest songs, and the still welcome, though now familiar, "Lost Chord.' We must con- fess to a feeling of slight disappoihtment at Miss Ilallwood's interpretation of one, at least, of these songs. "The Better Land" and "The Lost Chord"' succeed only in Proportion as they can be made climacteric and culMinative in their effects On the listeners. And although Miss Hallwood's singing Was marked by a high degree of. finish end refine- ment, she did not to our mind rise to the occasion, much of the' necessary dramatic fervour being want- ing to make an ideal performance. The 'credit of the • emphatic encore which greeted "The lost chord" most therefore be shared with the band, who, We believe, undertook the orchestral accom- paniments at a moment's notice, playing them in a subdued though effective manner, which showed how amenable the various elements in the orchestra had been brought to the will of the conductor. Miss Slater is not gifted with exceptional qualities either of voice or style. • Nevertheless she gave an intelli- gent and adequate rendering of "Will he Come?" and received a recall. A certain naivete was notice- able in Randeggeis "Second thoughts are .best:' which points to songs of this.class as being rather Miss Sa.ter's forte. "The White Squall," sung -by Mr. Reddisii was a marked success. The quality of his voice is sweet, and nicely adapted to the requirements of a small concert room, and his enunciation is Clear and articu- late. In acknowledgment of well-deserved plaudits Mr. Reddish gave with like. Success "My Sweetheart when a boy.', Mr. McDowell & contribution," The Skip- per," was in many respects a satisfactory performance. The song has a true nautical ring about it and Mr. Mc- Dowell's robust interpretation was quite in keeping with its character.' Sparing use should be made of the trenndo, an excess of which was more especially notice- able in "'the moon has raised her lamp.' It is a pity that the voices in this duet were so ill-matched in vol- ume and timbre. • Mr. Greenhouse sings entirely in this weak head register;:and in company with Mr. McDow- ell's full chest notes it was, of course, impossible to look for any blending of the parts. The performances of the band were undoubtedly a feature of the concert. It is a fitting commentary on the opinion which has been expressed in certain quarters in our midst that there is little or no material in Warrington available for the formation of an amateur orchestra. that Mr. Down is able to rally round him for practice and public perfor- mance a body of some forty instrumentalists capable of coping with the executive difficultiesof Suppe's overtures and the more refined subtleties of the duet, "Lo ! hear the gentle lark !" for elarionet and flute with orchestra. The precision and finish which charaqerised the playing of the six orchestral items included in !the programme not only reflect the, highest credit on Mr: Down in his capacity of conductor and trainer of what we may be pardoned describing as the raw material Which has come to his hands during the last few years, but is inciden- tally-a matter for self-congratulation amongst all lovers of instrumental music in the town. The soloists in the duet were Mi. F. Pendlebury (elarionet) and Mr. P. Brimelow (flute), and from the point of view of the audi- ence this was clearly thepike de reeistance of the evening. Some tasteful solos for bassoon, oboe, cornet, and eupho- nium were also heard in the selections from Sullivan's opera, "Princes S Ida." and the more recent work of Alfred Cellier, entitled " Dorothy." It should be men- tioned that the pianoforte accompaniments to the various songs were unobtrusivtay yet tastefully played by Mr. William James. • '

THE DISCOVERY OF GOLD IN WALES..-.-MT. Morgan in- tends to ask the Queen to accept the first bar of ',old taken from the Gwvnfynydd mine at Dolgelly.2bp- wards of one hundred miners are now engaged in the Wilts of the "Mount Morgan Gold Mine," in the • Mawd- , dach mountain, near DolgollY, a number of experienced , miners from Cornwall having just been brought into the 1 district by the owner of the mine. The excavations or headings have now been pushed into the hill a distance of nearly 400 ft.„ and upwards of 3.000 tons of quartz is stacked at the mouth of the; edits, and is guarded by watchmen day and night. RELAPSE OF THE_ CROWN PRINCE.—A despatch from San Remo says that in spite of the favourable state of the Crown Prince's general health and the optimistic views formed thereon, the physicians in attendance discovered On Tuesday night some new and alarming symptoms in the throat, and the Crown Prince desired that a telegram should be despatched to Sir Morell Mac- kenzie requesting him to Start for San Remo. A tele- gram was accordingly de.spatelied early on Wednesday morning. It is rumoured that a larger growth has •made its appearance, and that it is increasing at a somewhat ra,pid 'rate.

Sir A. B. Walker completed his sixty:third year on Thursday. ' Earl Lytton will leave London for Paris on Wednesday L evening next to assume his duties as British Ambassador to France. , The Baroness Grey de Ruthin died late on Thursday night at her residence, Warton Hall, Lytham,' after a painful illness. - Lord Cooper has written from Florence. withdrawing from the presidency of the Hertford Divisional Liberal Association. , In consequence of the discovery of a valuable gold mine on the estate of Mr. Morgan, of Brinterion, Dol- golly, several local landqwners engaged the services of Imining specialists to prostie, their properties, with the Iresult that more rich gold quartz has been found. VISIT OF THE QUEEN TO LONDON.—The Queen, accom- panied by the Princess Beatrice and the suite, left Wind- sor Castle at 35 'minutes past 12 on Friday afternoon for London; where she paid a visit to the Duchess of Cam- bridge. Her Majesty returned to the Castle about four o'clock. A MESSAGE FROM THE SEA.—The Board of Trade an- nounces a tin case as having been picked up containing the following message :—" Immediate help is required. The barque called the Helen, of Hobart, Captain Boom, is sinking fast in the Bay of Biscay. Send help for God's Isake." A WINDFALL.—On Friday Sergeant McOuffe, of tho Cumberland and Westmoreland police, stationed at Pen- rith, received an intimation that he is entitled to a legacy of £13,000 from an entirely unexpected source. The sergeant, who is very popular in the district, is mar- ried, and has a large family. MURDER IN IRBLAND.--An elderly man named Denis Flanagan was indicted at Wicklow Assizes, on Friday, for the murder of his wife at Shadbally,Queen's County, on the 9th July last. Evidence of the children and wit- nesses showed' that the prisoner stabbed his wife with a knife three times. The prisoner was found guilty, and sentenced to death. ALARMING ACCIDENT.—At Glindore, near Skibbereen, on Thursday evening, while some three hundred people were witnessing an amateur theatrical performance, in a large upper room, the flooring gave way, and the audi- ence were precipitated to the ground. Fortunately no lives were lost; but a large number of persons suffered injuries, some of which were serious. KILLED ON THE RAILWAY.—A terrible fatality hap- pened at Biusicough Junction, near Ormskirk, on the Lancashire and Yorkshire Railway, on Friday morning. A man, in the eniploy of a local firm, was assisting in the unloading of some goods from waggons when he was caught by the expresatrain for Liverpool, and killed in- stantaneously. The body was terribly mangled. MR. :GLADSTONR GOING TO ITALY.—A Chester corres- pondent states that Mr. Oladstone is going,to Italy, but not to Venice. The right hon. gentleman, for the first time for many years, will not be at Harwarden on the occasion of his birthday', which ,takes place on the 29th. He leaves Hawarden for London on the 26th, and crosses the channel on the following day, en route to the Mediter- ranean. THE TRIAL OF DR. Csioss.—At Cork Assizes; on Thurs- day, the trial was resumed of Dr. Cross, late.of the 53rd IRegiment, on the charge of poisoning his first wife. District-Inspector Tyocke deposed to finding different poisons at Shandy Hall, the residence of the prisoner, after his arrest. On Friday the last three witnesses for the Crown were examined. The first was Mr. Henry Tyndall, of London, the brother-in-law of the deceased Idy. He deposed to meeting the prisoner in London in Junelast, and he then teld him his wife died from angina pectoris. THE GERMAN CROWN PRINCE. A Central News telegram dated Vienna, Fri- day, states :—Telegrams from San Remo state that a careful examination was yesterday made of the throat of the German Crown Prince, and in the medical consultation which followed Sir M. Makenzie expressed his conviction that the new growth was in no way dangerous, neither was there any appear- ance of ceclema. No operation is considered necessary. DISASTROOS ' FLOODS IN—CHINA. • THASANDS OF LIVES LOST. A teleg,ram, dated New York, Friday, says :—Accord- ing to advices which have just reached San Francisco from China, most disastrous floods have taken place over a wide area during the autumn. It appears the Yellow River suddenly changed its course during Sep- tember, and overflowed in consequence some 7,000 square miles of country. Many thousands of persons have been drowned, whilst those deprived of home and shelter are reckoned by millions.
